topics.title: Introduction to Drivetrains: Wheel-Type Machines
topics.summary: This topic describes the basic drivetrain system components for wheel-type Caterpillar machines.

lessons.title: Wheel-Type Drivetrain Components
lessons.objective:
This segment introduces the major drivetrain system components used in Caterpillar wheel-type machines such as:

Wheel Loaders, Skidders, Integrated Tool Carriers (IT's), Wheel Dozers, Soil Compactors, Landfill Compactors, Off-Highway Trucks, Articulated Trucks, Backhoe Loaders and Tractor-Scrapers.
pages:
The torque converter connects the engine to the transmission. The purpose of the torque converter is to hydraulically transfer torque from the engine flywheel to the transmission.

The torque converter uses oil to send torque from the engine to the transmission. When a machine is working against a load, the torque converter can multiply the torque from the engine and send a higher torque to the transmission. The main components of a torque converter are the impeller, turbine, stator and output shaft.
The impeller is the driving member of the torque converter. It is splined to the flywheel and turns at engine RPM. The impeller contains blades which force oil against the blades of the turbine.

The turbine is the driven member of the torque converter with vanes that receive the oil flow from the impeller. The turbine causes the output shaft (which is splined to the turbine) to turn when oil from the impeller is forced against the turbine blades.

The stator is the stationary reaction member whose vanes multiply force by redirecting fluid flow from the turbine back to the impeller. The purpose of the stator is to change the direction of the flow of oil between the turbine and the impeller. This direction change increases the momentum of the fluid, thereby increasing the torque capacity of the converter.
The output shaft, which is splined to the turbine, sends torque to the input shaft of the transmission.

With the creation of the earliest Caterpillar wheel-type machines, one of the major challenges of the design engineer has been to find an efficient, reliable method of transmitting power from the engine to the final drive components.

The first specialized machines were equipped with transmission systems that were purely mechanical in design. While the transmissions had grown in size and complexity, their basic components remained unchanged. Power from the engine was transmitted to the drive line through a mechanical clutch and a series of gears. Gear movement and clutch operation were controlled by combinations of levers, shafts, and/or cables.

To help satisfy the continually increasing demand for higher productivity and greater efficiency, the concept of transmission design entered another era. The Caterpillar Powershift Transmission retained the advantages of the mechanical system, but added a feature that soon became an industry standard: hydraulically-activated clutches and controls. The introduction of hydraulics to power transmission systems also created an increased need for understanding of the terminology and service procedures that accompanied this system. In addition to pumps, hoses, valves, governors, accumulators and torque converters, service personnel were confronted with such new terms as "modulation," "clutch sequencing," and "primary pressure."

The major advantage of any powershift transmission is quicker response when shifting from one gear to another as well as changing speeds when the application calls for it. The powershift transmissions may be shifted under loads with no loss of productivity.

The basic components of the Planetary Powershift Transmission consist of:

• The Hydraulically Activated Clutches: which permit selection of the forward/reverse direction and speeds

• The Planetary Group: houses planetary gearing which depends on clutch engagement to supply speed and direction

The basic components of the Countershaft Powershift Transmission are:

• Clutch Shafts: that provide mounting for gears and clutch packs

• Constant Mesh Gears: that provide speed and direction which varies by clutch engagement

• Directional and Speed Clutches: that consist of clutch plates and friction discs (clutch packs), used to engage the various gears supplying speed and directionP

Some Cat machines have transfer gear trains that connect various power transmission units, change direction of power flow, or drop the axis of flow from the engine crankshaft to the transmission, or drop the axis of flow from the transmission to the final drive.

Transfer gears can reduce or increase torque as designed by the application it is being used for.

Input Transfer Gears are at the input side of the transmission. The torque converter connects to the input gear (drive gear) which in turn drives the driven (output gear) which is connected to the input of the transmission.

The Power flow through an Input Transfer Gear is as follows:

• From the yoke assembly to the drive gear.

• From the drive gear to the driven gear.

and

• From the driven gear to the transmission input 
 shaft.

YOutput Transfer Gears are at the output side of the transmission. The output carrier of the transmission connects to the input gear (drive gear) which in turn drives an idler gear which drives the driven gear (output gear) which is connected to the drive shaft that connects to the final drive system.

The Power flow through an Output Transfer Gear is as follows:

• From the drive gear to the idler gear.

• From the idler gear to the driven gear.

and

• From the driven gear to the drive shaft.

In wheel-type machines the axles provide the service brakes, a balance of power to the wheels during turns, and the final gear reduction and torque increase for the drivetrain. The main components of the axles are the bevel gear set/differential group, brake group, planetary group and axle group. P

The bevel ring and pinion gear set receives power from the driveshaft, turns it 90 degrees, and transmits it to the differential. The differential provides wheel speed differentiation, and transfers power to the final drives. The main components are the bevel pinion shaft, bevel ring gear, differential case assembly, pinion gears, side gears and spider.

The service brake group is generally an oil-cooled disc brake. There are three types found in wheel-type machines. In the "inboard axle brake" (used in small wheel loaders and backhoe loaders), the brake disc is splined to the sun gear shaft and housed in the axle. In the "axle shaft brake," the brake disc is splined to a hub on the long axle shaft and located between the axle housing and spindle (used in large loaders and landfill compactors). In the wheel speed brake (used in off-highway trucks), the brake disc is splined to the wheel casting and rotates at wheel speed.

Other types of brakes used on Caterpillar machines include dry caliper disc brakes and dry drum brakes. These are typically found on tractor-scrapers and articulated trucks.
The planetary group provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of a carrier, planet gears, ring gear, sun gear, shafts and bearings.

The axle group consists of the axle housing, axle shafts, and bearings. The function of the housing and bearings are to provide structure to support the weight of the machine. The axle shafts transmit power from the differential out to the wheels.

Hydrostatic drive systems have infinitely variable speed capability. Mechanical power from the engine is changed to hydraulic power by a variable displacement pump. This power is sent through hydraulic lines to the motor where it is changed back to mechanical power to drive a load. The pump is designed to produce a flow that can be varied. The flow is sent through either of two lines to the hydraulic drive motor. This allows the machine to be operated at different speeds and directions.

The major components of a hydrostatic drive system are as follows:

• The Variable Displacement Pump (1) which changes mechanical input to hydraulic output.

• The Hydraulic Oil Lines (2) which carry the flow to the motor.

and

• The Fixed or Variable Displacement Hydraulic Motor (3) which changes hydraulic power back to mechanical power.

The bevel ring and pinion gear set receives power from the transfer gears, turns it 90 degrees, and transmits it to the steering clutches and brakes. It consists of the bevel pinion shaft, bevel ring gear and bevel ring gear cross shaft.

The steering clutches and brakes are contained in one assembly and work together to brake and steer track-type machines. • The Variable Displacement Pump (1): which changes mechanical input to hydraulic output.

• The Hydraulic Oil Lines (2): which carry the flow to the control valves and the motors.

• The Hydraulic Control Valve (3): which directs flow from the pump

and

• The Fixed or Two-Position Hydraulic Motor (4): which changes hydraulic power back to mechanical power.

topics.title: Torque Converters
topics.summary: This topic describes torque converters and discusses their features, benefits and applications in Caterpillar machines.

lessons.title: Introduction to Torque Converters
lessons.objective: This segment describes the basic operation of the torque converter and how it is used in Caterpillar products.
pages:
The hydraulic coupling transmits power from an engine to a driven unit (in this case, a transmission is the driven unit). 

There are two types of hydraulic mechanisms used to transmit power - the fluid coupling and the torque converter. Both use the energy of a fluid in motion to transmit power. However, because fluid couplings operate on much the same principles as torque converters, an understanding of their operation will make the study of torque converters easier.

A fluid coupling consists of an impeller and turbine with internal vanes that face each other. The impeller, sometimes called the pump, is attached to the engine flywheel and the turbine is attached to the transmission input shaft. The impeller is the driving member, and the turbine is the driven member. 

When the engine is started, the impeller starts turning and forces oil from its center toward the outside edge. Centrifugal force causes the oil to strike the turbine blades. The force and energy of the oil starts the turbine turning, coupling the engine to the transmission, and transmitting the power required to move the machine.

A torque converter is a fluid coupling with the addition of a stator.

Like the fluid coupling, the torque converter couples the engine to the transmission, and transmits the power required to move the machine. Torque converter basic components are an impeller, turbine, stator and output shaft.

Unlike the fluid coupling, the torque converter can also multiply torque from the engine which increases torque to the transmission. The torque converter uses a stator which redirects fluid back into the impeller in the direction of rotation. The force of oil from the stator increases the amount of torque transferred from the impeller to the turbine creating torque multiplication.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment describes the features and benefits of torque converters.
pages: The torque converter provides Caterpillar machines with certain features and benefits.
A feature of the torque converter is that it multiplies torque from the engine to the drivetrain.
The benefit is that this provides increased output when working against a load.
A feature of the torque converter is that it automatically couples the engine to the transmission.
The benefit is that this allows Cat machines on-the-go shifting.
A feature of the torque converter is that it absorbs shock.
The benefit is that this provides longer life for the powertrain.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment discusses applications of torque converters in Caterpillar machines.
pages: Torque converters are the coupling devices used in most Caterpillar products.
The torque converter is standard with all powershift transmissions in track-type tractors. Some tractors are equipped with a flywheel clutch instead of a torque converter. P
Wheel type machines are equipped with torque converters with the exception of motor graders and hydraulic drive machines.

topics.title: Torque Converter Components and Operation
topics.summary: This topic describes torque converter components and explains torque converter operation including power flow.

lessons.title: Conventional Torque Converter Components
lessons.objective: This segment describes the conventional torque converter components used in Caterpillar machines.
pages: The torque converter consists of four components contained in a housing that is filled with fluid by the transmission pump: impeller (driving member), turbine (driven member), stator (reaction member) and output shaft.

The impeller is the driving member of the torque converter. It is connected to the engine flywheel and driven at engine speed. The impeller acts as a pump as it picks up the fluid in the torque converter and directs it toward the turbine. The vanes used in the impeller are curved to accelerate the oil flow as it leaves the impeller.

The turbine is the driven member of the torque converter whose vanes receive the oil flow from the impeller. The turbine rotates to turn the torque converter output shaft. The inlet sides of the turbine vanes are curved toward the impeller to absorb as much energy or power as possible from the fluid flow.

The stator is the stationary reaction member of the torque converter whose vanes multiply force by redirecting fluid flow from the turbine back to the impeller. The stator is fastened to the torque converter housing and does not rotate. The purpose of the stator is to change the direction of the flow of oil between the turbine and the impeller. This direction change increases the momentum of the fluid, thereby increasing the output torque of the converter.

The output shaft is splined to the turbine and sends power to the input shaft of the transmission. The output shaft is connected to the transmission through a yoke and driveshaft or directly to the transmission input gear.

lessons.title: Torque Converter Power Flow
lessons.objective: In this segment, torque converter power flow is described.
pages: The flow of oil through the torque converter creates the power flow for the drivetrain. We will examine the complete power flow process as it relates to creating torque for the transmission.
The impeller turns with the housing at engine speed and forces the oil toward the outside of the impeller, around the inside of the housing and against the blades of the turbine.

As the oil hits the turbine blades, the turbine begins to rotate causing the output shaft to turn. This sends power to the transmission. At this point in time, the torque is not multiplied and the torque converter is operating like a fluid coupling. P

As the oil hits the turbine blades, the oil is forced toward the inside of the turbine. Oil leaving the turbine, moves in a direction opposite the direction of impeller rotation. The stator redirects the oil back into the impeller in the direction of impeller rotation which causes torque multiplication.

topics.title: Special Application Torque Converters
topics.summary: This topic covers special application torque converters used in Caterpillar products.

lessons.title: One-Way Clutch Torque Converters
lessons.objective: This segment introduces One-Way Clutch Torque Converters and describes the features, benefits, applications and operation.
pages: The one-way clutch torque converter operates similarly to the conventional torque converter described earlier. The impeller, turbine and output shaft all accomplish the same function as in the conventional torque converter. The stator, however, is mounted on a one-way clutch which permits the stator to turn freely when torque multiplication is not required.

The clutch locks the stator in one direction of rotation and allows it to freewheel in the opposite direction. It is nothing more than a large ratchet. The components of the one-way clutch are the cam, rollers, springs and hub.
The cam connects the one-way clutch to the stator and is splined to the stator.
The rollers provide the mechanical connection between the cam and hub.
The springs hold the rollers in the cam opening.
The hub connects the one-way clutch to the carrier and is splined to the carrier.

When the machine is under load and in the torque multiplication phase, the force of the oil on the front of the stator vanes will try to turn the cam ring clockwise. This action will cause the rollers to be clamped between the cam and the hub, locking the stator in place. The stator will then redirect oil back to the impeller to multiply torque.

As the speed of the impeller and turbine increase, the force of the oil begins to strike the back of the stator vanes turning the stator counterclockwise. When rotating in this direction, there is no clamping action and the rollers are allowed to roll on the hub and the stator freewheels. The stator does not send oil back to the impeller, causing the torque converter to act more like a fluid coupling.

lessons.title: Variable Capacity Torque Converters
lessons.objective: This segment introduces Variable Capacity Torque Converters and describes the features, benefits, applications and operation.
pages: The purpose of the variable capacity torque converter is to allow the operator to limit the amount of torque increase in the torque converter to reduce wheel spin and to divert power to the hydraulic system. The components of the unit are: inner impeller, outer impeller, impeller clutch, turbine and stator. Only the outer impeller and impeller clutch will be covered here, since the inner impeller, turbine and stator function essentially the same as in the conventional torque converter previously covered.

The outer impeller is a second impeller within the torque converter. The outer impeller is engaged to the converter housing by oil pressure acting on the clutch piston to engage the clutch pack. Maximum oil pressure fully engages the clutch and the outer impeller turns with the inner impeller. When there is a reduction of oil pressure, there is clutch slippage resulting in the outer impeller turning slower and a reduction of torque converter capacity.

The impeller clutch is hydraulically activated and controlled by the transmission hydraulic system. The clutch engages the outer impeller with the clutch housing allowing the inner and outer impellers to turn together.

The variable capacity torque converter can operate at different capacities. The basic operation of the converter including power flow will be covered.

A change in the capacity of the torque converter impeller results in a change in output torque.

Oil flow inside the torque converter engages the impeller clutch and causes the outer impeller to turn with the inner impeller.

At maximum impeller clutch pressure, the clutch is completely engaged and there is no clutch slippage allowing the torque converter to operate as a conventional torque converter. 

At minimum impeller clutch pressure the outer impeller is not engaged and the torque converter capacity is at minimum. At minimum capacity, the operation of the variable capacity torque converter is similar to a conventional torque converter, except that the effective size of the impeller has been reduced due to impeller clutch slippage.

lessons.title: Impeller Clutch Torque Converters
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the Impeller Clutch Torque Converter and describes the features, benefits, applications and operation.
pages: The impeller clutch torque converter makes it possible to vary the output torque of the converter over a broad range. It is similar to the conventional torque converter but includes a clutch solenoid valve and multi-disc clutch pack which is mounted on the impeller input shaft. The impeller clutch solenoid valve, controlled by a transmission electronic control module (ECM), is activated by the left brake pedal.

The impeller clutch is hydraulically activated and controlled by the impeller clutch solenoid valve. It couples the impeller to the converter housing and consists of an impeller clutch piston, plates and discs. The impeller clutch solenoid valve controls oil flow through the impeller clutch torque converter. It is activated by the electronic control module (ECM). When the ECM increases the current to the solenoid, impeller clutch pressure is reduced. When the current from the ECM is at zero, the impeller clutch pressure is at the maximum and the converter operates like a conventional converter.

The operation of the impeller clutch torque converter includes an explanation of the power flow through the converter and how the impeller clutch interfaces with the conventional torque converter components. P

When the impeller clutch solenoid valve is not energized by the ECM, oil flows to the impeller clutch oil passage from the carrier and forces the impeller clutch piston (1) against the plates (2) and discs (3). The piston and plates are connected to the impeller clutch housing with splines. The adapter is fastened to the impeller (4) with bolts. The friction between the discs and plates causes the impeller to rotate at the same speed as the converter housing. This is the maximum torque output.

As the current flow to the solenoid is increased, oil pressure to the piston is decreased. The friction between the plates and discs decreases and the impeller turns slower, forcing less oil to the turbine. With less force on the turbine there is less torque at the output shaft.

lessons.title: Lock-up Clutch Torque Converters
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the Lock-up Clutch Torque Converter and describes the features, benefits, applications and operation.
pages: The lockup clutch torque converter provides a direct connection between the transmission and engine. It operates the same as a conventional torque converter when it is not in lockup mode. The lockup clutch torque converters are found in Wheel Tractor-Scrapers, Large Wheel Loaders, Off-Highway and Articulated Trucks.

The lockup clutch is automatically engaged anytime direct drive is demanded by the machine operating conditions.

The lockup clutch is located inside the torque converter housing. When the retarder is in operation, the lockup clutch is engaged, causing the impeller and turbine to turn at engine speed. The machine is now in direct drive. 

The lockup clutch consists of a piston and disc assembly, which receives oil pressure sent from the lockup clutch valve to lock the turbine to the converter housing causing direct drive.

When the lockup clutch is engaged, the converter is in direct drive providing the highest drivetrain efficiency. The lockup clutch consists of a clutch piston, plates and discs, which receives oil pressure to lock the turbine to the converter housing causing direct drive. The oil flow to the lockup clutch is controlled by the lockup clutch solenoid valve located on the outer cover. The lockup clutch solenoid is activated by the transmission electronic control module (ECM).
Four conditions must be present for the ECM to activate the lockup clutch:

• The lockup enable switch on the right side console must be in the ON (enabled) position.

• The torque converter output speed is greater than a specified rpm.

• The machine has been in the present speed and direction for at least 2 seconds.

• The left brake pedal must not be depressed.

The lockup clutch is disengaged during a shift and is reengaged when the four conditions are met in the new gear selected. The lockup clutch is also disengaged when the torque converter output speed drops below a specified rpm.

To help prevent engine overspeed, the lockup clutch cannot be engaged when the torque converter output is greater than a specified rpm.

When lockup clutch activation is demanded, oil pressure causes the lockup clutch to engage. The lockup clutch piston pushes the disc assembly against the rotating converter housing causing the disc to turn. The disc, which is splined to the hub turns the hub which turns the output shaft. This creates a direct connection between the engine and transmission, causing the transmission input shaft to turn at the same speed as the engine. The turbine and impeller are now turning at the same speed and there is no multiplication of torque from the torque converter.

When the lockup clutch solenoid is energized by the ECM, oil flows to the lockup clutch oil passage and through the oil passage in the output shaft to the lockup clutch piston (1). The lockup clutch piston and plates (2) are connected to the converter housing with splines. The discs (3) are connected to the adapter with splines and the adapter is fastened to the turbine (4) with bolts. The oil pressure on the piston forces the piston against the lockup clutch plates and discs, causing the turbine and output shaft to rotate at the same speed as the converter housing. The turbine and impeller are now turning at the same speed and there is no multiplication of torque from the torque converter.

When the impeller clutch solenoid is deenergized, the lockup clutch is not engaged and the torque converter multiplies torque like the conventional torque converter.

topics.title: Torque Converter Testing and Troubleshooting
topics.summary: This topic explains the performance tests used in troubleshooting torque converters.

lessons.title: Torque Converter Stall Test
lessons.objective: This segment describes the Torque Converter Stall Test used on torque converters.
pages:
The stall test is performed when a problem with the torque converter is suspected.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

Torque converter stall occurs when the output shaft speed is zero. The converter stall test is performed while the engine is operated at full throttle. This test will give an indication of engine and drivetrain performance based on engine speed. A lower or higher speed than specified is an indication of either engine or drivetrain problems. A low converter stall speed is generally an indication of an engine performance problem. A high converter stall speed is generally an indication of a drivetrain problem.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

lessons.title: Relief Valve Tests
lessons.objective: This segment describes the Relief Valve test used on torque converters.
pages: There are two converter relief valve tests, inlet relief (ratio valve) and outlet relief valve.

The ratio valve for the torque converter controls the maximum pressure to the converter. Its primary purpose is to prevent damage to the converter components when the engine is started with cold oil. The inlet relief pressure is tested with cold oil by raising engine rpm to high idle while observing a pressure gauge connected to the P3 pressure port.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

The outlet relief valve maintains pressure in the torque converter. Pressure must be maintained in the torque converter to prevent cavitation and assure efficient converter operation. Low pressure could be an indication of converter leakage, poor pump flow, or a malfunctioning relief valve. High pressure could be an indication of a malfunctioning relief valve or a blockage in the system. This test is performed by checking converter outlet relief valve pressure at the proper pressure port.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

topics.title: Torque Dividers
topics.summary: This topic describes torque dividers and discusses their features, benefits and applications.

lessons.title: Introduction to Torque Dividers
lessons.objective: This segment explains the use of a torque divider in the drivetrain.
pages:
The torque divider is a conventional torque converter with an integrated planetary gear set in front of it. This arrangement allows for a variable split of engine torque between the converter and planetary gear set. This split can be as high as 70/30 depending on the machine load. Both converter and planetary gear set output are connected to the torque divider output shaft.

The torque divider is attached to the engine flywheel. During operation the torque converter and planetary gear set work together to provide the most efficient split of engine torque.

The torque converter provides torque multiplication for heavy loads while the planetary gear set will provide nearly 30% direct drive during light load situations.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment describes the features and benefits of torque dividers.
pages: The torque divider provides Caterpillar machines with certain features and benefits.
A feature of the torque divider is that it multiplies torque from the engine to the drivetrain.
The benefit is that this provides increased output when working against a load.
A feature of the torque divider is that it absorbs shock.
The benefit is that by absorbing shock, the torque divider provides longer life for the powertrain.
A feature of the torque divider is that it permits direct drive operation of the machine.
The benefit is that this results in increased efficiency and better fuel economy.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment discusses applications of torque dividers.
pages: Some Track-Type Tractors are equipped with torque dividers.

topics.title: Torque Divider Components and Operation
topics.summary: This topic describes torque divider components and explains torque divider operation including power flow.

lessons.title: Torque Divider Components
lessons.objective: This segment describes torque divider components.
pages: Like the torque converter, the torque divider consists of four components contained in a housing that is filled with oil by the transmission pump: impeller (driving member), turbine (driven member), stator (reaction member) and output shaft. The torque divider also contains a planetary gear set.

The impeller is the driving member of the torque divider. It is connected to the engine flywheel and driven at engine speed. The impeller acts as a pump as it picks up the oil in the torque divider and directs it towards the turbine. The vanes used in the impeller are curved to accelerate the oil flow as it leaves the impeller.

The turbine is the driven member of the torque divider whose vanes receive the oil flow from the impeller. The turbine rotates to turn the torque divider output shaft. The inlet sides of the turbine vanes are curved toward the impeller to absorb as much energy or power as possible from the fluid flow.

The stator is the stationary reaction member of the torque converter whose vanes multiply force by redirecting fluid flow from the turbine back to the impeller. The stator is fastened to the torque converter housing and does not rotate. The purpose of the stator is to change the direction of the flow of oil between the turbine and the impeller. This direction change increases the momentum of the fluid, thereby increasing the output torque of the torque divider. P
The output shaft is splined to the turbine and sends power to the input shaft of the transmission. The output shaft is connected to the transmission through a yoke and driveshaft. P

The planetary gear set differentiates the torque divider from the torque converter. It provides direct drive when the machine is under light load. When under heavy load the torque divider acts as a conventional torque converter to increase output torque. The planetary gear set consists of the sun, ring, planet gears and planet carrier. The planetary gear set is connected to the components of the torque converter as follows:

• The ring gear which is splined to the turbine 

• The planet carrier which is splined to the output shaft

and

• The sun gear which is connected to the engine flywheel by splines and turns at engine rpmP

lessons.title: Torque Divider Operation
lessons.objective: This segment explanations torque divider operation.
pages: Operation of the torque divider and planetary gear set will be explained when the machine is under light load and in a stall condition.

With a load on the machine, the planet carrier has low resistance to rotation so the sun gear, planet gears, planet carrier and ring gear turn at the same speed. The torque from the converter and planetary gear set is transmitted through the planet carrier to the output shaft and to the transmission. Neither the torque converter nor the planetary gear set multiply the torque from the engine when they turn at the same speed.

When the machine is under heavy load, the planet carrier has a resistance to rotation. Since the sun gear is turning at the rpm of the engine, this resistance to rotation causes the planet gears to turn on their shafts. Their rotation is opposite the rotation of the ring gear. This causes a decrease in the speed of the ring gear. Since the turbine is connected to the ring gear, a decrease in speed will cause the torque converter to increase output torque. This torque is sent to the planet carrier and the output shaft through the ring gear.

Also with the decrease in the speed of the ring gear, the torque of the engine through the sun gear and the planetary gear set also multiplies. This torque is also sent to the planet carrier and output shaft.

If resistance to the rotation of the planet carrier becomes high enough, the ring gear will stop. During some very high load conditions, the rotation of the planet carrier and the output shaft will stop, this is referred to as converter stall. This will cause the ring gear to turn slowly in the opposite direction. At this time torque multiplication of the torque converter and sun gear is at its maximum.
