topics.title: Torque Divider Testing and Troubleshooting
topics.summary: This topic explains the performance tests used in troubleshooting torque dividers.

lessons.title: Stall Test for Torque Dividers
lessons.objective: This segment describes the Torque Converter Stall test which can be used to test the torque divider.
pages:
The stall test is performed when a problem with the torque converter is suspected.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

Torque converter stall occurs when the output shaft speed is zero. The converter stall test is performed while the engine is operated at full throttle. This test will give an indication of engine and drivetrain performance based on engine speed. A lower or higher speed than specified is an indication of either engine or drivetrain problems. A low converter stall speed is generally an indication of an engine performance problem. A high converter stall speed is generally an indication of a drivetrain problem.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

lessons.title: Relief Valve Tests
lessons.objective: This segment describes the Relief Valve test used on torque dividers.
pages: There are two converter relief valve tests, inlet relief (ratio valve) and outlet relief valve.

The ratio valve for the torque converter controls the maximum pressure to the converter. Its primary purpose is to prevent damage to the converter components when the engine is started with cold oil. The inlet relief pressure is tested with cold oil by raising engine rpm to high idle while observing a pressure gauge connected to the P3 pressure port.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

The outlet relief valve maintains pressure in the torque converter. Pressure must be maintained in the torque converter to prevent cavitation and assure efficient converter operation. Low pressure could be an indication of converter leakage, poor pump flow, or a malfunctioning relief valve. High pressure could be an indication of a malfunctioning relief valve or a blockage in the system. This test is performed by checking converter outlet relief valve pressure at the proper pressure port.

Always refer to the appropriate service manuals for safety and testing procedures.

topics.title: Transmissions
topics.summary: This topic describes what a transmission is, what the features and benefits of a transmission are and the applications transmissions are used for.

lessons.title: What Is a Transmission?
lessons.objective: This segment deals with what a transmission is and what it is used for.
pages: This power, coming from the engine via the flywheel to the driveshaft must be controlled as to its speed, direction and force. Controlling this power transfers it into useful power.

Transforming the power coming from the engine into useful power is done through the use of a transmission. The transmission accomplishes this using speed changing gears and/or hydraulically actuated planetary clutches which provide different ranges of machine ground speed.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment explains the different features and benefits of the various transmissions used in Caterpillar machines today.
pages: The following are just some of the features and benefits offered by Caterpillar Powershift Transmissions.
A feature of a powershift transmission is smooth automatic shifts.
The benefits are that this reduces operator fatigue and increases powertrain life.
A feature of a powershift transmission is that it contains modular components.
The benefit is this provides quicker service times.
A feature of a powershift transmission is that it has Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM).
The benefit is that this depresses torque spikes and abrupt shifts, reduces drivetrain wear and provides smoother shifts, which improves the ride.
A feature of powershift transmissions is electronic shifting.
The benefit is smooth consistent shifts with fingertip controls.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment details the different applications transmissions are used in.
pages: The following is a partial list of transmission applications used in Caterpillar machines. Included is the number of forward and reverse speeds. Because of the wide range of transmission applications, the different transmissions may be used within the same family of machines. Always refer to the appropriate service publications for the specific machine being serviced.

For Track-Type Tractors the Transmission Type is

 • Planetary Powershift

and the Speeds are

 • 3 Forward, and 3 ReverseP

For Integrated Toolcarriers and Wheel Loaders the Transmission Types include

 • Planetary Powershift

 • Countershaft Powershift

and

 • Hydrostatic Drive

The Speeds are

 • 3 to 4 Forward, and 3 to 4 Reverse (depending on model)

For Off-Highway Trucks the Transmission Type is

 • Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission

and the Speeds are

 • 5 to 7 Forward (depending on model), and 1 Reverse
P

For Wheel Tractor Scrapers the Transmission Type is

 • Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission

and the Speeds are

 • 8 Forward, and 1 Reverse

For Backhoe Loaders the Transmission Type is

 • Countershaft Powershift Transmission

and the Speeds are

 • 4 Forward, and 4 Reverse

For Challenger Tractors the Transmission Type is

 • Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission

and the Speeds are

 • Up to 16 Forward, and 3 Reverse

One type of transmission used on Caterpillar machines is the Planetary Powershift Transmission. This topic describes the major planetary powershift transmission components, operation (including power flow) and the performance testing and troubleshooting procedures.

Understanding planetary gear basics will help to understand how a planetary transmission functions. This segment explains the basics behind planetary gear sets and how they are used to make a planetary powershift transmission function.

Planetary gears are used in many ways in Caterpillar machines. Understanding planetary gear principles will help in understanding the basics of the planetary powershift transmission of which planetary gear sets are a large part.

Less space will be required in a transmission if planetary gear sets are used instead of external tooth gears, because all the gears can be inside the ring gear.

External tooth gears rotate in opposite directions, however, the direction of rotation is not changed with a ring gear. The pinion gear and the ring gear turn in the same direction.

Another advantage of planetary gearing (internal tooth gears) is that they have twice the tooth contact as external tooth gears. Planetary gears are stronger and have a longer wear life than the external tooth gears.

To change rotation, a planet gear is put between the pinion and ring gear.

Planet gears turn freely on their own bearings, and the number of teeth does not affect the ratio of the other two gears. With planetary gear sets there are three or four planet gears that turn on bearings.

The planet gears (1) are attached to a base or carrier (2) that's called a Planet Carrier.

The outer gear (3) is called the Ring Gear.

The pinion gear in the center (4) is called the Sun Gear.

The planetary gear set components got their names because they act the same as our solar system. The planet gears rotate around the sun gear just like the planets in our solar system rotate around our sun.

Speed, direction and torque changes are accomplished by restraining or driving various components of the planetary gear set. There are many different combinations possible, several examples will be shown.

To transmit power through a planetary set one member is held, one member is driving and one member is driven. The member held is not always the ring gear. In this example the planet carrier is held to get reverse rotation.

If the sun gear is driving in a counterclockwise rotation and the planet carrier is held, the ring gear is driven in the opposite direction of the sun gear.

If the sun gear is restrained and the ring gear is the drive gear, then the planet carrier will be driven. The planet gears rotate about their own axis, driving the planet carrier at a slower speed than the ring gear.

If the ring gear is restrained and the sun gear is the drive gear, then the planet carrier will be driven. The planet gears rotate about their own axis, driving the planet carrier at a slower speed than the sun gear.
If no member of the gear set is restrained the gears will idle and no power will be transmitted.
If two members are restrained or locked, the result is direct drive. The output speed is the same as the input speed.
If the sun gear is the drive gear and the ring gear is restrained, the planet carrier will be driven in low gear.
If the planet carrier is the drive gear and the ring gear is restrained, the sun gear will be driven in high gear.
If the planet carrier is restrained and the sun gear is the drive gear, the ring gear will be driven in reverse.

We have been studying drawings of a very simple planetary powershift transmission to get a basic understanding of the relationship of planetary gear sets. This picture shows an assembled planetary powershift transmission.

This picture shows a two-piece shaft similar to those used in the transmission arrangement we have been studying.

This (red) shaft is the input shaft. The sun gears of the reverse and forward planetary gear sets are mounted on the input shaft.

This (blue) shaft is the output shaft. The sun gears for the second speed and first speed planetaries are mounted on the output shaft.

Let's add some planet gears to each sun gear to build up a basic planetary powershift transmission. Planetary sets are usually referred to by numbers starting from the input (left) end; they are numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4.

This is a typical carrier. Note that the planet gears are supported by large round shafts mounted in the carrier housing.

Carriers appear in many shapes and sizes, but all have the same function--to support the planet gear shafts.
The front carrier of the reverse planetary gear set has been added to this illustration. Half of the carrier is omitted to show how it is mounted and how it holds the planet gears.
The center carrier connects the (red) input shaft to the (blue) output shaft. It contains the planet gears for forward speed and for second speed.
All three carriers are mounted in this illustration. From left to right, they are the front carrier, the center carrier, and the rear carrier.

In this illustration, the four planetary gear sets have been installed. From the input end (left) they are: No. 1 (reverse), No. 2 (forward), No. 3 (second) and No. 4 (First).

To make a complete transmission, ring gears and clutches must be added and the entire assembly put into a protective housing.

For more specific information on Planetary Powershift Transmission components, refer to the Segment titled "Planetary Powershift Transmission Components" in this module.

In the planetary powershift transmission there is a planetary gear set for each transmission speed--a set for forward and a set for reverse.

This drawing shows, assembled into a compact group, four planetary gear sets.

This drawing is a schematic representation of a two-speed, two-direction planetary powershift transmission. It is an exploded view of the assembled transmission shown in the previous picture.

Engine power is transmitted to the (red) input shaft through a torque converter or a torque divider. The sun gears for both the forward and reverse directions are mounted on the input shaft, and always rotate when the input shaft is driven. The (gray) member in the center is the carrier for the planet gears of the reverse set and the second speed set. The (blue) output shaft and the sun gears for the second and first speeds are mounted on it.

This slide shows the planetary gear sets for forward and reverse--the directional half of the transmission. Power is transmitted from the engine to the (red) input shaft. The ring gear of the planetary gear set for forward is stopped. This portion of the transmission is now engaged in forward gear. The input shaft is driven and because the (red) sun gears are mounted on the input shaft, the sun gears are also driven. The reverse sun gear (the one on the left) is rotating the planet gears. However, no power is transmitted through the reverse planetary because no member of the planetary is held.

The sun gear of the forward planetary rotates with the input shaft. Therefore, the planet gears rotate in the opposite direction. Because the ring gear is stopped the planet gears must revolve in the same direction as sun gear rotation. This causes the planet carrier to rotate in the same direction. This is the power flow for the forward direction.

This picture shows the power flow when the planet carrier for the reverse gear planetary is stopped.

The (red) input shaft drives the sun gear of the reverse planetary. The sun gear drives the (green) planet gears. Because the planet carrier is stopped the planet gears must rotate in place and drive the ring gear. Ring gear rotation is now opposite sun gear rotation.

The ring gear of the reverse planetary is fastened to the carrier of the planet gears of the forward planetary. Therefore, the planet carrier of the forward planetary also rotates in a direction opposite to input gear rotation.

This is the speed part of the transmission. The planet carrier on the left is part of the planet carrier of the forward planetary and is driven either clockwise or counterclockwise, depending upon which planetary gear set (forward or reverse) is transmitting power.

In this picture the ring gear of the planetary for second gear is stopped. Because the planet carrier is rotating and the ring gear is stopped, the sun gear of the second gear planetary is driven. The sun gear and output shaft rotate in the same direction as the planet carrier.

No member of the first gear planetary is held. Therefore, all components are free to rotate and no power is transmitted through the first gear planetary.

For first gear operation, the ring gear of the second gear planetary is released and the ring gear of the first gear planetary is stopped. The planet carrier at the left is still driven through the directional half of the transmission. The load on the output shaft provides resistance to sun gear rotation. Therefore, the ring gear of the second gear planetary must rotate. This ring gear is fastened to the planet carrier of the first gear planetary. Because the ring gear of the first gear planetary is stopped, the sun gear is driven. Its rotation is in the same direction as the rotation of the carrier on the left.

In review, the center carrier is driven. It drives the second speed ring gear that is connected to the first speed planet carrier. Because the first speed ring gear is stopped, the planet gears walk around the inside of the ring gear and drive the first speed sun gear and the output shaft.

Let's review the basic two-speed planetary powershift transmission we have been studying. It has two basic groups; a directional group (forward and reverse), and a speed group that determines how fast the vehicle moves in either direction.

Remember the arrangement of the planetary gear sets: reverse is nearest the engine; then forward; then second gear; and then first gear.

Let's follow the power flow when the ring gear of the forward planetary is stopped.

The input shaft is driven counterclockwise. No member of the reverse planetary is held. Therefore, the reverse planetary is rotating freely and is not transmitting power.

The ring gear of the forward planetary is stopped. The driven sun gear makes the planet gears rotate clockwise. Because the ring gear is stopped, rotation of the planet gears causes the gears to revolve around the sun gear in a counterclockwise direction. The carrier of the planet gears must also rotate counterclockwise. The carrier of the forward planetary is connected to the carrier of the second speed planetary.

There is no power flow through the speed section of the transmission because no member of the two speed planetaries is stopped, so there is no power delivered to the output shaft. The speed planetary gears are idling, because nothing is held.

In this picture the only member stopped is the ring gear of the first gear planetary. Trace the power flow. The input shaft is the driving member of the directional group but no other member of the directional group is held. Therefore, no member is driven and no power is transmitted through the directional group. Consequently, stopping the ring gear of the first speed planetary does not cause any power to be transmitted to the output shaft. The transmission is still in neutral.

Both a direction ring gear and a speed ring gear must be stopped before the transmission delivers power to the output shaft.

In this picture the ring gears of the forward and first speed planetaries are stopped. No power is transmitted through the reverse planetary because no member is held. The ring gear of the forward planetary is stopped, and the rotating sun gear causes the planet gears to revolve around the sun gear. The forward planet gears are mounted on the center carrier, and the center carrier must rotate.

The rotating center carrier drives the ring gear of the second gear planetary. The sun gear of the second gear planetary is the held member because its rotation is restricted by the load on the output shaft. The ring gear of the second speed planetary is connected to the carrier of the first speed planetary. Because the first speed ring gear is held the planet gears drive the first speed sun gear and deliver power to the output shaft. The vehicle moves forward in first speed.

In this picture, the ring gears of the forward and second speed planetaries are stopped. Power from the input shaft causes the forward sun gear to drive the forward planet gears. Because the forward ring gear is stopped the planet gears revolve around the sun gear and cause the center carrier to rotate. The planet gears of the second speed planetary are mounted on the center carrier and must revolve around the sun gear of the second speed planetary. 

Because the ring gear of the second speed planetary is stopped the rotation of the planet gears drives the sun gear. Power is transmitted to the output shaft.

The combination here is reverse and second speed. The carrier in the reverse planetary and the ring gear of the second speed planetary are held.

To transmit power through a planetary set one member is held, one member is a driving member, and one member is driven. The member held is not always the ring gear. As shown here, the carrier of the reverse planetary is held to get reverse rotation.

Any member of one planetary set may be connected to any member of a second planetary set. For example, locking up a ring gear of one set can lock up the carrier of a second planetary.

In this picture input shaft rotation is counterclockwise. Rotation of the input shaft and reverse sun gear make the planet gears rotate clockwise. Because the planet carrier is stopped the planet gears cannot revolve around the sun gear. Therefore, the ring gear must rotate in a clockwise direction. Because the center carrier is connected to the ring gear of the reverse planetary it also has clockwise rotation opposite to the rotation of the input shaft.

For first speed reverse operation the carrier of the reverse planetary and the ring gear of the first gear planetary are held. Remember that in reverse the carrier is held and the planet gears rotate and drive the reverse ring gear. The reverse ring gear causes the center carrier to rotate and drive the second speed ring gear. The second speed ring gear connects to the carrier of the first speed planetary set and the first speed planetary gears must revolve around the first speed sun gear. Because the first speed ring gear is held the planet gears revolve around the inside of the ring gear and drive the first speed sun gear and the output shaft.

lessons.title: Planetary Powershift: Components
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification, function and location of the major components that make-up the Planetary Powershift Transmission.
pages: This portion of the program will define the major components of a powershift transmission control valve. This control valve is used with many Caterpillar powershift transmissions. The following content for the transmission control valve should be treated as non-machine specific. Use the respective machine service manual powertrain modules for machine specific information.
The speed selector spool directs oil to the appropriate speed clutch for operation in each gear range.
The directional selector spool routes oil to the appropriate directional clutch for operation in Forward or Reverse.
The screened orifice controls the rate of flow to the load piston to control speed and direction clutch engagement time.
The modulating relief valve and load piston provide a controlled gradual pressure rise in the clutches and limit the maximum speed clutch pressure (P1 pressure).

The pressure differential valve controls directional clutch pressure (P2). This valve provides a set difference in pressure between speed clutch pressure and directional clutch pressure. This difference in pressure assures speed clutch engagement before directional clutch engagement. Typically this differential in pressure is 55 psi.

The pressure differential valve also prevents machine movement if started in gear.

Planetary gear sets are the heart of the planetary powershift transmission. Planetaries are made up of a number of different gears that rotate around or inside each other like a miniature solar system. The main components of a planetary gear set are the ring gear, planet (idler) gears, planet carrier and sun gear.
The ring gear is the outer gear which has teeth on the inside of the ring for the planet gears to engage with.
The planet gears (sometimes called the idler gears), rotate freely on their own bearings and engage with the internal teeth of the ring gear and the external teeth of the sun gear.
The planet carrier provides a mounting surface for the planet gears.

The transmission clutches are the disc-type and are housed in separate housings. Each clutch has a number of discs and plates. The inside teeth of the discs are engaged with the outside teeth of the ring gear. Notches on the outside diameter of the plates are engaged with pins in the clutch housing. The pins keep the plates from rotating.

Springs are located between the clutch housing and the piston. The springs keep the clutches disengaged (not engaged) by keeping the clutch piston from pushing against the plates. The clutches engage when oil is sent into the area behind the piston. When the pressure of the oil in the area behind the piston increases, the piston moves to the right against the force of the spring and pushes the discs and plates together. The clutch is now engaged and the ring gear is held stationary. When the pressure of the oil holding the piston decreases, the spring forces the piston back into the housing releasing the discs and plates. The ring gear is no longer held and rotates freely.
The clutch plates are mounted inside the clutch housing. Notches on the outside diameter of the plates are engaged with pins in the clutch housing that keep the plates from rotating.

The clutch discs are fitted to the ring gear and rotate with the gear. The inside teeth of the discs are engaged with the outside teeth of the ring gear.

Caterpillar clutch discs are made of special friction materials based on the requirements of the application.

Each clutch in the transmission has its own housing. The housing provides the clutch with a place to hold the piston that engages the clutch using hydraulic pressure. The housing also retains the clutch plates and using pins prevents the plates from turning.

The transmission shafts are mounted in the center of the planetary gear sets. In the case of a track-type tractor application both shafts are at the front of the transmission. In other applications the shafts are at each end of the transmission case.

In a track-type tractor application the input shaft rides inside the hollow output shaft and is splined to the input sun gears inside the transmission. In other applications the input shaft enters the transmission on one end of the case.

In a track-type tractor application the output shaft is hollow to accommodate the input shaft. This is due to the fact that on the track-type tractors the transmission is installed at the rear of the machine. Both the power input and output are at the front of the transmission unit.

In other applications the output shaft leaves the rear of the transmission case.
The transmission system is equipped with a positive displacement gear-type pump. Refer to the appropriate service manual for pump location.
The scavenge pump removes oil from the torque converter case and or transmission case. The scavenge oil is then transferred to the powertrain reservoir.
The transmission pump, takes oil from the case and sends it to the oil filter. Oil through the oil filter goes to the transmission control valve.

lessons.title: Planetary Powershift: Operation and Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment describes the operation and power flow of the Planetary Powershift Transmission.
pages: The following transmission control valve operation describes the oil flow through the valve of a transmission with three speeds forward and three speeds reverse. In this portion of the program only the oil flow through the valve while in the NEUTRAL position is detailed.

lessons.title: Planetary Powershift: Testing and Troubleshooting
lessons.objective: This segment details the major performance testing and troubleshooting procedures for the Planetary Powershift Transmission.
pages:
One of the most important pieces of diagnostic information required to troubleshoot transmissions is the clutch engagement chart. This chart explains what clutches are engaged for each speed and direction. By knowing these combinations a proper diagnosis of which clutch pack has failed can be made. This particular chart applies only to the transmission in the D8N Track-Type Tractor and is used for illustration purposes only.

Some of the performance testing procedures that can be performed on a powershift transmission include:

 • Pump Pressure Check
 • Speed Clutch Pressure Check (P1)
 • Directional Clutch Pressure Check (P2)
 • Converter Inlet Relief Pressure Check (Ratio Valve) (P3)
 • Converter Outlet Relief Pressure Check
 • Lube Pressure Check

Before performing any testing or troubleshooting procedures on any Caterpillar machine, always refer to the appropriate service manual for the machine being serviced. Contact the Technical Communicator (TC) at your Caterpillar Dealer for the latest specifications and procedures.

READ AND UNDERSTAND ALL SAFETY PRECAUTIONS AND WARNINGS BEFORE PERFORMING REPAIRS ON ANY CATERPILLAR MACHINE.

Basic safety precautions, skills and knowledge are listed in the SAFETY section of all Caterpillar service manuals and in the descriptions of operations where hazards exist.

The pump pressure check is used to assure proper system pressure is reached during operation. Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge tap and procedure.

For example the pump pressure tap location on most tractors is on top of the transmission oil filter.

The speed clutch pressure check determines if there is enough system pressure to fully engage the speed clutches and to assure proper operation of the modulating relief valve and load piston. If there is not enough pressure to fully engage the speed clutches, the transmission will not perform properly.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge tap and procedure.

For example the speed clutch (P1) pressure tap on a D4H Tractor is located on the rear housing of the transmission.

The directional clutch pressure check determines if there is enough system pressure to fully engage the directional clutches. This check also determines if sufficient differential exists between P1 and P2, to assure speed clutch engagement before directional clutch engagement. If there is not enough pressure to fully engage the directional clutches, the transmission will not perform properly.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

For example the direction clutch (P2) pressure tap on a D4H Tractor is located on the rear housing of the transmission.

When the machine is first started, especially on a cold morning, the "Converter Inlet Pressure" P3 can be as high as 145 psi. When the machine warms up the pressure drops due to warm oil versus cold oil. The converter inlet relief valve is flow tested at the factory and has no adjustment. If the pressure rises above 145 psi. it could cause internal damage to the torque converter impeller and high operating temperatures. On the other hand, if "running pressure" (about 60 psi.) on various machine models, drops for any reason, or the valve sticks open serious damage to the torque converter may result.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge tap and procedure.

For example the torque converter inlet (P3) pressure tap on a D4H Tractor is located on the rear housing of the transmission.

The converter outlet relief pressure check determines if the torque converter has an adequate supply of oil and that the converter outlet relief is operating properly. Oil must be maintained in the torque converter to prevent cavitation. If the pressure is low, the power transferred by the converter could be less efficient. Inadequate oil flow will also cause overheating. This test is usually ran when a torque converter stall speed test is performed.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

For example the converter outlet relief pressure tap on a D4H Tractor is located on the torque converter outlet relief valve.

This test indicates if there is enough pressure within the system to keep the transmission clutch plates and gears properly lubricated. Lack of lubrication can seriously damage any transmission. A lack of pressure in this system can be an indication of inadequate oil flow or a leak in another system component.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

For example the transmission lubrication pressure tap on a D8N Tractor is located on the rear housing of the transmission.

One type of transmission used on Caterpillar machines is the Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission. This topic describes the major counter-shaft powershift transmission components, operation (including power flow) and the performance testing and troubleshooting procedures.

lessons.title: Countershaft Powershift: Overview
lessons.objective: This segment will provide an overview of the Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission.
pages: Counter-Shaft transmissions differ from planetary transmissions in that counter-shaft transmissions use constant mesh spur gears. The transmission does not have sliding collars. Speed and directional shifts are accomplished by hydraulically engaging various clutch packs.
What is a Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission?

Advantages of this transmission include: fewer parts, less weight and controlled failure mode protection. Electrically operated shift solenoids provide automatic shifting while eliminating the cable control linkage from the operators station to the transmission control valve.

lessons.title: Countershaft Powershift: Components
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification, function and location of the major components that make-up the Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission.
pages: The control valve body houses electrically actuated solenoids that route oil flow to the directional and speed selector spools. The illustrations and text used here apply to Integrated Toolcarriers and Small Wheel Loaders.

The upper portion of the control valve contains the three directional selector spools. The directional selector spools shift to allow directional clutch pressure oil (P2) to be routed to one of the three directional clutch packs.

The directional selector spools route pressurized P2 oil to directional clutches #1 (Forward Low), #2 (Forward High), and #3 (Reverse). The P2 supply to the selector spools is in parallel for Forward and Reverse but cascaded for Forward High and Forward Low. This is to prevent engagement of more than one directional clutch at one time.

The load piston (1) is located in the middle section of the control valve. The load piston works with the modulating relief valve (2) to provide a controlled pressure rise (modulation) in the clutches and to limit maximum P2 pressure.

The modulating relief valve is located in the middle section of the control valve. The modulating relief valve works with the load piston to provide a controlled pressure rise (modulation) in the clutches and to control P2 pressure. It also sends excess oil to the torque converter.

The lower portion of the control valve houses the three speed selector spools. These spools route speed clutch pressure oil (P1) to one of the three speed clutches.

The speed selector spools route P1 oil to speed clutches #4, #5, and #6. Each selector spool is controlled by an electric solenoid. When a solenoid is activated, the solenoid is shifted. This directs oil through the solenoid to the selector spool. The oil pressure shifts the selector spool, which then directs oil to the selected clutch.

P1 supply oil is cascaded through the three selector spools to prevent engagement of more than one speed clutch at one time. Cascading means that supply oil is first available to the number 4 solenoid and selector spool, then the number 5 solenoid and selector spool, and finally to the number 6 solenoid and selector spool. Therefore, in any default situation, the transmission will either shift down or shift to a neutral condition.

The solenoids consist of two basic components. They are the stem and the coil. All six solenoids and/or components are interchangeable. Loss of electrical power to any speed or directional solenoid will neutralize the transmission by dropping out that particular clutch.

Supply oil is directed to the end of the solenoid stem. When the solenoid is activated, a pin shifts upward inside the stem and unseats a ball that allows oil to pass out through the oil passage to the selector spool.
Pressure tap ports are located on the control valve to check P1 speed clutch pressure, P2 directional clutch pressure and P3 torque converter inlet pressure.

The pressure differential valve and spring are located between the control valve and the separator plate. The pressure differential valve maintains P1 pressure at a specified pressure greater than P2.
The clutches are engaged hydraulically and disengaged by spring force. The clutches are engaged in a manner that provides the proper speed reduction and direction to the transmission output shaft.

The clutch piston has an inner and outer seal. When the discs have worn one half the oil groove depth, the clutch piston travels far enough to unseat (blow) the outer seal. This prevents the discs and plates from ever running metal to metal.

Speed or directional clutch pressure fills the cavity behind the clutch piston and moves the piston to the left against the piston spring and engages the clutch discs and plates.

The clutch plates are mounted inside the clutch housing. Splines on the outside diameter of the plates are engaged with splines in the clutch housing. Both the plates and the housing rotate together. The clutch discs are stacked between the clutch plates. The inside teeth of the discs are engaged with the outside teeth of the hub. The clutch discs have a friction material bonded to their surface so there is no metal to metal contact between the clutch discs and the clutch plates.
The hub is the component in the clutch pack that the gear is splined to. When the clutch piston engages the clutch plates and discs power is transferred through the hub to the gear.

Each of the transmission shafts have three internal oil passages. One passage is for carrying the oil for the lubrication and cooling of the clutches, bearings and gears. The other two passages are for carrying pressure oil for the engagement of the clutches on each shaft.

One pump supplies oil for all of the powertrain hydraulic system. It is a positive displacement, gear type, single section pump. The pump is driven by the pump gear bolted to the torque converter impeller.

On some machines the pump is located at the transmission input shaft. and is driven by the torque converter impeller hub.

Always refer to the appropriate service manual for the machine being serviced for component locations.

lessons.title: Countershaft Powershift: Operation and Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment describes the operation and power flow of the Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission.
pages: Torque from the engine is transferred through the torque converter shaft to the transmission. The torque converter shaft is splined to and drives the transmission input shaft assembly. Since the REVERSE or FORWARD clutches are not engaged, there is no torque transfer from the input shaft assembly to any countershaft assembly or the output shaft assembly.

To transmit power one directional clutch and one speed clutch must be engaged.

Directional clutch packs that are engaged are indicated by red and white stripes. Speed clutch packs that are engaged are indicated by solid red.

The transmission example used in this portion of this program is the transmission used in the 910F and 916F Wheel Loaders and the IT12B and IT14B Tool Carriers.

Always refer to the appropriate service manual for the specific machine being serviced.

With the forward clutch engaged, power is transmitted from a gear on the input shaft to a gear on the Fwd Lo/Hi shaft. The gear on the Fwd Lo/Hi shaft drives a gear on the Rev/2nd shaft. Power is transmitted from a gear on the Rev/2nd shaft to a gear on the 3rd/1st shaft.

When the 1st gear clutch is engaged, power is transferred from the gear to the shaft. The gear on the 3rd/1st shaft transfers power to a gear on the output shaft.

With the reverse clutch engaged power is transmitted from a gear on the input shaft to a gear on the Rev/2nd shaft.

When the second gear clutch is engaged, power flows from the Rev/2nd shaft to a gear which is in mesh with another gear on the 3rd/1st shaft. This transmits power to a gear in mesh with another gear on the output shaft, which turns the shaft.

lessons.title: Countershaft Powershift: Testing and Troubleshooting
lessons.objective: This segment details the major performance testing and troubleshooting procedures for the Counter-Shaft Powershift Transmission.
pages:
One of the most important pieces of diagnostic information required to troubleshoot transmissions is the clutch engagement chart. This chart explains what clutches are engaged for each speed and direction. By knowing these combinations a proper diagnosis of which clutch pack has failed can be made. This particular chart applies only to the transmission in the 910F/916F/IT12B/IT14B and is used for illustration purposes only.

Some of the performance testing procedures that can be performed on a counter-shaft powershift transmission include:

 • Pump Pressure Check
 • Speed Clutch Pressure Check (P1)
 • Directional Clutch Pressure Check (P2)
 • Converter Inlet Relief Pressure Check (P3)
 • Converter Outlet Relief Pressure Check
 • Lube Pressure Check

Before performing any testing or troubleshooting procedures on any Caterpillar machine, always refer to the appropriate service manual for the machine being serviced. Contact the Technical Communicator (TC) at your Caterpillar Dealer for the latest specifications and procedures.

READ AND UNDERSTAND ALL SAFETY PRECAUTIONS AND WARNINGS BEFORE PERFORMING REPAIRS ON ANY CATERPILLAR MACHINE.

Basic safety precautions, skills and knowledge are listed in the SAFETY section of all Caterpillar service manuals and in the descriptions of operations where hazards exist.

The speed clutch pressure check determines if there is enough system pressure to fully engage the speed clutches and to assure proper operation of the modulating relief valve and load piston. If there is not enough pressure to fully engage the speed clutches, the transmission will not perform properly.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

The directional clutch pressure check determines if there is enough system pressure to fully engage the directional clutches. This check also determines if sufficient differential exists between P1 and P2, to assure speed clutch engagement before directional clutch engagement. If there is not enough pressure to fully engage the directional clutches, the transmission will not perform properly.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

When the machine is first started, especially on a cold morning, the "Converter Inlet Pressure" P3 can be as high as 80 psi. When the machine warms up the pressure drops due to warm oil versus cold oil. The converter inlet relief valve is flow tested at the factory and has no adjustment. If the pressure rises above 80 psi. it could cause internal damage to the torque converter impeller and high operating temperatures. On the other hand, if "running pressure" (about 60 psi.) on various machine models, drops for any reason, or the valve sticks open serious damage to the torque converter may result.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

This test indicates if there is enough pressure within the system to keep the transmission clutch plates and gears properly lubricated. Lack of lubrication can seriously damage any transmission. A lack of pressure in this system can be an indication of inadequate oil flow or a leak in another system component.

Refer to the appropriate machine service manual for gauge taps and procedures.

One type of transmission used on Caterpillar machines is the Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission. This topic describes the major individual clutch modulation powershift transmission components, operation (including power flow) and the performance testing and troubleshooting procedures.

lessons.title: ICM Powershift: Overview
lessons.objective: This segment will provides an overview of the Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission.
pages: The Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission is a planetary powershift transmission. The difference is found in the control valve in that each clutch is modulated and decays individually to provide smoother shifting under load. Speed and directional shifts are accomplished by individual control valves which hydraulically engage various clutch packs.
What is an Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission?
Advantages of this transmission include: smoother shifts, improved ride and increased component life and is adaptable to electronic shifting.

lessons.title: ICM Powershift: Components
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification, function and location of the major components that make-up the Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission.
pages:
The ICM transmission hydraulic control consists of a number of components or groups. These components or groups include:

 • Downshift Solenoid (for electronic shifting)

 • Upshift Solenoid (for electronic shifting)

 • Pressure Control Group

 • Selector Group

 • Rotary Actuator

All of these components or groups are located within the transmission hydraulic control unit.

In the case of Tractor-Scrapers the transmission hydraulic control unit is located at the center rear portion of the tractor part of the machine.

The downshift and upshift solenoids are located on top of the transmission. The solenoids are the connection between the electrical and hydraulic systems of the transmission.

When the downshift or upshift solenoids are activated electrically, they send oil to the rotary actuator.

The pressure control group is part of the transmission hydraulic control group and contains the pressure modulation reduction valves. These valves, one valve for each clutch in the transmission are commonly referred to as "Stations". The modulation reduction valves for the transmission clutches give separate control of the pressure and time that it takes to engage and release each clutch.

This is known as Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM).

Each load piston body has a letter identification on it for disassembly and assembly purposes. Pilot passages (for the transmission clutches) are connected to passages from the rotary selector spool of the selector group.

The selector group is part of the transmission hydraulic controls. The selector group controls the pressure of the oil that goes to the two electric solenoids, the torque converter and the pressure control group. It consists of five valves including:

 • Priority Reduction Valve (1) - Controls the pressure of the oil to the neutralizer valve

 • Neutralizer Valve (2) - Prohibits machine movement if the engine is started with the transmission selector lever in a gear other than NEUTRAL

 • Rotary Selector Spool (3) - Determines which selector pistons in the pressure control group get pilot oil and which selector pistons get drained

 • Relief Valve (4) - Controls the maximum pressure of the oil in the transmission hydraulic system

 • Inlet Relief Valve (5) - Controls the maximum pressure of the oil to the torque converter
The rotary actuator is part of the transmission hydraulic control group. The rotary actuator turns a rotary selector spool in the selector group which directs pilot oil to the pressure control group.

On machines equipped with electronic control of the transmission, the electrical system is made up of a sealed, solid state transmission control, a transmission switch, a shift lever switch, two solenoids (upshift and downshift that control the shift and engagement of the transmission) and a neutral start control.

The transmission control must get information from four sources: the shift lever switch, the transmission switch, the transmission speed sender and the transmission hold switch. From this information the transmission control will send current to one of the two solenoids: upshift or downshift.
The transmission clutches are the disc-type and are housed in separate housings.

Each clutch has a number of discs and plates. The inside teeth of the discs are engaged with the outside teeth of the ring gear. Notches on the outside diameter of the plates are engaged with pins in the clutch housing. The pins keep the plates from rotating. This is basically the same clutch setup as in the Planetary Powershift Transmission except for the transmission used in Challenger Tractors. Refer to the Topic titled Planetary Powershift Transmission for more information.

lessons.title: ICM Powershift: Operation and Testing
lessons.objective: This segment describes the operation of the Individual Clutch Modulation Valves of the (ICM) Powershift Transmission. Also included in this segment are the performance testing and troubleshooting procedures for the ICM transmission.
pages: Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission Operation, Performance Testing and Troubleshooting
All of the modulation reduction valves of the transmission hydraulic control - pressure control group operate in a similar way. For this reason, only the basic operation of one valve is given.

When a shift is started (a clutch is to be engaged), a pilot passage gets pilot oil at the correct sequence from the rotary selector spool. This causes the selector piston (1) along with the load piston (2) to move against the force of their springs causing the modulation reduction valve to move against the force of a spring closing the passage to drain. At this time a passage is opened which sends the oil to fill the clutch.

Oil also goes through the load piston orifice and passage. This oil goes between the selector piston and the load piston.

After the clutch is full of oil, the pressure of the pump oil increases in the selected clutch. This causes the load piston (2) to again move against the force of its springs. Clutch oil also goes through an orifice in the modulation reduction valve, opens the check ball and goes into the slug chamber at the end of the valve.

This pressure works against the pressure at the end of the load piston. The pressure increases until the load piston is moved all the way to the left against its stop. The pressure in the clutch is now at its maximum.

The Modulation Reduction valve moves to the right and left to keep the pressure in the passage constant.

Two components control the amount of time it takes for the pressure in the clutch to get to its maximum: the size of the load piston orifice (3) and the force of the springs. The force of the springs can be changed by the removal or addition of shims (4) in the load piston.

The power flow of the Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission is the same as a Planetary Powershift Transmission. Please refer to the Topic titled "Planetary Powershift Transmission" for more information.

Always refer to the appropriate service manual for complete details of transmission operation and power flow.

The performance testing and troubleshooting procedures for the Individual Clutch modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission are similar to those of the Planetary Powershift Transmission. Please refer to the Topic titled "Planetary Powershift Transmission" for more information.

One of the most important pieces of diagnostic information required to troubleshoot transmissions is the clutch engagement chart. This chart explains what clutches are engaged for each speed and direction. By knowing these combinations a proper diagnosis of which clutch pack has failed can be made. This particular chart applies only to the transmission in the 621E/623E Wheel Tractor-Scraper and is used for illustration purposes only.
Individual Clutch Modulation (ICM) Powershift Transmission Performance Testing and Troubleshooting

Some of the performance testing procedures that can be performed on a powershift transmission include:

 • Pump Pressure Check
 • Transmission Clutch Pressure Check
 • Converter Inlet Relief Pressure Check
 • Converter Outlet Relief Pressure Check
 • Lube Pressure Check

Before performing any testing or troubleshooting procedures on any Caterpillar machine, always refer to the appropriate service manual for the machine being serviced. Contact the Technical Communicator (TC) at your Caterpillar Dealer for the latest specifications and procedures.

topics.title: Transfer Gear Principles
topics.summary: This topic introduces the basic transfer gear principles including what a transfer gear is, what they are used for, the features and benefits of transfer gears and transfer gear applications.

lessons.title: What Is a Transfer Gear?
lessons.objective: This segment describes what a transfer gear is and what transfer gears are used for.
pages: Some Cat machines have one or more transfer gear cases (sometimes called drop boxes) that connect various power transmission units, change the direction and speed of the power flow, or drop the axis of the power flow. They can be used to connect the engine to the transmission input driveshaft, or the transmission to the output driveshaft. The transfer gear case is referred to as a "drop box" because it often lowers (drops) the power axis from one elevation to another elevation.

Since there is a continuous mechanical connection between the output transfer gears and the wheels of the machine, various components can be attached to the transfer gear case. These may include supplemental steering pumps and parking brakes.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment details the features and benefits of transfer gears.
pages: The following are some of the features and benefits of transfer gear systems.
A feature of transfer gears is that they allow speed reduction and torque increase.
The benefit is more power to move heavy machinery in a compact design configuration.
A feature of transfer gears is that they allow a change in the power flow direction.
The benefit is that it allows various powertrain component configurations.
A feature of transfer gears is that they can drive auxiliary pumps.
The benefit is that it eliminates the need for additional pump drives.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment shows the various applications for transfer gears used in a drivetrain system.
pages: Transfer gear cases are used on most Caterpillar equipment. The configuration of the transfer gear case, how many gears and the layout, varies by application.
Because of the wide variety of transfer gear case configurations, always refer to the appropriate service literature for specific transfer gear case applications and configurations.

topics.title: Transfer Gear Systems
topics.summary: This topic describes the two major transfer gear systems and where they are used.

lessons.title: Input Transfer Gear System
lessons.objective: This segment details the transmission input transfer gear system including when, where and why it is used.
pages: A transmission input transfer gear system is most commonly used when the machine transmission is not in direct line with the machines engine and torque converter.

For example, the transmission in a 988F Wheel Loader is mounted lower than the engine in the frame of the machine. In order for the power flow from the engine and torque converter to be used by the transmission the axis line for the power flow must be dropped to reach the transmission. This is accomplished by an input transfer gear system.

lessons.title: Output Transfer Gear System
lessons.objective: This segment details the transmission output transfer gear system including when, where and why it is used.
pages: A transmission output transfer gear system is most commonly used when the machine axles are not in direct line with the machines transmission output shaft.

Again as an example we'll use the 988F Wheel Loader. As you can see in the picture the power flow axis line for the axles does not meet or line up with the output shaft on the transmission. A transmission output transfer gear system is used to drop the power flow from the transmission to the driveshafts that transfer the power to the axles. 

The transmission output transfer gear system at this point can also be used to reduce the speed of the power flow and increase the torque to the axles for more power to move the machine.

topics.title: Transfer Gear Components
topics.summary: This topic describes the identification, function, and location of the basic transfer gear system components.

lessons.title: Drive Gears
lessons.objective: This segment identifies the transfer gear system drive gears including their function and location.
pages: A transfer gear system uses a drive gear (red) that accepts the incoming power flow and transfers it either directly to the driven gear or through an idler gear to the driven gear.

In the case of the 988F Wheel Loader Input Transfer Gear System, the drive gear (red) is splined to the yoke assembly that has the driveshaft from the torque converter connected to it. The ratio of the transfer gears depend on the requirements of the machine.

lessons.title: Driven Gears
lessons.objective: This segment identifies the transfer gear system driven gears including their function and location.
pages: In a two-gear transfer gear system the drive gear rotates and drives a driven gear (red). P

In the case of the 988F Wheel Loader Input Transfer Gear System, the drive gear is splined to the yoke assembly that has the driveshaft from the torque converter connected to it. The drive gear rotates and drives the driven gear (red).

The driven gear is connected to and turns the input shaft of the transmission. The ratio of the transfer gears are designed by the requirements of the machine. In a two-gear transfer gear system the drive gear and the driven gear rotate in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Idler Gears
lessons.objective: This segment identifies the transfer gear system idler gears including their function and location.
pages: In some cases, such as the output transfer gear system on the 988F Wheel Loader, the drive gear and the driven gear need to rotate in the same direction. This is accomplished with an idler gear.

On the 988F Wheel Loader, the output shaft of the transmission is connected to the drive gear. The drive gear is engaged with and turns the idler gear. The idler gear is engaged with and turns the driven gear. The driven gear is connected by yokes to the driveshafts that drive the axles. Because of the three gear setup the drive gear and the driven gear turn in the same direction. The gear ratios between the gears determine the speed reduction and torque increase required by the machine.

topics.title: Transfer Gear Operation and Power Flow
topics.summary: This topic shows how the different transfer gear systems operate and the power flow through each.

lessons.title: Input Transfer Gear Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment shows the operation and power flow through the Input Transfer Gear System.
pages: The following shows the Input Transfer Gear System operation as it applies to the 988F Wheel Loader. All Input Transfer Gear Systems on Caterpillar equipment operate under the same principles.
The input transfer gears are at the input side of the transmission. The upper driveshaft from the torque converter connects to a yoke assembly on the transfer gear case.
The yoke assembly is connected to the drive gear by splines. As the driveshaft turns the yoke the drive gear also turns.
The drive gear is engaged with the driven gear. As the drive gear turns the driven gear turns in the opposite direction.
The driven gear is connected to the input shaft of the transmission. As the driven gear rotates so does the input shaft to the transmission.

lessons.title: Output Transfer Gear Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment shows the operation and power flow through the Output Transfer Gear System.
pages: The following shows the Output Transfer Gear System operation as it applies to the 988F Wheel Loader. All Output Transfer Gear Systems on Caterpillar equipment operate under the same principles.
The output transfer gears are at the output side of the transmission. The output carrier of the transmission is connected to the drive gear by splines.
As the output carrier of the transmission turns so does the drive gear. The drive gear is engaged with and drives the idler gear. These gears rotate in opposite directions.
As the drive gear rotates it turns the idler gear. The idler gear is engaged with and turns the driven gear.

As the idler gear rotates it turns the driven gear. The idler gear and the driven gear turn in the opposite directions, but because this is a three gear system, the drive gear and the driven gear turn in the same directions.
The driven gear is splined to a shaft that has yokes on each end attached by splines. As the driven gear turns so does the shaft. The yokes are connected to driveshafts that turn the axles.

Chap. 1
Torque Converters and Torque Dividers

topics.title: Introduction to Drivetrains: Wheel-Type Machines
topics.summary: This topic describes the basic drivetrain system components for wheel-type Caterpillar machines.

lessons.title: Wheel-Type Drivetrain Components
lessons.objective:
This segment introduces the major drivetrain system components used in Caterpillar wheel-type machines such as:

Wheel Loaders, Skidders, Integrated Tool Carriers (IT's), Wheel Dozers, Soil Compactors, Landfill Compactors, Off-Highway Trucks, Articulated Trucks, Backhoe Loaders and Tractor-Scrapers.
pages:
The torque converter connects the engine to the transmission. The purpose of the torque converter is to hydraulically transfer torque from the engine flywheel to the transmission.

The torque converter uses oil to send torque from the engine to the transmission. When a machine is working against a load, the torque converter can multiply the torque from the engine and send a higher torque to the transmission. The main components of a torque converter are the impeller, turbine, stator and output shaft.
The impeller is the driving member of the torque converter. It is splined to the flywheel and turns at engine RPM. The impeller contains blades which force oil against the blades of the turbine.

The turbine is the driven member of the torque converter with vanes that receive the oil flow from the impeller. The turbine causes the output shaft (which is splined to the turbine) to turn when oil from the impeller is forced against the turbine blades.

The stator is the stationary reaction member whose vanes multiply force by redirecting fluid flow from the turbine back to the impeller. The purpose of the stator is to change the direction of the flow of oil between the turbine and the impeller. This direction change increases the momentum of the fluid, thereby increasing the torque capacity of the converter.
The output shaft, which is splined to the turbine, sends torque to the input shaft of the transmission.

With the creation of the earliest Caterpillar wheel-type machines, one of the major challenges of the design engineer has been to find an efficient, reliable method of transmitting power from the engine to the final drive components.

The first specialized machines were equipped with transmission systems that were purely mechanical in design. While the transmissions had grown in size and complexity, their basic components remained unchanged. Power from the engine was transmitted to the drive line through a mechanical clutch and a series of gears. Gear movement and clutch operation were controlled by combinations of levers, shafts, and/or cables.

To help satisfy the continually increasing demand for higher productivity and greater efficiency, the concept of transmission design entered another era. The Caterpillar Powershift Transmission retained the advantages of the mechanical system, but added a feature that soon became an industry standard: hydraulically-activated clutches and controls. The introduction of hydraulics to power transmission systems also created an increased need for understanding of the terminology and service procedures that accompanied this system. In addition to pumps, hoses, valves, governors, accumulators and torque converters, service personnel were confronted with such new terms as "modulation," "clutch sequencing," and "primary pressure."

The major advantage of any powershift transmission is quicker response when shifting from one gear to another as well as changing speeds when the application calls for it. The powershift transmissions may be shifted under loads with no loss of productivity.

The basic components of the Planetary Powershift Transmission consist of:

• Hydraulically Activated Clutches - which permit selection of the forward/reverse direction and speeds

• The Planetary Group - houses planetary gearing which depends on clutch engagement to supply speed and direction

The basic components of the Countershaft Powershift Transmission are:

• Clutch Shafts: that provide mounting for gears and clutch packs

• Constant Mesh Gears: that provide speed and direction which varies by clutch engagement

• Directional and Speed Clutches: that consist of clutch plates and friction discs (clutch packs), used to engage the various gears supplying speed and directionP

Some Cat machines have transfer gear trains that connect various power transmission units, change direction of power flow, or drop the axis of flow from the engine crankshaft to the transmission, or drop the axis of flow from the transmission to the final drive.

Transfer gears can reduce or increase torque as designed by the application it is being used for.

Input Transfer Gears are at the input side of the transmission. The torque converter connects to the input gear (drive gear) which in turn drives the driven (output gear) which is connected to the input of the transmission.

The Power flow through an Input Transfer Gear is as follows:

• From the yoke assembly to the drive gear.

• From the drive gear to the driven gear.

and

• From the driven gear to the transmission input 
 shaft.

YOutput Transfer Gears are at the output side of the transmission. The output carrier of the transmission connects to the input gear (drive gear) which in turn drives an idler gear which drives the driven gear (output gear) which is connected to the drive shaft that connects to the final drive system.

The Power flow through an Output Transfer Gear is as follows:

• From the drive gear to the idler gear.

• From the idler gear to the driven gear.

and

• From the driven gear to the drive shaft.

In wheel-type machines the axles provide the service brakes, a balance of power to the wheels during turns, and the final gear reduction and torque increase for the drivetrain. The main components of the axles are the bevel gear set/differential group, brake group, planetary group and axle group. P

The bevel ring and pinion gear set receives power from the driveshaft, turns it 90 degrees, and transmits it to the differential. The differential provides wheel speed differentiation, and transfers power to the final drives. The main components are the bevel pinion shaft, bevel ring gear, differential case assembly, pinion gears, side gears and spider.

The service brake group is generally an oil-cooled disc brake. There are three types found in wheel-type machines. In the "inboard axle brake" (used in small wheel loaders and backhoe loaders), the brake disc is splined to the sun gear shaft and housed in the axle. In the "axle shaft brake," the brake disc is splined to a hub on the long axle shaft and located between the axle housing and spindle (used in large loaders and landfill compactors). In the wheel speed brake (used in off-highway trucks), the brake disc is splined to the wheel casting and rotates at wheel speed.

Other types of brakes used on Caterpillar machines include dry caliper disc brakes and dry drum brakes. These are typically found on tractor-scrapers and articulated trucks.
The planetary group provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of a carrier, planet gears, ring gear, sun gear, shafts and bearings.

The axle group consists of the axle housing, axle shafts, and bearings. The function of the housing and bearings are to provide structure to support the weight of the machine. The axle shafts transmit power from the differential out to the wheels.

Hydrostatic drive systems have infinitely variable speed capability. Mechanical power from the engine is changed to hydraulic power by a variable displacement pump. This power is sent through hydraulic lines to the motor where it is changed back to mechanical power to drive a load. The pump is designed to produce a flow that can be varied. The flow is sent through either of two lines to the hydraulic drive motor. This allows the machine to be operated at different speeds and directions.

The major components of a hydrostatic drive system are as follows:

• The Variable Displacement Pump (1) which changes mechanical input to hydraulic output.

• The Hydraulic Oil Lines (2) which carry the flow to the motor.

and

• The Fixed or Variable Displacement Hydraulic Motor (3) which changes hydraulic power back to mechanical power.

topics.title: Introduction to Drivetrains: Track-Type Machines
topics.summary: This topic describes the basic drivetrain system components for track-type Caterpillar machines.

lessons.title: Track-Type Drivetrain Components
lessons.objective:
This segment introduces the major drivetrain system components used in Caterpillar track-type machines such as:

Track-Type Tractors, Excavators, Pipe Layers, Track Loaders, Cold Planers, Log Loaders, Feller Bunchers, Asphalt Pavers and Track Skidders.
