Gear movement and clutch operation were controlled by combinations of levers, shafts, and/or cables.

To help satisfy the continually increasing demand for higher productivity and greater efficiency, the concept of transmission design entered another era. The Caterpillar Powershift Transmission retained the advantages of the mechanical system, but added a feature that soon became an industry standard: hydraulically-activated clutches and controls. The introduction of hydraulics to power transmission systems also created an increased need for understanding the terminology and service procedures that accompanied this system. In addition to pumps, hoses, valves, governors, accumulators and torque converters, service personnel were confronted with such new terms as "modulation," "clutch sequencing," and "primary pressure."

The major advantage of any powershift transmission is quicker response when shifting from one gear to another as well as changing speeds when the application calls for it. The powershift transmissions may be shifted under loads with no loss of productivity.

The basic components of the Planetary Powershift Transmission consist of:

• The Hydraulically Activated Clutches: which permit selection of the forward/reverse direction and speeds

• The Planetary Group: houses planetary gearing which depends on clutch engagement to supply speed and direction

The basic components of the Countershaft Powershift Transmission are:

• The Clutch Shafts: that provide mounting for gears and clutch packs

• Constant Mesh Gears: that provide speed and direction which varies by clutch engagement

and

• The Directional and Speed Clutches: that consist of clutch plates and friction discs (clutch packs), used to engage the various gears supplying speed and direction

Some Cat machines have transfer gear trains that connect various power transmission units, change direction of power flow, or drop the axis of flow from the engine crankshaft to the transmission, or drop the axis of flow from the transmission to the final drive.

Transfer gears can reduce or increase torque as designed by the application it is being used for.

In track-type machines, the lower drivetrain system provides steering, braking and the final gear reduction and torque increase for the drivetrain. The main components of the lower drivetrain system are the bevel gear set, steering clutches and brakes, and final drive. A differential steering system is available on some tractors and will be discussed in Module 3 - "Axles and Lower Drivetrain Systems."P

The bevel ring and pinion gear set receives power from the transfer gears, turns it 90 degrees, and transmits it to the steering clutches and brakes. It consists of the bevel pinion shaft, bevel ring gear and bevel ring gear cross shaft.

The steering clutches and brakes are multiple disc oil-cooled units that transfer power from the bevel gear to the final drives. The steering clutches and brakes are contained in one assembly and work together to brake and steer track-type machines. The steering clutches and brakes consist of many components and will be covered in greater detail in Module 3 - "Axles and Lower Drivetrain Systems."

The final drive is a planetary gear set(s) or bull gear which provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. The final drive receives power from the sun gear shaft and then transfers power to the sprocket which drives the track.

Hydraulic drive systems have infinitely variable speed capability. Mechanical power from the engine is changed to hydraulic power by a variable displacement pump. This power is sent through hydraulic lines to the control valve and from the control valve to the motor where it is changed back to mechanical power to drive a load. The pump is designed to produce a flow that can be varied. The flow is sent through either of two lines to the hydraulic drive motor. This allows the machine to be operated at different speeds and directions.

The major components of a hydraulic drive system are as follows:

• The Variable Displacement Pump (1): which changes mechanical input to hydraulic output.

• The Hydraulic Oil Lines (2): which carry the flow to the control valves and the motors.

• The Hydraulic Control Valve (3): which directs flow from the pump

and

• The Fixed or Two-Position Hydraulic Motor (4): which changes hydraulic power back to mechanical power.

topics.title: Axles
topics.summary: This topic describes axles and discusses their features, benefits and applications in Caterpillar wheel-type machines.

lessons.title: Axles in the Drivetrain
lessons.objective: This segment explains the use of axles in the drivetrain of Caterpillar wheel-type machines.
pages: The purpose of the front and rear axle arrangements is to transfer power from the drive shafts to the tires to both drive and stop the machine. While the front and rear axle housings are slightly different, the internal components and operation are identical.

There are four basic functions of an axle. Transmit power from the drive shaft to the ground, provide a balance of power to each wheel during turns, stop (brake) the machine and provide torque increase/speed reduction before the power reaches the tires.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits of Axles, Brakes and Final Drives
lessons.objective: This segment describes the features and benefits of axles, brakes and final drives.
pages: Axles in wheel-type machines are equipped with certain features and benefits for dependable performance.
A feature of Caterpillar axles is that they are equipped with duo-cone seals.
The benefit is that they provide Cat machines with a superior seal.
A feature of Caterpillar axles is that many wheel-type machines are equipped with an oscillating rear axle.
The benefit is that this provides traction and stability.
engineer has been to find an efficient, reliable method of transmitting power from the engine to the final drive components.

A feature of Caterpillar axles is that they have a traction aids option. The following types of traction aids are found on some wheel-type machines:

• NoSPIN Differential
• Limited Slip Differential
• Differential Lock
- Traction Control System (TCS)

and

• Automatic Electronic Traction Aid (AETA)
The benefit is that these aids provide improved traction and stability.
Brakes in wheel-type machines are equipped with certain features and benefits for optimum stopping. Caterpillar brakes meet a variety of legal requirements depending upon type of machine.
A feature of Caterpillar brakes is that they are enclosed and sealed.
The benefit is that they are protected from environmental contaminants.
A feature of Caterpillar brakes is that they are adjustment free.
The benefit is that this results in lower maintenance costs.
Final drives in wheel-type machines, consisting of sun gears, ring gears and planetary carrier assemblies, are equipped with certain features and benefits.
A feature of Caterpillar final drives is that they are equipped with full-floating bronze sleeve planet bearings.
The benefit is that they provide durability and are adjustment free.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment discusses applications of axles used in Caterpillar products.
pages: Wheel-Type machines are equipped with outboard and inboard axles.
Inboard axles can be found on Small and Medium Wheel Loaders and Backhoe Loaders.
Outboard axles can be found on Large Wheel Loaders, Compactors, Wheel Dozers, Off-Highway and Articulated Trucks and Wheel Tractor-Scrapers.

topics.title: Inboard Axle Components
topics.summary: This topic describes the inboard axle components used in Caterpillar wheel-type machines.

lessons.title: Bevel Gear Set and Differential Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the bevel gear set and differential group.
pages: The bevel gear set consists of the bevel pinion shaft and bevel ring gear. The bevel gear set receives power from the drive shaft, turns it 90 degrees, provides a speed reduction/torque increase and transmits the power to the differential. P

The bevel pinion shaft is splined to the drive shaft yoke assembly at one end. The other end intersects with the bevel gear at a 90 degree angle. Bevel gear teeth are tapered in thickness and height. The bevel pinion shaft is supported by tapered roller bearings in the pinion housing. Bevel gears must be precisely adjusted. The bearings are preloaded to maximize bearing life.
The bevel ring gear is driven by the bevel pinion shaft and bolted to the differential case assembly, which provides power to the differential.
The differential provides a balance of power to the wheels and transfers power to the final drives. The main components are the differential case assembly, pinion gears, side gears and spider.

The differential case assembly houses the components of the differential group. The bevel ring gear is bolted to the case assembly. The case assembly turns the spider and pinions (spider gears) which intersect with the side gears to turn the final drive sun shafts. The differential case also provides support to the sun shafts.

The pinion gears or spider gears ride on the spider and transmit power from the differential case to the side gears and then sun shafts. There are two to four pinion gears, depending on model, mounted to the spider. The pinion gears remain stationary except during a turn or during wheel slippage. When a machine is turned, the pinions "walk around" the side gears to permit wheels to turn at different speeds.
The spider is driven by the differential case and provides the mounting for the pinion gears. P
The side gears are splined to the sun gear shafts. The pinion gears drive the side gears causing the sun gear shafts to turn.

lessons.title: Brake and Planetary Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the brake and planetary group.
pages: The service brakes are located in the axle housing next to the differential. There is one brake on each side of the differential. The service brakes may be in both the front and rear axles and are cooled by the lubricant in the axles. The brakes are hydraulically activated and spring released. Each service brake consists of a piston, disc, plate, guides and springs.

The piston is kept from rotating in the differential housing by the guides. The piston pushes the brake plate and disc together to slow or stop the machine. Hydraulic oil is used to move the piston. The spring retracts the piston which releases the brakes when oil pressure drops.

The disc has splines on the inside diameter that fit on the splines of the sun shaft. The disc turns with the sun gear. The friction of the disc pushing against the plate is what slows or stops the machine. The disc is pushed against the plate by the piston.
Like the piston, the plate is kept from rotating in the axle by the guides. The piston pushes the disc against the stationary plate to slow or stop the machine.
The guides keep the plate from rotating in the differential housing.
The springs force the piston away from the brake pack when oil pressure drops.
The planetary group (final drive) provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of sun, ring, and planet gears, a planet carrier, planet shaft and bearings.
The sun shaft is splined to the differential side gear. It receives power from the side gear and then transfers that power to the planet gears. P
The ring gear is pressed into the axle housing and does not rotate. The ring gear reacts torque from the planet gears.

The planetary gear set consists of three planet gears, shafts and bearings mounted in a carrier. The planetary gears are driven by the sun gear and revolve around the inside of the stationary ring gear. The internal splines of the planet carrier mate with the axle shaft splines and transmit power to the axle shaft.

lessons.title: Axle Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the axle group such as: axle shafts and housing.
pages: The axle group consists of the axle housings and axle shafts, and bearings. The function of the housing and bearings are to provide structure to support the weight of the machine. Axle shafts transmit power from the differential to the wheels.

VThe housings contain the components of the drivetrain from the drive shaft yoke to the wheel assemblies. They provide a mounting for the bevel pinion shaft bearing races, and brake pistons. The front axle is rigidly mounted to the machine frame and the rear axle is capable of oscillating up and down +/- 15 degrees. The inboard axle consists of four housings.

• Axle Shaft Housings (1)- Bolted to the intermediate housing and center housing. The axle shaft housings provide support for the axle shafts.

• Pinion Housing (2) - Bolted to the center housing and supports the bevel pinion gear.

• Center Housing (3) - Bolted to the intermediate housing and axle shaft housing. The center housing supports the differential.

and

• Intermediate Housing (4) - Bolted to the center housing and axle shaft. The intermediate housing provides an access for removal and installation of the differential.

The axle shafts transmit power from the planetary gears to the wheels and are splined to the planetary carrier. The rim bolts to a flange at the end of the axle shaft. The axle shafts rotate on bearings located at each end of the shafts and are supported by the axle housing.
The bearings allow the axle shafts to rotate easily and not slide. They are located at each end of the axle shafts. The type of bearings used in the axle are tapered roller bearings.

topics.title: Inboard Axle Operation
topics.summary: In this topic inboard axle operation is explained.

lessons.title: Inboard Axle Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment explains the power flow through the inboard axle used on wheel-type machines.
pages: Power from the driveshaft enters at the bevel pinion shaft, flows through the bevel ring gear, differential, planetary gear set and axle shafts to the wheels.

topics.title: Outboard Axle Components
topics.summary: This topic describes the outboard axle components used in Caterpillar wheel-type machines.

lessons.title: Bevel Gear Set and Differential Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the bevel gear set/differential group.
pages: The bevel gear set consists of the bevel pinion shaft and bevel ring gear. The bevel gear set receives power from the drive shaft, turns it 90 degrees, provides a speed reduction/torque increase and transmits the power to the differential. P

The bevel pinion shaft is splined to the drive shaft yoke assembly at one end. The other end intersects with the bevel gear at a 90 degree angle. Bevel gear teeth are tapered in thickness and height. The bevel pinion shaft is supported by tapered roller bearings in the pinion housing. Bevel gears must be precisely adjusted. The bearings are preloaded to maximize bearing life.
The bevel ring gear is driven by the bevel pinion shaft and bolted to the differential case assembly, which provides power to the differential.
The differential provides a balance of power to the wheels and transfers power to the final drives. The main components are the differential case assembly, pinion gears, side gears and spider.

The differential case assembly houses the components of the differential group. The bevel ring gear is bolted to the case assembly. The case assembly turns the spider and pinions (spider gears) which intersect with the side gears to turn the axle shafts. The differential case also provides support to the axle shafts.

The pinion gears or spider gears ride on the spider shaft and transmit power from the differential case to the side gears and then axle shafts. There are two to four pinion gears, depending on model, mounted to the spider. The pinion gears remain stationary except during a turn or during wheel slippage. When a machine is turned, the pinions "walk around" the side gears to permit wheels to turn at different speeds.
The spider is driven by the differential case and provides the mounting for the pinion gears.
The side gears are splined to the axle shafts. The pinion gears drive the side gears causing the axle shafts to turn.

lessons.title: Brake Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the brake group.
pages: Axle shaft brakes are found in some large wheel loaders and landfill compactors. The brakes are located between the axle housing and spindle and are fully hydraulic. The main components are the pistons, discs, plates, springs, brake anchor and brake hub.

The piston pushes the brake plates and discs together to slow or stop the machine. Hydraulic oil is used to move the piston. "Retraction" springs retract the piston and release the brakes when oil pressure drops.

Multiple discs are used in the braking system. The discs are splined to the hub on the long axle shaft. The discs turn with the hub on the axle shaft. The discs are pushed against the plates by the piston. The friction of the discs (rotating with the axle) pushing against the plates (held stationary by the brake anchor) is what slows or stops the vehicle.

Multiple plates are used in the braking system. The plates are splined to the brake anchor remaining stationary. The friction of the discs (rotating with the axle) pushing against the plates (held stationary by the brake anchor) is what slows or stops the vehicle. The discs are pushed against the plates by the piston.
The springs, always under compression, retract the piston when hydraulic pressure is released.
The brake anchor is fastened between the spindle and the axle housing. It does not turn. There are splines on the inside of the anchor which engage with the plates.
The brake hub has outer splines which engage the brake friction discs and inner splines which engage the axle shaft.

The wheel speed brake is used in off-highway trucks and some large wheel loaders. Wheel speed brakes are splined to the wheel and rotate at the same rpm as the tires. Wheel loaders use brakes at each wheel, while some models of off-highway trucks have these brakes only on the rear axles. Wheel speed brakes are cooled by the transfer of heat to the oil sump. Brakes which operate in an oil sump without oil flow are called "dipped" brakes. Brake systems which feature coolers and force oil through the brakes are referred to as "forced cooled brakes." Wheel speed service brakes are hydraulically applied and spring released. The main components are the pistons, discs, plates, springs and pins.

The piston pushes the brake plates and discs together to slow or stop the machine. Hydraulic oil is used to move the piston. "Retraction" springs retract the piston and release the brakes when oil pressure drops.

Multiple discs are used in the braking system. The discs are splined to the wheel hub and rotate at wheel speed. The discs are pushed against the plates by the piston. The friction of the discs (rotating with the wheel hub) pushing against the plates (stationary in the wheel housing) is what slows or stops the vehicle.

Multiple plates are used in the braking system. The plates are splined to the wheel housing remaining stationary. The friction of the discs (rotating with the wheel hub) pushing against the plates (stationary in the wheel housing) is what slows or stops the vehicle. The discs are pushed against the plates by the piston.

lessons.title: Single and Double Reduction Planetary Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the single reduction and double reduction planetary group.
pages: The planetary group (final drive) provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of sun, ring, and planet gears, a planet carrier, planet shaft and bearings. P
The sun gear is splined to the axle shaft. It receives power from the side gear through the axle shaft and then transfers that power to the planet gears.
The planetary ring gear is fastened to the wheel hub and does not rotate. The ring gear reacts torque from the planet gears.

The planetary gear set consists of three or more planet gears, shafts, and bearings mounted in a planet carrier. The carrier is fastened to the wheel assembly. The planetary gears are driven by the sun gear and revolve around the inside of the stationary ring gear transmitting torque to the wheel assembly.

The double reduction planetary group (final drive) provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain on some larger machines. It consists of two sun gears, two ring gears and two planetary gear sets. For explanation purposes, the components will be identified as part of planetary #1 (1st reduction) and planetary #2 (2nd reduction).

The #1 sun gear is splined to the axle shaft. It receives power from the side gear through the axle shaft and then transfers that power to the #1 planet gears. The #2 sun gear driven by the #1 planet carrier in turn drives the #2 planet gears.
The ring gears are fastened to the spindle hub and do not rotate. Like the single reduction, the ring gear reacts torque from the planet gears.

Each planetary gear set consists of three or more planet gears, shafts and bearings mounted in each planet carrier. Carrier #1 is splined to and drives sun gear #2. Carrier #2 is fastened to and drives the wheel assembly. The planetary gears are driven by the sun gears and revolve around the inside of the ring gears transmitting torque to their respective carriers.

lessons.title: Axle Group
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the axle group.
pages: The axle group consists of the axle housings and axle shafts. The function of the housing is to provide structure to support the weight of the machine. Axle shafts transmit power from the differential to the wheels.

The axle housing supports the components of the drivetrain from the drive shaft yoke to the wheel assemblies. It provides a mounting for the differential carrier, spindle, and brake piston housing. The front axle housing is rigidly mounted to the machine frame and the rear axle is capable of oscillating up and down +/- 13 degrees.

The axle shafts transmit power from the differential side gears to the final drive sun gear and support the hub for the brake discs. The axle shafts rotate and are supported by the gears into which they are splined.

topics.title: Outboard Axle Operation
topics.summary: In this topic outboard axle power flow is explained.

lessons.title: Outboard Axle Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment explains the power flow through the outboard axle used on wheel-type machines.
pages: Power from the driveshaft enters at the bevel pinion shaft, flows through the bevel ring gear, differential, axle shafts and planetary gear sets to the wheels.

Power from the drive shafts enters the axle groups through the bevel pinion shaft, which drives the bevel ring gear. The bevel ring gear is fastened to and drives the differential case assembly. The differential case contains the spider which turns with the case. The pinion gears are mounted on and driven by the spider. The pinion gears drive the differential side gears which transmit power through the axle shafts to the planetary final drives. When the machine moves in a straight direction with the same amount of traction under each drive wheel, the pinions do not turn on the spider.

During a turn or wheel slippage one wheel must turn faster than the other. This is accomplished by the differential.

The spider turns with the differential case and bevel gear, and drives the side gears through the pinions. Since it takes more force to turn one wheel than the other, the pinions turn on the spider. As the pinions turn, they move around the side gears. This lets the outside wheel turn faster than the inside wheel. The same amount of torque is sent through the final drives to both the inside and outside wheels. This torque is only equal to the amount needed to turn the wheel with the least resistance.

The sun gear is driven by the axle shaft and turns the planet gears. The planet gears are forced to revolve around the inside of the stationary ring gear which is splined to the hub. The movement of the planet gears around the ring gear causes the planet carrier, which is fastened to the wheel assembly, to rotate. The wheel assembly transfers power to the tire.

topics.title: Traction Aids
topics.summary: This topic discusses the different types of traction aids available in the wheel-type products. P

lessons.title: NoSPIN Differentials
lessons.objective: This segment introduces NoSPIN Differentials including applications and operation.
pages: The NoSPIN Differential is an automatic locking type differential which forces both wheels to turn at the same speed regardless of tractive conditions. It effectively locks the wheels together sending up to 100% of available torque to one wheel if needed. During a turn the outside wheel will disengage and overrun and the NoSPIN differential sends the torque to the inside wheel that turns slower. The NoSPIN differential group is a direct replacement for the standard differential internal components. It fits directly into the standard differential case assembly. The main components of the NoSPIN differential are the side gears, driven clutches, center cam and spider.
The side gears are connected to the sun gears and driven clutches. The side gears are turned by the driven clutches and send power through the sun gears to the final drives.

The driven clutches are splined to the side gears and engage with the teeth of the spider. Both driven clutches engage with the spider in straight ahead maneuvers and one driven clutch disengages from the spider in a turn.

topics.title: Traction Aids (continued)
topics.summary: In this topic inboard axle operation is explained.

lessons.title: Why Traction Aids Are Needed
pages:
The travel of the outside wheel, during a turn, is a longer distance than the travel of the inside wheel. When the machine turns with power, the NoSPIN differential allows the outside wheel to turn faster than the inside wheel. The NoSPIN spider continues to drive the inside wheel.

The driven clutch for the outside wheel turns faster than the spider. The driven clutch teeth of the cam for the outside wheel move up the teeth of the center cam. This causes the outside driven clutch to move away from and disengage from the spider.

When the machine comes out of a turn the driven clutch from the outside wheel reengages with the spider and both wheels turn at the same speed.

lessons.title: Limited Slip Differentials
lessons.objective: This segment introduces Limited Slip Differentials including applications and operation.
pages: The Limited Slip Differential (LSD) is a locking type differential designed to give equal power to both wheels until ground conditions between the left and right wheel have a pulling difference. The Limited Slip Differential transfers lost power from the least tractive side to the side with the most traction. The Limited Slip differential is a direct replacement for the standard differential group. It replaces the differential case assembly and all its components. The main components of the Limited Slip Differential are the side gears, clutch pack, pinion gears, pinion shafts and actuator housing.

The inside splines of the side gears are connected to the sun shaft for the final drives. The outside splines of the side gears are meshed with the inner friction discs in the clutch packs. The side gears send power through the sun gears to the final drives.

The clutch pack contains discs which are splined to the side gears and plates which are splined to the LSD case housing. When loaded, the clutch pack tries to force the side gear and the case housing to move together.
The pinion gears perform identical to pinion gears in a standard differential. The pinion shafts function the same as the spider in a standard differential.

The actuator housing fits in the grooves of the case housing and is held with the discs from moving radially. The actuator is the component that applies the load to the clutch pack when a wheel slips.
The Limited Slip Differential was developed for machines that must work on steep grades or in poor underfoot conditions. It is available in both the front and rear axle groups.
The Limited Slip Differential is available in Integrated Tool Carriers and Wheel Loaders.

The differential case housing is driven by the bevel ring gear. The differential case drives the actuator housings. The actuator housings drive the pinion shafts which impart a side load to the actuator housings. This side load compresses the clutch pack partially locking the side gear to the differential case housing.

The Limited Slip Differential is now capable of sending up to 72% of the input torque to one wheel if needed. When the machine is in normal straight forward or reverse the limited slip differential provides 50% of the input torque at each wheel. When wheel slip occurs, torque at the non-slipping wheel is 2.6 times the torque at the slipping wheel.

lessons.title: Differential Lock
lessons.objective: This segment introduces Differential Lock including applications and operation.
pages: Without a differential lock, when a drive wheel is in poor underfoot conditions and cannot develop traction, it will spin freely while the other wheel is stationary. Forward machine motion is stopped when this occurs. A differential lock locks the differential, preventing differential action, and forces both wheels to rotate together at the same speed. There are two types of differential lock systems. The jaw clutch differential lock system is activated by a foot pedal. The multi-disc differential lock system is activated by the differential lock switch in the operator's cab.

The jaw clutch lets the differential engage or release while the vehicle is under power and when the wheels are rotating at the same speed. The operator chooses when to engage the jaw clutch. An example of such a need is; when one wheel starts to spin. Machine speed should be reduced prior to engaging the clutches if wheels are turning at different speeds.

The differential lock pedal engages the jaw clutch which locks the axle shaft to the differential case, both wheels are locked together and forced to rotate at the same speed. Jaw clutch activation can be either mechanical or pneumatic.

The multi-disc differential lock lets the differential engage or release while the vehicle is under full power independent of wheel spin. The operator chooses when to engage the differential lock. An example of such a need is; when one wheel starts to spin. Machine speed does not need to be reduced prior to engaging the differential lock if wheels are turning at different speeds.

The differential lock switch pressurizes the multi-disc differential lock which locks the differential side gear to the differential case. Both wheels are locked together and forced to rotate at the same speed.
Differential lock is available on many Caterpillar machines, such as; Wheel Tractor-Scrapers, Backhoe Loaders, Motor Graders, Articulated Trucks and Log Skidders.
Operation of the jaw clutch differential lock and multi-disc differential lock will be covered.

When the differential lock switch is activated, pressurized oil forces the piston against the clutch pack, locking the side gear to the differential case. The pinions cannot move in relation to the differential housing. This gives the same effect as one solid axle drive.

When the switch is turned off the multi-disc clutch pack is released and the side gear is free to turn.

lessons.title: Traction Control System for Wheel Loaders
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the Traction Control System for wheel loaders including applications and operation.
pages: The Traction Control System (TCS) is an automatic four wheel drive traction aid system that transfers torque to the wheel with the best traction when a tire slips. P

The TCS collects information from four wheel speed sensors and an articulation sensor to determine the wheel speed ratio required to behave like open differentials while the machine is turning. When tire slip occurs, TCS applies the service brake to the slipping tire(s) transferring torque to the tire(s) on more solid footing. The system only provides traction assistance when needed because it only reacts when wheel slip occurs. The TCS provides information which is displayed by the machine monitoring system, to aid in problem diagnosis. The main electrical and hydraulic components of the TCS are covered.

The TCS electrical components provide input to the Electronic Control Module (ECM) so that the ECM can process the information and provide a corresponding response through the outputs. Electrical components also respond to the ECM's output to create action or provide information.

The ECM makes decisions based on input and memory information, then the corresponding response is made through the outputs. The inputs and outputs of the control are joined to the machine harness by a 40 contact ECM connector.

The TCS Test Enable/Off/Enable is a three position system power switch. It is an input to the TCS control. The purpose of this switch is to turn TCS ON or OFF and tell the control in which setting (high or low gain) to operate. The switch is located in the operator's compartment on the right console.

The TCS display is located in the operator's compartment. This display is equipped with five alert indicators. Four of these indicators are used to show when a brake is being applied and to which wheel the brake is being applied. The fifth indicator is a power ON indicator and will light when the TCS Test/ Enable switch and the display power switch are both in the ON position.

A wheel speed sensor is mounted in the axle housing at each axle and provides input signals to the TCS control when the TCS is enabled. The purpose of the wheel speed sensors is to let the ECM know the individual wheel speeds.

The articulation angle position sensor is mounted at the machine's articulation center. The ECM uses input from this sensor to determine the correct speed ratio between the left and right side wheels.

The option code plug connects to the harness code inputs of the TCS control. The purpose of the options code plug is to tell the TCS control, the module characteristics of the machine it is installed on.
The hydraulic components of the TCS system control the hydraulic application and release of the brakes based on information from the electrical system.

The function of the accumulator charging valve is to keep the hydraulic brake pressure in the accumulators at a constant range while the engine is running. The charging valve also holds a lower level of pressure for the TCS.
The On/Off Valve will allow oil under pressure to be supplied to four proportional brake control valves.

A pressure control valve is used at each individual wheel brake to apply pressure to that brake when the valve is supplied with hydraulic pressure and the solenoid has an electrical current signal supplied to it.
The pressure reducing valve governs pressure supplied to the On/Off pilot valve, by balancing a force created by the input pressure from the pump line, with a spring inside the valve cartridge.

The shuttle valves are located in the TCS manifold. The shuttle valves are ball checks that receive inputs from the service brake system and from the four proportional valves. There is one shuttle check valve for each brake. The shuttle check valve uses the higher system pressure (from the TCS or the service brake) to shut off the other and apply the wheel brake.

The Traction Control System operates like a standard differential and uses the brakes to provide traction assist. It is equally suited for straight ahead or turning applications in good and poor underfoot conditions.

Speed sensors at each axle read the individual wheel speeds. These wheel speed signals are sent back to the ECM. The signals are measured by the ECM which determines if there is unwanted wheel slippage by comparing wheel speeds as well as the angle at which the machine is being steered. The ECM compares these wheel speeds from side to side. The desired speeds are calculated by the ECM and compared with the actual wheel speed. When the actual wheel speed exceeds the desired speed an electrical signal is sent to the proportional solenoid brake valve for that wheel and the actual wheel speed is brought back to the desired speed by applying the brake at that wheel.

lessons.title: Automatic Electronic Traction Aid (AETA)
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the Automatic Electronic Traction Aid (AETA) for off-highway trucks including applications and operation.
pages:
The Automatic Electronic Traction Aid (AETA) is used to improve traction at the drive wheels. If either drive wheel starts to spin (lose traction), the AETA can increase power to the wheel that has better traction. This is done by applying the parking brake of the wheel that has the loss of traction. The AETA is functional at ground speeds under 12 mph.

The components of the AETA system are the control box, hydraulic control valve, selector solenoid valve, proportional solenoid valve, speed sensors, brake and retarder switches and the transmission speed distributor.

The control box is located in the cab behind the operator's seat on smaller trucks and behind the buddy seat in larger trucks. The control box processes signals from the speed sensors and sends signals to the hydraulic controls to select the spinning wheel and apply that wheel's parking brake. The AETA has many self checks to help locate problems. These are in the form of lamps on the front of the AETA control box.

The hydraulic control valve is located on the inside of the left or right frame rails. The exact location varies from model to model, but the valve is near the transmission. The hydraulic control valve contains two reducing spools which control the left and right parking brake release flow.

The selector solenoid valve is mounted on the hydraulic control valve. The valve receives electrical signals from the control box, which causes it to shift and select either the left or right parking brake. When the selector solenoid valve is shifted, it drains control oil and allows a reducing spool to shift and apply the parking brake.

The proportional solenoid valve is mounted on the hydraulic control valve. The valve controls the volume of oil being drained from the selected parking brake control circuit. Proportional solenoid valve oil flow is controlled by an electrical signal from the control box.

There are three speed sensors. One is located at each of the drive wheels and one at the transmission output shaft. These speed sensors monitor rotational speeds and send electrical pulse signals to the control box. P
These air switches are located at the rear of the operator's compartment behind an access panel. The switches disable the AETA whenever the vehicle is moving and the brakes or retarder are activated.

The transmission speed distributor is located at the rear of the operator's compartment under an access cover on smaller trucks and inside the center console in the operator's compartment under an access panel on larger trucks. The transmission speed distributor will take signals from the transmission speed pickup and change them to a signal the AETA control box and speedometer can use.

The AETA system uses the rear parking brakes (spring engaged and hydraulically released) to decrease the revolutions of a spinning wheel. AETA allows the tire with better underfoot conditions to develop an increased amount of torque. The controls for the system are contained in the AETA control box.

The AETA Control Box monitors the drive wheels through three input signals: one at each drive axle, and one at the transmission output shaft. When a spinning drive wheel is detected, the sensors at the drive wheels and transmission output shaft send a signal to the control box.

The control box processes the signal from the sensors and sends a signal to the selector and proportional valves which in turn engage the brake of the affected wheel. When the condition has improved, and the ratio between the right and left axle returns to 1:1, the control box sends a signal to release the brake.

topics.title: Lower Drivetrain Systems
topics.summary: This topic describes lower drivetrain systems and discusses their features, benefits and applications.

lessons.title: Introduction to Lower Drivetrain Systems
lessons.objective: This segment explains the lower drivetrain systems used in Caterpillar track-type machines.
pages: The purpose of the lower drivetrain system in track-type machines is to transfer power from the transmission out to the tracks, steer and stop the machine, and provide a final gear reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. The track-type machines are equipped with two types of lower drivetrain systems; the "Steering Clutch" system and the "Differential Steer" system, and will be discussed separately, including component identification and operation.

Power is transferred from the transmission output shaft to the transfer gears. The bevel gear set receives power from the pinion gear, turns it 90 degrees and transmits it through the axle shafts to the steering clutches and brakes.

A track-type machine is steered by causing one track to turn faster than the other. In the Steering Clutch system, a steering clutch interrupts the power flow to one of the tracks. In the Differential Steer system, the steering differential uses hydraulic motor power input to increase the speed of one track and equally decrease the speed of the other track.

The lower drivetrain includes the service brakes to slow or stop the machine. In the Steering Clutch system, the brakes are part of the steering clutch assembly and also assist in turning the machine. In the Differential Steer system, the brakes are part of the steering differential group on the left side of the tractor and the planetary group on the right side of the tractor. The brakes do not assist in turning the tractor with the Differential Steer system.
The final drives provide the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. The final drives can be bull gears or planetary gear sets. P

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment describes the features and benefits of lower drivetrain systems.
pages: The Steering Clutch system in elevated sprocket track-type tractors has certain features and benefits for dependable performance.
A feature of Caterpillar elevated sprocket track-type tractors is modular design final drives.
The benefit is that this greatly reduces removal time.
A feature of Caterpillar elevated sprocket track-type tractors is the elevated sprocket design.
The benefit is that this isolates the final drives from ground impact and blade induced loads for long service life.
A feature of the steering clutches and brakes is that they are multiple disc and oil cooled.
The benefit is that they provide high load carrying capability and long life. They require no adjustment and are enclosed from contaminants.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment covers applications of lower drivetrain systems used in Caterpillar products.
pages: The Steering Clutch System and the Differential Steer System are the types of lower drivetrain systems used on Track-Type Tractors, Track Loaders and Challenger Agricultural Tractors.
The Steering Clutch system is found on Track-Type Tractors and Small Track-Type Loaders.
The Differential Steer system is available on some Track-Type Tractors and standard on Challenger Agricultural Tractors.

topics.title: Steering Clutch System Components
topics.summary: This topic describes the Steering Clutch system components.

lessons.title: Steering Clutch
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the steering clutch.
pages: The steering clutches transfer power from the bevel gears to the final drives and turn the machine. They are hydraulically engaged. The main components of the steering clutches are the clutch plates, clutch discs, clutch piston, clutch housing, input hub and output hub.
The clutch discs turn with the input hub and are forced against the clutch plates to transmit power to the clutch housing. The discs are splined to the input hub and typically oil cooled.

The clutch plates are splined to the clutch housing and turn the clutch housing when the clutch discs are forced against the plates by the piston. Power is then transmitted to the output hub through the clutch housing.

The piston pushes the discs and plates together to connect the input hub to the clutch housing. Hydraulic oil is used to move the piston. When oil pressure drops, spring pressure retracts the piston and the input hub disengages from the clutch housing.

The clutch housing is splined to the output hub and turns the output hub when the discs and clutches are engaged. The plates are splined to the internal teeth of the clutch housing. The discs are splined to the input hub. P
The input hub transfers power from the inner axle shaft to the clutch housing. It is splined to the inner axle shaft and the clutch discs.
The output hub transfers power from the clutch housing to the outer axle shaft. It is splined to the clutch housing and outer axle shaft.

lessons.title: Brakes
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the brake components used in the Steering Clutch system.
pages: The brakes are typically oil-cooled multiple disc, spring applied and hydraulically released. The brakes slow or stop the machine and assist in turning. The main components of the service brakes are the Belleville spring, brake plates, brake discs, brake piston and brake housing.

The Belleville spring(s) force the piston to engage the brakes. A brake module is equipped with one or two Belleville springs depending on the tractor model. Hydraulic pressure is used to release the brakes.

The brake plates are splined to the brake housing which is stationary. When the brake discs are forced against the plates by the piston, the clutch housing slows or stops. The clutch housing then holds the output hub and the outer axle shaft stationary. P

The brake discs are splined to the clutch housing and rotate with it. When the brake discs are forced against the plates by the piston, the clutch housing slows or stops. The clutch housing then holds the output hub and the outer axle shaft stationary.

The piston forces the discs and plates together to slow or stop the clutch housing. Belleville springs are used to push the piston against the discs and plates. The piston is retracted by hydraulic pressure.

The brake housing is bolted to the spindle housing and remains stationary. It contains the discs, plates and pistons. When the brakes are engaged, the clutch housing is locked to the brake housing to slow or stop the tractor.

lessons.title: Bevel Gear Set
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the bevel gear set.
pages: The bevel gear set consists of the bevel pinion shaft and bevel ring gear. The bevel gear set receives power from the transfer gear, turns it 90 degrees and transmits it to the steering clutches.

The pinion shaft is splined to the transfer gears at one end. The other end intersects with the ring gear at a 90 degree angle. The pinion shaft turns the ring gear which sends power through the inner axle shafts to the steering clutches. Pinion shaft teeth are tapered in thickness and height.

The ring gear is bolted to the ring gear shaft and driven by the pinion shaft. The ring gear shaft is supported by roller bearings and connects to the inner axle shafts which transmit power to the steering clutches. Like the pinion shaft, the ring gear has tapered teeth to mate with the pinion.

lessons.title: Planetary Final Drives
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the planetary final drives.
pages: The planetary gears provide the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. The main components are the sun gear, ring gear and a planetary gear set. The planetary final drive gears transmit power from the steering clutches to drive the tracks.
The sun gear is located at the outboard end of the axle shaft. The sun gear transfers power from the steering clutches and axles to the planet gears.

The ring gear is fastened to the hub of the spindle housing and does not rotate. Unlike most gears, the ring gear has internal teeth. The ring gear mates with the planet gears and allows the planet gears, which are driven by the sun gear, to walk around the ring gear.

The planetary gear set consists of three or more planet gears mounted in a carrier. The carrier is bolted to the sprocket hub. The planetary gears are driven by the sun gear and revolve around the inside of the ring gear transmitting power through the carrier to the sprocket hub.

lessons.title: Bull Gear Final Drives
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the bull gear final drives.
pages: The bull gear final drive provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of a pinion gear and bull gear.

The pinion gear mates with the bull gear. The pinion gear receives power from the steering clutches through the outer axle shaft. The pinion gear turns the bull gear, which is much larger, causing a speed reduction and torque increase.
The bull gear teeth intersect with the pinion gear. The bull gear is turned by the pinion and transmits power through the axle shaft to the sprocket which drives the track.

lessons.title: Shafts
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the shafts used in the Steering Clutch system.
pages: The axle shafts transfer power from the bevel gear set to the steering clutches and from the steering clutches to the final drives. There are two inner and two outer axle shafts in the Steering Clutch System.
The inner axle shafts transfer power from the bevel gear set to the steering clutches on both sides of the machine. They are splined to the bevel ring gear shaft and steering clutch input hub.
The outer axle shafts transfer power from the steering clutches to the final drives through the sun gear on both sides of the machine.

topics.title: Steering Clutch System Operation
topics.summary: In this topic Steering Clutch System power flow is explained.

lessons.title: Steering Clutch Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment explains the power flow through the Steering Clutch system as it is transmitted through the bevel gear set, steering clutches and brakes, and the final drives.
pages: The bevel gear set receives power from the transmission and transmits it to the steering clutches.

Power from the transmission is transferred to the bevel gear set through the transfer gear. The transfer gear is splined to the bevel pinion. The bevel pinion is turned by the transmission output shaft and transmits power to the bevel gear. The bevel gear is bolted to the bevel gear shaft. As the bevel gear turns, it transmits power through the bevel gear shaft. The bevel gear shaft is splined to the inner axle shafts. The bevel gear shaft turns the axle shafts, sending power to the steering clutches.

The power flow through the steering clutches will be explained as follows:

• Basic power flow

• Power flow during straight movement of the machine

• Power flow during a gradual turn

• Power flow during a sharp turn

• Power flow when brakes are applied

During straight movement of the machine, oil pressure is sent to the brake pressure chamber and clutch pressure chamber through internal passages. This oil pressure holds the brakes in the released position and holds the steering clutches in the engaged position. When power from the bevel gear is sent through the inner axle shaft to the input hub, the clutch housing turns the output hub and the outer axle shaft sends power to the sun gear and final drives.
The final drives receive power from the steering clutches and transmit it to the sprockets and tracks. Power flow in the planetary final drives and bull gear final drives will be covered.

topics.title: Differential Steer System Components
topics.summary: This topic describes the Differential Steer system components.

lessons.title: Steering Motor and Pump
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the steering motor and steering pump.
pages: In the Differential Steer System, the steering motor controls the turning direction of the machine and the pump provides the oil flow to operate the steering motor.

The steering motor is a fixed displacement, bent-axis piston motor that controls the turning direction of the machine. It is operated by oil pressure from the variable displacement piston pump. A change in the direction of oil flow through the motor will not change the amount of output torque from the shaft of the motor.

There are two types of steering pumps. One is a variable displacement over center axial piston pump, the other is a hydrostatic pump. Both pumps are fastened to the transmission pump drive which uses power from the engine to turn the input shaft. The pump provides the oil flow to operate the steering motor.

lessons.title: Steering Planetary Gear Sets
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the steering planetary gear sets.
pages: There are three planetary gear sets in the Differential Steer System. They are often referred to as the "steer planetary," the "drive planetary," and the "equalizing planetary." There are two power inputs to the planetary gear set. One of the power inputs is the pinion and bevel gear which are driven by the transmission output shaft through the transfer gears. The second input is a pinion which is driven by the steering motor. All three planetary gear sets are interconnected by a common shaft which connects the three sun gears.

The steer planetary is driven by the steering motor through a bevel pinion gear and bevel ring gear. It transmits the power for turning the tractor. The steer planetary components are the ring gear, sun gear, planet gears and carrier.

The drive planetary is driven by the transmission output shaft through the transfer gears, bevel pinion gear and bevel ring gear. It transmits the power for moving the tractor in forward or reverse directions. The drive planetary components are the ring gear, sun gear, planet gears and carrier. P

The equalizing planetary converts high speed low torque input into a lower speed higher torque output to the right final drive. The equalizing planetary components are the ring gear, sun gear, planet gears and carrier.

lessons.title: Brakes
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the brake components used in the Differential Steer system.
pages: The brakes are oil-cooled multiple disc, spring applied and hydraulically released. They are part of two different modules of the tractor. One module is the steering differential group installed on the left side of the tractor and the other module is the planetary group installed on the right side of the tractor. The brakes are used to stop the tractor and do not assist in turning. The main components of the brakes are the hub, pistons, retainer, Belleville springs, housings, discs and plates.

The brake hub is splined to the outer axle shaft on the left side of the tractor. It is also connected to the brake housing through plates and discs. The brake discs are splined to the hub. When the brakes are engaged, the hub is locked to the brake housing, slowing or stopping the tractor.

The piston forces the discs and plates together to slow or stop the brake hub and planet carrier. Belleville springs are used to push the piston against the discs and plates. The piston is retracted by hydraulic pressure.
The retainer is used on the left side brake group to retain the brake plates and discs. The brake plates and discs on the right side brake group are retained by the ring gear.

The Belleville spring(s) force the piston to engage the brakes. A brake module is equipped with one or two Belleville springs depending on the tractor model. Hydraulic pressure is used to release the brakes.

The brake housings are bolted to the spindle housings and remain stationary. They contain the discs, plates and pistons and provide the support needed to slow or stop the vehicle. When the brakes are engaged, the hub is locked to the brake housing to slow or stop the tractor.

The brake discs are splined to the brake hub and rotate with it. When the brake discs are forced against the plates by the piston, the brake hub slows or stops. The brake hub then hold the outer axle shafts stationary.

The brake plates are splined to the brake housings which are stationary. When the brake discs are forced against the plates by the piston, the brake hub slows or stops. The brake hub then holds the outer axle shafts stationary.

lessons.title: Steering and Transmission Bevel Gear Sets
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the steering bevel gear set and transmission bevel gear set.
pages: The steering gear set receives power from the steering motor to turn the vehicle. It consists of a pinion gear and ring gear.

The pinion gear is splined to the steering motor at one end. The other end intersects with the ring gear, attached to the steering differential, at a 90 degree angle. The pinion gear turns the ring gear which sends power through the steering differential. P
The ring gear is turned by the pinion gear, and attached to the steering differential housing. The ring gear transmits power through the steering differential.

The bevel gear set receives power from the transfer gear, turns it 90 degrees and transmits it to the differential. The transmission bevel gear set consists of the bevel pinion gear and bevel ring gear.

The pinion gear is splined to the transfer gear at one end. The other end intersects with the ring gear at a 90 degree angle. The pinion gear turns the ring gear which sends power through the steering differential. Bevel gear teeth are tapered in thickness and height.

The ring gear is turned by the pinion gear and attached to the ring gear shaft. The ring gear transmits power through the ring gear shaft to the steering differential. Like the pinion gear, the ring gear has tapered teeth to intersect with the pinion gear.

lessons.title: Planetary Final Drives
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the planetary final drives.
pages: The planetary gears provide the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. The main components are the sun gear, ring gear and a planetary gear set. The planetary final drive gears transmit power from the steering differential to drive the tracks.
The sun gear is splined to the outer axle shaft. The sun gear transfers power from the steering differential and center axle to the planet gears.

The ring gear is fastened to the hub of the spindle housing and does not rotate. Unlike most gears, the ring gear has internal teeth. The ring gear mates with the planet gears and allows the planet gears, which are driven by the sun gear, to walk around the ring gear.

The planetary gear set consists of three or more planet gears mounted in a carrier. The carrier is bolted to the sprocket hub. The planetary gears are driven by the sun gear and revolve around the inside of the ring gear transmitting power through the carrier to the sprocket hub.

lessons.title: Bull Gear Final Drives
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the components used in the bull gear final drives.
pages: The bull gear final drive provides the last speed reduction and torque increase in the drivetrain. It consists of a pinion gear and bull gear.

The pinion mates with the bull gear. The pinion gear receives power from the steering differential through the center axle shaft. The pinion gear turns the bull gear, which is much larger, causing a speed reduction and torque increase.
The bull gear teeth intersect with the pinion gear. The bull gear is turned by the pinion and transmits power through the axle shaft to the sprocket which drives the track.

lessons.title: Shafts
lessons.objective: This segment discusses the shafts used in the Differential Steer system.
pages: The axle shafts transfer power from the bevel gear set through the steering differential to the final drives. There are two outer axle shafts and a center axle shaft in the Differential Steer System.
The outer axle shafts transfer power from the steering differential to the final drives on both sides of the machine. They are splined to the planet carriers and sun gear.
The center axle shaft is splined to the sun gears of all three planetary gear sets. It transfers power through the steering differential to the outer axle shafts.

topics.title: Differential Steer System Operation
topics.summary: In this topic Differential Steer system basic operation and power flow are explained.

lessons.title: Basic Operation
lessons.objective: This segment covers basic operation of the Differential Steer system.
pages: Basic operation of the Differential Steer system will be explained as the tractor is traveling straight, turning and when the transmission is in neutral. A differential steer demonstrator will be used. P

Let's go through an operational explanation. The operator uses a steering tiller with a twist grip to control the tractor. You twist for forward, neutral, and reverse and point the tiller in the direction you wish to steer. When operating straight ahead, the tiller would be in the forward detent and centered. The drive planetary of the steering differential receives power only from the transmission. The steering motor is not activated and the gears driven by it are stopped. The sprockets are both going in the same direction at the same speed.

When making a turn the differential receives two inputs. Still one from the transmission and now another one from the steering motor. The direction the motor rotates, determines the direction you turn. For a left turn, the steering motor turns one way, speeding up the right side while slowing down the left. For a right turn, the steering motor turns the other way, causing the left track to speed up and the right track to slow down.

When the transmission is in neutral, you are still able to turn the tractor because of the speed change generated by the steering motor. As you can see the sprockets are going in opposite directions. Counter rotation is beneficial for maneuvering in tight quarters and for changing your heading during directional shifts.

lessons.title: Differential Steer Power Flow
lessons.objective: This segment explains the power flow through the Differential Steer system as it is transmitted through the steering differential and the final drives.
pages:
With the steering pinion and bevel ring gear in the hold position, power from the transmission goes through the transmission pinion to the bevel ring gear. The bevel ring gear transmits the power through the bevel gear shaft to the carrier. Power through the carrier goes in two directions. Most of the power goes through the planet gears to the ring gear and the rest of the power goes through the planet gears to the sun gear. The ring gear sends the power through the carrier to the outer axle shaft. The sun gear sends its power through the center axle shaft to the sun gear. The sun gear, planet gears, carrier and stationary ring gear multiply the power and send it to the outer axle.

Power to both outer axles is the same and the direction of axle rotation is the same. This results in the tractor moving straight ahead or straight backward.

With the transmission in NEUTRAL, power from the steering motor goes through the steering pinion to the bevel ring gear. The bevel ring gear sends power through the housing, ring gear and the planet gears to the carrier. Power through the carrier goes in two directions. Half of the power goes through the planet gears to the sun gear, and half of the power goes to the outer axle shaft. The sun gear sends its power through the center axle shaft to the sun gear. The sun gear, planet gears, carrier and stationary ring gear multiply the power and send it to the outer axle shaft.

Power to both outer axle shafts is the same but the direction of axle rotation is opposite. This results in the tractor rotating about its own center.

When power from the steering motor and transmission act together on the differential steering system, power from the transmission input flows through the system the same as when it acts individually. The steering input power, rather than going in two directions, now goes one direction or the other through the system. A left turn will be used to animate the power flow.

This results in the power to one axle shaft being greater which causes the speed of that axle shaft to increase and the other axle shaft to equally decrease its speed. The amount of power to the axle shafts and their rotation is controlled by the transmission. The amount of speed difference between the axle shafts and the direction of the turn are controlled by the steering motor. Rotation of the steering motor and steering pinion controls which way the tractor turns. The speed of the motor and pinion determines how sharp or gradual the tractor turns. 

When the tractor makes a left turn, the rotation of the steering pinion and transmission pinion are in the same direction. Power to the steering pinion goes through the bevel gear and housing to the ring gear. The ring gear sends the power through the planet gears to the sun gear. The steering planetary sun gear sends power to the center axle shaft adding power to the drive planetary sun gear. The combined power through the center axle shaft goes to the equalizing planetary sun gear. The sun gear, planet gears, carrier and stationary ring gear multiply the power and send it to the outer axle shaft. This causes the outer axle shaft to increase its speed. As with any differential, when one side speeds up, the other side slows down an equal amount. This is accomplished when the power to the steering planetary sun gear adds to the power at the drive planetary sun gear. The increase in power causes the speed of the sun gears to increase. When the speed of the drive planetary sun gear increases, the speed of the ring gear decreases. The decrease in the speed of the ring gear causes the carrier to decrease its speed as well as the speed of the outer axle shaft. The resulting speed difference between outer axle shafts causes the tractor to turn left.
The final drives receive power from the steering differential and transmit it to the sprockets and tracks. Power flow in the planetary final drives and bull gear final drives will be covered.

topics.title: Hydrostatic Drive Systems
topics.summary: This topic describes the Hydrostatic Drive System, its features and benefits, and the applications of Hydrostatic Drive Systems.

lessons.title: What Is a Hydrostatic Drive?
lessons.objective: This segment describes a Hydrostatic Drive System.
pages:
A Hydrostatic Drive system is a closed loop hydraulic system which provides infinitely variable travel speeds.

The Hydrostatic Drive system consists of pump(s), lines, motors, control valves and a reservoir tank.

The major differences between a hydraulic drive system and a hydrostatic drive system are:

• In Hydrostatic Drive systems the direction of flow from the pump determines the direction (forward/reverse) of machine travel.

• The return oil from the motors in a hydrostatic drive system returns to the pump(s) (closed loop). In a hydraulic drive system the return oil goes through the control valves back to the tank (not closed loop).

A hydrostatic drive system is a closed loop hydraulic system that converts mechanical power to hydraulic power and then converts the hydraulic power back to mechanical power to move the machine. The hydraulic oil flows from the pump to the motor and then back to the pump. Control valves direct the action of the pumps and direction of oil flow. Excess oil not needed by the system flows through an oil cooler and back to the reservoir tank.

The required basic components of a hydrostatic drive system are:

• A variable displacement piston pump,
• Two hydraulic lines (used for forward and reverse),
• Control Valves,
• A drive motor.

These components make up a basic single hydrostatic "Drive Loop". A complete drive system may require two or more drive loops.

The drive loop changes the mechanical power to hydraulic power and then changes the hydraulic power back into mechanical power to drive a load. The mechanical power, provided by the engine, is changed to hydraulic power (flow) by the variable displacement piston pump. The rate and direction of flow is determined by a swashplate inside the pump. The pump delivers varied rates of flow to the drive motor, through the hydraulic lines. The motor drives the machine in either forward or reverse. The direction of flow from the pump determines the direction of machine movement. In the case of a wheeled machine such as a vibratory compactor, the motors can drive the rear axle and the drum to propel the machine.

The pressure in the drive line is determined by the load on the drive motor. If the load on the motor increases, the pressure in the drive line increases. The drive line providing the flow to the motor is referred to as the "high pressure side" of the drive loop. The drive line providing the path for the return oil from the motor to the pump is referred to as the "low pressure side" of the drive loop.

Other components in a hydrostatic drive system include:

• Charge Pump (1) - which supplies oil to the propel pump and provides makeup oil to the system.

• Charge Pressure Relief Valve (2) - which limits charge system pressure.

• Crossover and Main Relief Valve (3) - which limits maximum pressure in the high side of the drive loop, and during high pressure spikes transfers oil from the high pressure side of the drive loop to the low pressure side.

• Low Pressure Charge Relief Valve (4) - which limits return loop pressure, sends some oil to the case drain circuit for cooling and lubrication.

• Shuttle Valve (5) - which directs the low pressure side of the drive loop to the low pressure charge relief valve

• Flushing Valve - (some systems use a flushing valve in place of the low pressure charge relief and the shuttle valve) which directs the low pressure side of the drive loop to the low pressure charge relief valve which limits return loop pressure and sends some oil to case drain for cooling and lubrication.

and

• Flow Divider Valve (6) - (if equipped) which divides the oil flow between the front and rear drives. This valve is only used on systems that have one pump for both the front and rear drives.

During normal operation, the low pressure side of the drive loop does not require all the flow provided by the charge pump. Most of the oil from the low pressure side is sent through the charge relief valve to the transmission oil cooler. The cooler reduces the temperature of the oil before it returns to the tank.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment explains the different features and benefits of the Hydrostatic Drive systems used in Caterpillar machines today.
pages: The following are some of the features and benefits of a Hydrostatic Drive system.
Which of the following is not a basic component of the Planeta
A feature of the Hydrostatic Drive system is hydrostatic pumps.
The benefit is that they provide infinitely variable speed ranges.
A feature of the Hydrostatic Drive system is the drum drive units on vibratory compactors which have a patented hydraulic flow divider valve (CS-323) or a dual pump circuit arrangement.
The benefit is that this increases the machines ability to maneuver in a wide variety of soil types and conditions and improves gradeability.
A feature of the Hydrostatic Drive system is the direct hydrostatic drive to both drums on dual drum vibratory asphalt compactors.
The benefit is that this provides dependable, responsive propulsion effort and maximum gradeability.
A feature of the Hydrostatic Drive system is the hydrostatic drivetrain on Track Loaders.
The benefit is that this offers independent control of each track, infinitely variable speeds, fast acceleration and counter-rotation for increased production.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment details the different applications of Hydrostatic Drive systems.
pages: A number of Caterpillar machines use a hydrostatic drive system for machine travel. The basic principles of hydrostatic drive (closed loop, variable speed) apply to all hydrostatic drives.

The biggest difference will be found in the location and function of the components that make-up the hydrostatic drive system. For example, a hydrostatic drive system may have one pump with the flow divided between the motors or the system may have two or more pumps one for each drive motor. One kind of system uses a Hydrostatic Power Control Unit (HPCU) which is a complex hydrostatic drive system with the pumps and controls contained in one unit. 

No matter which type of hydrostatic drive system the machine has, always refer to the appropriate service manuals for the machine being serviced.

topics.title: Hydrostatic Drive Components
topics.summary: This topic introduces the identification, function and location of the major components that make-up the Hydrostatic Drive System.

lessons.title: Variable Displacement Pump
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification and function of the major components that make-up the variable displacement hydraulic piston pump.
pages: Hydraulics perform many different functions on Caterpillar machines. The main component of any hydraulic system including hydrostatic drives is the pump. Without the flow delivered by the pump, a hydrostatic drive cannot function. The pumps are axial piston slipper design and are driven by the engine. The major components of the pump are the pistons, barrel, swashplate, retraction plate, servo piston and port plate.

The driveshaft is connected to the cylinder barrel. As it turns, the pistons move back and forth in the cylinder because they're connected to the swashplate. As the piston retracts it pulls oil into the cylinder through the inlet port, and then ejects it on the downstroke through the outlet port.

The amount of oil pumped depends on the angle of the swashplate.

The pump contains a swashplate that has a wear plate on which the piston slippers ride. The swashplate does not turn with the rotating group. The angle of the swashplate determines the amount of flow supplied to the system. The pistons will move in and out of the barrel as the drive shaft, barrel and pistons turn anytime the swashplate is not at zero angle. The in and out movement is the result of the piston slippers following the angle of the swashplate. The greater the angle of the swashplate, the farther the pistons move in and out of the barrel.
Each pump contains a retraction plate that keeps the piston slippers down on the wear surface of the swashplate.

Movement of the control lever moves the servo control spool. The spool routes charge oil to activate and adjust the servo piston. As the charge oil moves the servo piston, the angle of the swashplate changes. This changes the amount of oil flow from the pump.
Each pump has a port plate that rides on top of the barrel and does not turn. The port plate helps the hydraulic oil flow smoothly in and out of the pump.

lessons.title: Drive Motor
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification and function of the major components that make-up the hydraulic drive motor.
pages: The propel motor is a bi-directional, piston motor. Some motors use a two position servo control to provide two travel speeds. The major components of the motor are the pistons, barrel, port plate, servo piston assembly and swashplate.

The pistons are installed and housed in the barrel. As hydraulic oil under high pressure enters the barrel through the port plate, it pushes the piston out of its bore. The force of the oil pushes the piston against the swashplate. The piston reacts by trying to reach maximum outward stroke. Since the swashplate is at an angle, the piston will start to move along the swashplate. This movement causes the barrel, and output shaft, to rotate.

The barrel houses the pistons and is splined to the output shaft. As the pistons in the barrel cause the barrel to rotate, the output shaft also rotates converting the hydraulic power back to mechanical power.

The swashplate is connected by a pin to the servo piston assembly and does not rotate. The pistons that are housed in the barrel react against the swashplate causing the barrel to turn. The servo piston assembly controls swashplate angle. Two-speed motors can operate either at maximum displacement (low speed) or at minimum displacement (high speed).
Each motor has a port plate that rides on top of the barrel and does not turn. The port plate helps the hydraulic oil flow smoothly in and out of the motor.
Two-speed motors use a servo piston assembly to change the operating angle of the swashplate. The assembly is controlled by the pump charge pressure through the speed shift control valve. P

lessons.title: Motor Flush Valve
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the flushing or motor flush valve.
pages: The motor flush valve is located in the drive motor of the propel closed loop circuit. The direction of tilt of the pump swashplate, either FORWARD or REVERSE operation, determines direction of flow in the loop. Direction of flow in the loop determines whether a line is high pressure or low pressure. The motor flush valve operates on whichever line of the drive loop is acting as the low pressure line of the loop.

Pilot pressure on the high pressure side shifts the spring-centered crossover shuttle check valve. The low pressure side opens to the low pressure relief valve. The low pressure relief valve allows charge pressure oil and flow to a flush port to the motor case. This oil cools and flushes the motor and pump.

lessons.title: Charge Pump
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the charge pump. Its identification and function are included.
pages: The charge pump is used to provide make-up oil to the drive loop. This make up oil is needed due to normal leakage in the drive loop and is used to lubricate the pump and motor components.
The charge pump is a fixed displacement pump. The pump is usually bolted directly to the propel pump.

Two matched gears rotate inside a housing producing hydraulic flow. The drive gear is driven at engine speed and turns the driven gear. Oil is drawn through the inlet and is forced through the outlet to the system.
The inlet and outlet may be externally attached hoses to carry the oil to and from the pump, or internal passages in the pump housing.
