This is a typical hydrostatic drive system used by Caterpillar today. Always refer to the appropriate service manual for the specific machine you are working on.

The driveshaft is connected to the cylinder barrel. As it turns, the pistons move back and forth in the cylinder because they're connected to the swashplate. As the piston retracts it pulls oil into the cylinder through the inlet port, and then ejects it on the downstroke through the outlet port.

The amount of oil pumped depends on the angle of the swashplate.

lessons.title: Crossover and Main Relief Valve
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the operation and power flow through the crossover and main relief valve that is used in a hydrostatic drive system.
pages: The crossover and main relief valves protect the propel system from excessive high pressure spikes.

lessons.title: Charge Relief Valves
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the operation and power flow through the charge relief valves that are used in a hydrostatic drive system.
pages: The propel pumps have a charge relief valve. The charge relief valve is located in the pump housing.

Charge oil enters the pump through the charge circuit oil line. When the system is in NEUTRAL the charge relief valve regulates system pressure. When the charge relief valve opens, excess oil goes to the hydraulic oil tank.

lessons.title: Motor Flush Valve
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the operation and power flow of the motor flush valve that is used in a hydrostatic drive system.
pages: On models using the motor flush valve, the valve is located in both the drum motor and axle motor of the propel closed loop circuits. P

lessons.title: Axle Propel Motor
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the operation and power flow of the axle propel motor that is used in a hydrostatic drive system.
pages: The hydraulic oil in the main circuit of the propel system flows in a continuous closed loop from the propel pump. The direction of the hydraulic flow in the circuit, and the direction the motor turns, is determined by the direction the pump swashplate is tilted from the NEUTRAL position (FORWARD or REVERSE operation). The speed of the motor is determined by the volume of hydraulic oil supplied by the pump.

High pressure oil enters the motor through one of the drive loop lines (1). Oil flows through the port plate (2) to the pistons (3) in the barrel (4). The force of the oil pushes the piston against the swashplate (5). The piston reacts by trying to reach maximum outward stroke. Since the swashplate is at an angle, the piston will start to move along the swashplate. This movement causes the barrel and output shaft (6) to rotate.

lessons.title: Safety Warnings Before Service
lessons.objective: This segment contains the warnings that should be read and observed before any hydrostatic drive system service is performed. Also included are the first steps that should be done before any other service is started.
pages: Before performing any testing or troubleshooting procedures on any Caterpillar machine, always refer to the appropriate service manual for the machine being serviced. Contact the Technical Communicator (TC) at your Caterpillar Dealer for the latest specifications and procedures.

When the oil in the system gets hot, it causes the air to expand and build up pressure in the system. This pressure can remain in the system after the engine and pumps are stopped. Personal injury can be caused if this pressure is not released before any service is done on the drive system. To prevent possible injury, remove the cap from the oil filler tube before any fitting, hose or component on the drive system is loosened, tightened, removed or adjusted. 

The cap must be replaced when the testing is completed. The bucket and other implements must always be flat on the ground before service is started. When it is necessary for an implement to be raised while tests and adjustments are being done, be sure to have the correct support. In the case of the bucket, it must be in the FULL DUMP position. Always move the machine to a location away from the travel of other machines. Always wear the seat belt, and be sure that other personnel are not near the machine when the engine is running and tests or adjustments are being made.

The following are the tests available to help in diagnosis of a Hydrostatic Drive system:

• Zero Pump Angle Check
• Charge Relief Valve Pressure Check
• Crossover Relief Valve Check
• Low Pressure Charge Relief Valve Check

topics.title: Hydraulic Drive Systems
topics.summary: This topic describes what a Hydraulic Drive system is, what the features and benefits of a Hydraulic Drive system are and the applications Hydraulic Drive systems are used for.

lessons.title: What Is a Hydraulic Drive?
lessons.objective: This segment provides a description of what a Hydraulic Drive System is including its function.
pages:
A hydraulic drive system is a hydraulic transfer of power from the engine to the tracks on certain Caterpillar machines. Unlike a conventional direct drive or powershift transmission, the hydraulic drive does not require steering clutches, bevel gears, pinions or similar mechanical drive components to control track movement on track-type machines.

The hydraulic drive consists of pumps, lines, motors, control valves and a reservoir tank.
The major difference between a hydraulic drive system and a hydrostatic drive system is that the return oil from the motors in a hydraulic drive system goes through the control valves back to the tank (this is not a closed loop system). In a hydrostatic system, return oil from the motors goes back to the pumps (in a closed loop), and excess oil not needed by the system returns to the tank.

A hydraulic drive system converts mechanical power to hydraulic power and then converts the hydraulic power back to mechanical power to move the machine. In a hydraulic drive system, the hydraulic oil flows from the pump to the motor and then back to the tank. Control valves direct where the oil flows.

The basic components of a hydraulic drive system are:

• Variable displacement piston pumps (1)

• Hydraulic lines (used for forward and reverse)

• Control valves (2)

• Fixed or variable displacement piston motors (3)

• Hydraulic oil reservoir (4)

The drive system changes mechanical power to hydraulic power and then changes the hydraulic power back into mechanical power to drive a load. The mechanical power, provided by the engine, is changed to hydraulic power (oil flow) at the variable displacement piston pump. The rate of flow is determined by a swashplate inside the piston pump. The piston pump delivers varied rates of flow to the control valves which direct oil to the motors driving the machine in either forward or reverse. The direction of flow from the control valve determines the direction of machine movement.

The pressure in the drive system is determined by the load on the drive motor. If the load on the motor increases, the pressure in the system increases. The hydraulic line providing the flow to the motor is referred to as the "high pressure side" of the drive system. The hydraulic line providing the path for the return oil from the motor to the tank is referred to as the "low pressure side" of the drive system.

lessons.title: Features and Benefits
lessons.objective: This segment explains the different features and benefits of the Hydraulic Drives used in Caterpillar machines today.
pages: The following are some of the features and benefits of hydraulic drive systems used on Caterpillar machines today.
A feature of the hydraulic drive system is independent, two-speed, axial-piston hydraulic motors (available on some models).
The benefit is that this provides infinitely variable speed ranges.
A feature of the hydraulic drive system is using existing hydraulics for machine movement.
The benefit is that this costs less (as opposed to a separate transmission system), and they have fewer components to wear.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.objective: This segment gives a brief listing of the different Caterpillar machines that use a Hydraulic Drive System.
pages: In the current Caterpillar product line, all hydraulic excavators use a hydraulic drive system for machine travel.

The hydraulic drive system used on these machines includes:

• Two hydraulic pumps - also used for other hydraulic systems (implement, swing etc.)

• Two drive motors - one for each track

• The drive motors on these hydraulic drive systems are two-position motors capable of two different speeds of travel.

lessons.title: Hydraulic Drive Components
lessons.objective: This segment introduces the identification, function and location of the major components that make-up the Hydraulic Drive.
pages: A component of the Hydraulic Drive system is a Variable Displacement Hydraulic Pump. This segment introduces the identification and function of the major components that make-up the Variable Displacement Hydraulic Pump.

Hydraulics perform many different functions on Caterpillar machines. The main component of any hydraulic system, including hydraulic drive systems is the pump. Without the flow delivered by the pump, a hydraulic drive cannot function. The pumps used in hydraulic excavators are variable displacement piston pumps. It should be noted that the valve plates used in pumps on current Caterpillar hydraulic drive systems perform the same function as the swashplates and port plates on other models.
The main pump in a hydraulic excavator consists of two pumps coupled in a housing. The pumps are identical in construction, operation and control.
The major components of the pump are the gear, pistons, barrel, valve plate, retraction plate and servo pistons.

Each pump contains a number of pistons. The pistons are installed and housed in the barrel.

As the barrel and pistons turn with the valve plate at an angle, the pistons will move in and out of the barrel. The in and out movement is the result of the piston slippers following the angle of the valve plate. The greater the angle of the valve plate, the farther the pistons move in and out of the barrel. As a piston moves out of the barrel, oil from the inlet side of the pump is pulled in to fill the space at the end. As the pump continues to turn, the piston will be forced back into the barrel by the valve plate. As a result, the oil in the chamber at the end of the piston will be forced through the outlet in the valve plate to the control valves. An increase in valve plate angle results in an increase in the volume of oil pulled into the chambers at the ends of the pistons. This, of course, results in an increase in the flow provided to the system.

Each pump contains a gear with depressions for the head of the piston to ride in. The retraction plate holds the piston head in the gear. The gear turns with the rotating group. The angle of the valve plate riding on top of the barrel determines the amount of flow supplied to the system. The pistons will move in and out of the barrel, as the gear, barrel and pistons turn. The in and out movement is the result of the piston slippers following the angle of the valve plate. The greater the angle of the valve plate, the farther the pistons move in and out of the barrel.

Each pump has a valve plate that rides on top of the barrel and does not turn. The valve plate helps the hydraulic oil flow smoothly in and out of the pump. Servo pistons control the angles of the valve plates. The angle of the valve plates determines the direction and amount of flow delivered by the pumps.
The servo pistons are the components inside the head of the pumps that use hydraulic signals from the control valves to control the angles of the valve plates.

A component of the Hydraulic Drive system is the Fixed or Two-Speed Hydraulic Motor. This segment introduces the identification and function of the major components that make-up the Fixed or Two-Speed Hydraulic Motor.

The hydraulic motors used in a hydraulic drive system are sometimes referred to as the drive motors or travel motors. The motors used with hydraulic drives are Caterpillar designed and built, piston motors. The motors can be fixed or two-speed motors (two-speed system). When servicing the piston-type motor on any hydraulic drive system, care must be taken to prevent damage to the valve plate and barrel.

On a hydraulic drive system the two track motors are the same. Each motor gets its oil supply from one of the variable displacement pumps. A change in direction of oil flow through a motor changes the output direction but does not change the amount of torque available from the shaft of the motor.

Travel motors can be either bent axis or axial piston swashplate design. Displacement of the swashplate can be changed from minimum angle to maximum angle for slow speed travel. The swashplate will be at either minimum or maximum angle.

The major components of the motor can be divided into the following groups:

• Rotary Group: Major components include, drive shaft, barrel, piston and slipper, and retainer.

• Parking Brake Group: Major components include, friction plates, separator plates and piston.
Part of the rotating group the drive shaft connects the motor to the final drive of the track system. The barrel inside the motor is splined to the drive shaft, providing rotation.

Part of the rotating group, the pistons are installed and housed in the barrel. As hydraulic oil under high pressure enters the barrel through the valve plate, it pushes the piston out of its bore. Because of the angle between the barrel assembly and the cam plate (the piston slipper rides on the cam plate), the barrel turns as the pistons are forced out of their cylinders. The barrel being splined to the drive shaft turns the drive shaft as it rotates.
The retainer is part of the rotating group. Its function is to hold the piston slippers on the cam plate.

The friction plates are part of the parking brake group and are splined to the barrel. When no pump oil is supplied to the motor a spring pushes the separator plates against the friction plates keeping the motor from turning. The separator plates, also part of the parking brake group, separate the friction plates. The separator plates are splined to the motor body. When no pump oil is supplied to the motor a spring forces the separator plates against the friction plates to keep the motor from turning.

The parking brake piston, part of the parking brake group, uses pump oil to release the parking brake. When pump oil is supplied to the motor, the piston releases the separator and friction plates allowing the motor to turn.
The parking brake springs, part of the parking brake group, force the parking brake piston against the friction and separator plates anytime system oil is not present.
Control valves are used to control a Hydraulic Drive system. This segment introduces the identification and function of the Control Valves on a Hydraulic Drive system.

The main control valves on a hydraulic excavator are right and left bodies coupled together by bolts to make one assembly.

Oil from the pumps is directed to the valve bodies and then to the drive system as requested by operator input. Return oil from the motors enters the control valves and flows out return ports back to the hydraulic tank.

The hydraulic oil from the pumps is directed to the control valves where it is distributed as needed to perform the operations requested by the operator.

These operations include more than driving the machine. Implement operation is also controlled by the control valves. For detailed operation and function of the control valves on a specific Cat machine, refer to the specific service manual for the machine being serviced.

For illustration purposes the following information applies to the 325 Hydraulic Excavator. Always refer to the appropriate service literature for specific machine information.

The hydraulic control valves on a 325 Excavator are mounted vertically between the frame rails behind the base of the boom. 

The control spools are all open center control valves.

The following components are part of the hydraulic control valve group. Only the components that control the hydraulic drive system will be covered in detail.

The Main Relief valve is a single relief valve with two check valves. The check valves direct the flow from the pump with the highest system pressure to the relief valve. The main relief valve is a dual stage relief valve. When only the travel circuits are operated, the main relief setting is higher than when the implement or swing circuits are operated.
Pilot pressure from this orifice shifts the main relief valve to increase system pressure to the travel circuits.

When activated, the straight travel valve performs a crossover function that directs top pump flow to both travel control valves, and bottom pump flow is directed to the parallel feeder flow paths in each side of the hydraulic control valve.

Displacement of the swashplate in the motor can be changed from minimum angle to maximum angle for low speed travel.

title: Engine Basics and Engine Systems
overview: Chapter 1, Diesel Engine Basics, explains combustion concepts, the four-stroke cycle, diesel engine components and how they operate. This introduction section explains the objectives and overall course structure of Fundamentals of Diesel Engines.

This course will help you:

1. Understand basic operating principles of internal combustion, four-stroke cycle diesel engines. 

2. Understand how the cooling, lubrication, charge air, fuel, and starting systems operate. 

3. Perform basic maintenance procedures on Caterpillar engines.

Knowing how the engine works normally means you will be able to recognize when the engine or engine system is not operating correctly.

lessons.title: Course Introduction
pages:
Diesel power... power to move mountains... power to move goods... power to transform dry desert to lush farmland... power to extract the raw materials used worldwide...

Caterpillar diesel power has changed the way we do work... from ocean vessels and oil rigs, to the trucks traveling the highways, diesels help get the job done.

And you can help get the job done too, whenever you service or repair an engine. A thorough and efficient repair keeps the machine out where it should be... working.

The key to doing your job well is knowledge. Knowledge about the engine, how it works, how the systems operate under normal conditions. It all comes down to basics.

Mastering the basics is what this course is all about. FUNDAMENTALS OF DIESEL ENGINES lays the groundwork, preparing you for advanced training on repair and maintenance procedures used on Caterpillar diesel engines.

Diesel Engine Basics explains:

1. Combustion concepts
2. The four-stroke cycle
3. Diesel engine components

The information in this chapter is the cornerstone for additional training on repair and maintenance procedures performed on a diesel engine.

Diesel Engine Systems discusses:

1. The cooling system - basic components, flow of fluids, and properties of coolant.
2. The lubrication system - basic components, flow of fluids, and properties of oil.
3. The air intake and exhaust system - basic components, and flow of air. 
4. The fuel system - basic components, flow of fuel, injection principles, and properties of fuel. 

Your understanding of diesel engine systems and their normal operation is critical for future troubleshooting.

Diesel Engine Systems Tests discusses tests you might have to perform during routine maintenance on:

1. The cooling system
2. The lubrication system
3. The air intake/exhaust system
4. The fuel system

General Maintenance Procedures provides information on:

1. How to gather information about the engine prior to performing maintenance.
2. How to determine a service interval.
3. How to perform filter and fluid changes on the lubrication system.
4. How to perform filter and fluid changes on the cooling system.
5. How to perform filter changes on the fuel system.
6. How to perform filter changes on the air system.
7. How to take an S·O·S sample and read an S·O·S report.

Maintenance procedures are critical to the life of the engine. Performing the procedures properly ensures long-running engines and satisfied customers.

lessons.title: The Combustion Process
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn:

1. The combustion process and how the combustion chamber and its components operate.
2. How the engine uses reciprocating and rotary motion to transmit energy.
3. How combustion occurs during a four stroke cycle.
4. Top Dead Center, Bottom Dead Center, and stroke.
pages: Think of an engine as a clock. Everything works in synchronization to keep good time. In a diesel engine, all the components work together to convert heat energy into mechanical energy.

The heating of air and fuel together produces combustion, which creates the force required to run the engine. Air, which contains oxygen, is required to burn the fuel. Fuel produces the force. When atomized, diesel fuels ignite easily and burn efficiently. Combustion occurs when the air fuel mixture heats up enough to ignite. It must burn quickly in a controlled fashion to produce the most heat energy.

Air + Fuel + Heat = CombustionP

Combustion is controlled by three factors:

1. The volume of air compressed.
2. The type of fuel used.
3. The amount of fuel mixed with the air.

The combustion chamber is formed by:

1. Cylinder liner
2. Piston
3. Intake valve
4. Exhaust valve
5. Cylinder head
When air is compressed, it heats up. The more you compress air, the hotter it gets. If it is compressed enough, it produces temperatures above the fuel's ignition temperature.

%The amount of fuel is also important because more fuel produces more force. When injected into an enclosed area containing sufficient air, a small amount of fuel produces large amounts of heat and force.

More Fuel = More Force
The type of fuel used in the engine affects combustion because different fuels burn at different temperatures, and some burn more thoroughly.
"In a diesel engine, air is compressed inside the combustion chamber until it is hot enough to ignite the fuel. Then, fuel is injected into the hot chamber and combustion occurs.
In a gasoline engine, compressed air does not provide enough heat for combustion to begin. A spark plug ignites the mixture which creates combustion.

)In both engine types, combustion produces heat energy which causes the gasses trapped in the combustion chamber to expand pushing the piston down. As the piston moves down, it moves other mechanical components that do the work.

The components work together to transform reciprocating motion into rotary motion. When combustion occurs, it moves the piston and connecting rod in an up and down motion called reciprocating motion. The connecting rod turns the crankshaft which converts the reciprocating motion into circular motion called rotary motion.

This is how the engine transforms the heat of combustion into useable energy.

The cycle starts with the intake stroke. First the intake valve opens. At the same time the piston moves to bottom dead center, or BDC, its lowest point, pulling air into the combustion chamber. The crankshaft turns 180 degrees, or half a revolution. The exhaust valve remains closed.

During the second or compression stroke the intake valve closes, sealing the combustion chamber. The piston moves up to its highest point in the cylinder liner, called top dead center or TDC. The trapped air is compressed and very hot. The amount the air is compressed is called the compression ratio. Most diesel engines have a compression ratio between 13 to 1 and 20 to 1. The crankshaft has turned 360 degrees or one complete revolution.

Compression Ratio = 
BDC Volume/TDC Volume

²Diesel fuel is injected near the end of the compression stroke. This creates combustion and starts the power stroke. the intake and exhaust valves remain closed to seal the combustion chamber. The force of combustion pushes the piston down which causes the connecting rod to turn the crankshaft another 180 degrees. The crankshaft has now made one and a half revolutions since the cycle started.

_The exhaust stroke is the final stroke in the cycle. During the exhaust stroke the exhaust valve opens as the piston moves up forcing the burned gasses out of the cylinder. At TDC, the exhaust valve closes, the intake valve opens, and the cycle begins again. The connecting rod had turned the crankshaft another 180 degrees.

At the end of the exhaust stroke the entire process is complete. During this time the crankshaft has completed two 360 degree rotations. Taken together, the intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes are called a cycle... thus the name "The Four-Stroke Cycle." Cat engines use the four-stroke cycle, and the cycle occurs over and over as long as the engine is running. The sequence in which each cylinder comes to the power stroke is called the firing order of the engine.

Four Strokes of Piston = 
Two Revolutions of CrankshaftP

lessons.title: Comparing Diesel and Gasoline Engines
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn the differences between diesel and gasoline engines.
pages: Like diesel engines, gasoline engines use combustion from the four-stroke cycle to create energy to do work. But there are some slight differences in the process. Let's see what those differences are.

Probably the most obvious difference between diesel and gasoline engines is that diesel engines do not require a spark for ignition.

Instead, air is compressed to such a high ratio that it heats the air in the combustion chamber enough to ignite the fuel.

Combustion chamber design is also different between diesel and gasoline engines.

In diesels, there is very little room between the cylinder head and the piston at top dead center, producing the high compression ratio.

Most diesel pistons have the combustion chamber formed right into the top of the piston.
In gasoline engines the combustion chamber is formed into the cylinder head. The space between the piston and cylinder head is larger than in a diesel, resulting in a lower compression ratio.

Another major difference is the amount of work the engine is capable of performing at lower rpm. In general, diesel engines usually operate between 800 and 2200 RPM and provide more torque, and more power to do work.
Both engines convert heat energy to motion using the four-stroke cycle.

Diesel engines are generally more fuel efficient for the amount of work output than gasoline engines. It requires relatively small amounts of fuel to produce the rated horsepower output in a diesel engine.
Diesel engines are generally heavier than gasoline engines because the diesel engine must withstand higher combustion pressures and temperatures.

Diesel engines generally use higher compression ratios to heat the air to combustion temperatures. Most diesel engines generally have a 13:1 to 20:1 compression ratio. Gasoline engines generally use compression ratios between 8:1 to 11:1.

lessons.title: Spark-Ignited Engines
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn how a spark ignited engine operates.
pages: Spark ignited engines run on gaseous fuels like propane, methane and ethanol. These fuels and the requirements for low pressure fuel lines required significant modifications of the engine design.

Since World War II, Caterpillar has marketed a limited number of gas engines. Today Caterpillar produces gas engines for the irrigation, industrial, cogeneration and generator set markets.

In recent years, the United States and other countries have instituted strict emissions guidelines to protect and preserve the environment. Natural gas has emerged as an environmentally clean and abundant fuel. To meet the changing market, Caterpillar has made the commitment to supply gas engines throughout its product line. These engines run on gaseous fuels like propane and methane. Based on Cat diesel engine design, many gas engine parts are the same, but significant modifications have been made primarily in the fuel delivery system. 

The air intake, exhaust, cooling and fuel systems have been changed to accommodate leaner air-fuel mixtures, and a high voltage spark ignition system has been added.

On some engines, the piston has also been redesigned with a deep cup to facilitate combustion. On others, a flat top piston is available. Electronic sensors and timing devices have been added to improve engine performance on these low emission engines. Gas engines are currently available from the 3300, 3400, 3500, and 3600 families. Currently gas engines are used to compress and transport gas in natural gas fields, run irrigation pumps and power cogeneration plants.

lessons.title: Engine Terminology and Performance
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn the common terminology used to describe how an engine functions and how well the engine operates.
pages:
Engines are described using many terms and phrases. Some describe how an engine functions, while others describe how well the engine operates.

There are three main categories of terminology in this topic: laws of mechanics, power output, and engine efficiency.
Laws of mechanics terms describe the motion of objects and the effects of motion.

Friction is the resistance to motion between two surfaces in contact with each other. 

For example, friction exists between the piston and cylinder wall as the piston moves up and down. Friction produces heat which is one of the biggest contributors to wear and component damage.
Inertia is the tendency of an object at rest to stay at rest or an object in motion to stay in motion. The engine uses force to overcome inertia.
Force is a push or pull that starts, stops, or changes the motion of an object. Force is created by combustion during the power stroke. The higher the generated force, the more power is produced.
Pressure is a measure of the force exerted per unit area. During the four stroke cycle, a lot of pressure is produced on the top of the piston during the compression and power strokes.

There are three ways to create pressure. Increase temperature, decrease volume or restrict flow. Many systems and components of internal combustion engines operate under or generate specific pressures. Knowledge and measurement of specific pressures throughout the engine can provide a great deal of information about the overall engine health.
Here are four terms associated with the Laws of Mechanics. Match each term with its definition.
A measure of the force exerted per unit area.
A push or pull that starts, stops, or changes the motion of an object.
The resistance to motion between two surfaces in contact with each other.
The tendency of an object at rest to stay at rest or of an object in motion to stay in motion.
Engine power is described according to the quality and quantity of certain characteristics.
Torque is a turning or twisting force. A crankshaft exerts torque to force flywheels, torque converters or other mechanical devices to turn.

Torque is also a measure of the load carrying capacity of the engine.

The formula for torque is:

Torque (lb. ft) = (5252 x horsepower) / rpmP

Torque Rise is an increase in torque that occurs when an engine is lugged down from rated RPM. This increase in torque occurs until a certain rpm is reached, after which torque drops rapidly. The maximum torque level reached is called peak torque.

Legend: 
TR = Torque Rise
HP + T = Horsepower and Torque
TC = Torque Curve
HC = Horsepower Curve
PT = Peak Torque
RT = Rated TorqueP

6Horsepower is a rating given to the engine that describes the amount of work output over a period of time or the rate of doing work.
Brake horsepower is the useable power available for work at the flywheel. Brake horsepower is less than true horsepower because some energy is used to move the engine components.
The formula for horsepower is:

Horsepower = rpm x torque / 5252
Heat is a form of energy produced by the combustion of fuel. Heat energy is converted into mechanical energy by the piston and other engine components in order to produce power suitable for work.
Temperature is a measurement of relative warmth or coolness of an object. It is usually measured with either a Fahrenheit or Celsius scale.

The British Thermal Unit, or BTU, is used to measure the heat value of a specific amount of fuel, or the amount of heat transferred from one object to another. A BTU is the amount of heat required to raise one pound of water one degree Fahrenheit.
BTU is used to describe a fuel's heating value. Fuels with higher BTU ratings generate more heat and therefore more power. In general, diesel fuel has a higher BTU rating than gasoline.
BTU is also used to describe how well the cooling system works. The more BTUs the coolant removes, the more efficient the cooling system.

Bore is the interior diameter of the cylinder measured in inches or millimeters.

The bore of the cylinder determines the volume of air available for combustion. With all other things being equal, the larger the bore the more powerful the engine.

Stroke is the name for the distance the piston travels from top dead center to bottom dead center. Stroke length is determined by the design of the crankshaft. A longer stroke allows more air into the cylinder which allows more fuel to be burned, creating more power.
There are four main concepts used to describe engine efficiency. Match the terms to their definitions.

topics.title: Engine Components
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will be able to identify the components in the block, cylinder head, and gear train assemblies and understand the function of each component.

lessons.title: Block Assembly
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about each component in the block assembly and be able to describe the function of each component.
pages: The block assembly is where the power is created. Let's look at each of the block assembly components and how they work together to make the engine operate.
The engine block is the structure that supports all the components for the engine.

The cylinders are holes in the engine block. They perform a number of tasks:

1. House the pistons
2. Form the combustion chambers
3. Move heat away from the pistons

Pistons perform three primary jobs:

1. Transmit force of combustion to connecting rod and crankshaft
2. Seal the combustion chamber
3. Transmit excess heat away from the combustion chamber P

Each piston has two or more rings that fit into grooves on the piston. They have three primary jobs:

1. Seal the combustion chamber
2. Control lubrication of the cylinder walls
3. Cool the piston by transferring heat generated by combustion
Connecting rods are attached to every piston via the piston pin. The connecting rod transmits combustion force from the piston to the crankshaft.
The other end of the connecting rod turns the crankshaft located at the bottom of the engine block. The crankshaft transmits rotary motion to the flywheel providing energy suitable for work.

The camshaft is driven by a gear on the crankshaft. The camshaft controls the valve opening and closing and may control fuel injection when unit injectors are used. The camshaft gets it name from the egg shaped lobes or cams. As the camshaft rotates, the lobes turn. Valve train components linked to the camshaft follow the motion, moving up and down. When the nose of the lobe faces up, the valve is all the way open.

The flywheel assembly is the link between the engine and the load. It is bolted to the rear of the crankshaft. A flywheel performs three jobs:
1. Stores energy for momentum between power strokes.
2. Smoothes out the speed of the crankshaft.
3. Transmits power.
Push rods are steel tubes with seats on both ends. The camshaft moves the push rod causing it to lift the rocker arms.
A valve lifter or cam follower rests on each cam lobe. As the camshaft turns, the lifter moves, following the shape of the lobe.
Engine blocks come in different designs. In-line engines (1) have the cylinders all in one row. V-engines (2) separate the cylinders into two rows, and the block has a “V” shape.
Blocks are normally gray cast iron. Coolant (1) and lubricant (2) passages are cast into the block.
Cylinders can be cast permanently into the block called a Parent Bore (1), or they may be removable cylinder liners (2).

Wet liners have O-rings to seal the water jacket and prevent coolant leakage. Dry liners are often used to repair or “sleeve” parent bore engines should a cylinder fail. The liners are called “dry” because they fit against pre-existing cylinder bore walls in the block.

KA cylinder liner is made of cast iron. A typical wet cylinder liner has several parts:

1. Inside Surface - holds the piston, also called the bore.
2. Fire Dam - seals the combustion chamber.
3. Flange - supports the liner in the block.
4. Filler Band Groove - holds filler band which helps the liner fit into the bore and reduces liner vibration.
5. Outside Surface - forms the water jacket wall.
6. O-Ring Grooves - hold O-Rings which seal the water jacket.

The piston, which transmits the force of combustion, is made up of many parts:

1. Crown - contains the combustion chamber.
2. Ring Grooves and Lands - hold the compression and oil control rings.
3. Wrist Pin Bore - contains a pin that connects the piston to the connecting rod.
4. Retaining Ring - keeps the piston pin inside the pin bore.
5. Thrust Skirt - carries side loads.

There is an undercrown area (1) on the inside of the piston. 

Some pistons contain oil cooling galleries (2) inside the piston crown which cannot be seen.

Pistons are constructed using a variety of methods.

1. Cast aluminum crown with a forged aluminum skirt, electron beam welded.
2. Composite, a steel crown and forged aluminum skirt bolted together.
3. Articulated, a forged steel crown with pin bores and bushings, and a separate cast aluminum skirt. The two pieces are held together by the wrist pin.
4. The most common type is the single piece cast aluminum piston with an iron band that carries the piston rings.

There are two styles of pistons which relate to fuel system and combustion chamber design.
 
Precombustion pistons have a heat plug in the crown.

Direct injection pistons do not have a heat plug.

There are two types of piston rings: (1) compression rings and (2) oil control rings. Compression rings seal the bottom of the combustion chamber by preventing combustion gasses from leaking out past the pistons.

There is usually one oil control ring below the compression rings. Oil control rings lubricate the walls of the cylinder liner as the piston moves up and down. The oil film reduces wear on the cylinder liner and piston.
Behind the oil control ring is an expander spring which helps maintain an even film of oil on the cylinder wall.
All rings have a hard facing to increase ring life.
Every piston ring has a gap between the two ends of the ring. To prevent leakage, ring end gaps should not line up when installed.

Connecting rods link the piston to the crankshaft.
There are several parts to a connecting rod:

1. Rod Eye
2. Piston Pin Bushing
3. Shank
4. Cap
5. Rod Bolts and Nuts
6. Connecting Rod Bearing

The rod eye holds the piston pin bushing. The piston pin bushing is inside the rod eye. Bushings are a type of bearing which distribute load and can be replaced when worn.
P
The shank extends the length of the connecting rod. It has an I-beam shape for strength and rigidity.
The crankshaft bore and cap are at the large end of the connecting rod. They surround the crankshaft's rod bearing journal and attach the connecting rod to the crankshaft.
The rod bolt and nut secure the rod and cap to the crankshaft. This is called the crank end or big end of the connecting rod.
The connecting rod bearings are in the crank end of the connecting rod. The crankshaft turns inside the connecting rod bearings which carry the load.

The connecting rod bearing's top half fits in the rod and is called the upper half shell. The other half fits in the cap, and is called the lower half shell.
P

The crankshaft transfers the piston's reciprocal motion into a rotary motion that is used in performing work. There are many parts to the crankshaft.

1. Rod Bearing Journals
2. Counterweights
3. Main Bearing Journals
4. WebP

Crankshafts for in-line engines generally have only one rod bearing journal for each cylinder while “V” engines share a single rod bearing journal between two cylinders.
P

/The Rod Bearing Journals determine the position of the pistons. When the journals are up, the pistons are at top dead center. When the journals are down, the pistons are at bottom dead center. The firing order of the engine determines when each rod bearing journal comes to top dead center.
Some rod bearing journals have lightening holes to reduce the weight of the crankshaft and to help balance the crankshaft.
The crankshaft has drilled oil holes to get oil from the main bearings to the connecting rod bearings.
Drilled oil passages are plugged at one end by a cup plug or set screwP
Main bearing journals (1) and rod bearing journals (2) are held together by webs (3). The radius between the web and the journal is called a fillet (4).
Some webs have counterweights to help balance the crankshaft. These counterweights may be part of the crankshaft forging or in some cases they are bolted on.
Crankshafts use main bearings to support the crankshaft in the block. Main bearings are in line with each other.
This is a thrust main. It is one of the main bearing journals. Its web has wide ground sidewalls. It works with the thrust main bearing to limit crankshaft back and forth movement called end play.

The crankshaft turns inside main bearings that are tightly clamped in bores located at the bottom of the block.
P

There are two halves to each main bearing called shells. The lower half shell fits into the main bearing cap, and the upper half shell fits into the main bearing bore in the block. Generally, the lower half shell carries more load and wears faster.

The main bearing assemblies consist of the main bearing bores in the engine block, the main bearing caps which are held on with bolts or studs, and the main bearings themselves.
P

The upper halves of main bearings have an oil hole and usually a slot so lubricating oil is continuously fed into the oil hole in the main journal.
P

Thrust main bearings minimize back and forth movement of the crankshaft.

There are two types of thrust main bearings.

1. Insert bearings are two pieces.

2. Flanged thrust bearings are one piece.
P
The thrust main works together with a thrust bearing to minimize back and forth movement of the crankshaft within the block. This movement is called End Play.

The flywheel is bolted to the rear of the crankshaft in the flywheel housing.

The crankshaft turns the flywheel on the power stroke, and the flywheel's momentum keeps the crankshaft turning smoothly during the intake, compression and exhaust strokes.
P
The ring gear, which is located around the flywheel, is used for starting the engine.

The flywheel performs three functions:

1. Stores energy for momentum between power strokes.
2. Smooths out the speed of the crankshaft.
3. Transmits power to a machine, torque converter or other load.

On the front of the crankshaft you may find a vibration damper. Dampers control torsional or twisting vibrations of the crankshaft.

A damper resembles a miniature flywheel that is either pressed on or bolted to the front of the crankshaft.

Vibration dampers are available in two basic designs: a rubber damper and a viscous damper.
Rubber vibration dampers (left) use dense rubber to absorb the vibrations.

Viscous dampers (right) use heavy oil to absorb the vibrations.
P

The camshaft is driven by a gear on the crankshaft. As the camshaft rotates, the cam lobes turn. Valve train components linked to the camshaft follow the motion, moving up and down. When the nose of the lobe faces up, the valve is all the way open. The camshaft turns at half the speed of the crankshaft so that the valves open and close at the correct time during the four-stroke cycle.
The purpose of the camshaft is to control intake and exhaust valve operation. All camshafts have (1) bearing journals and (2) lobes.

Separate lobes operate the (1) intake and (2) exhaust valves for each cylinder. Some cams have (3) fuel injection lobes which operate unit injectors. These control when fuel is injected into the cylinder.

XEvery lobe is made up of three main parts: 

1. Base Circle
2. Ramps
3. NoseP
The distance from the base circle diameter to the top of the nose is called Lift. Cam lift determines how far valves are opened.

The shape of the opening and closing ramps determine how fast the valves open and close. 

The shape of the nose determines how long the valve is fully opened.

1. Fast opening
2. Long open period
3. Fast close
4. Slow closeP
The camshaft journals turn in the camshaft bearings. Camshaft bearings are press fit into bores in the engine block. They contain an oil hole that aligns with an oil passage in the block.

A valve lifter or cam follower rests on each lobe of the camshaft. As the (1) camshaft turns, the (2) valve lifter follows the shape of the lobe. The valve lifter transmits the motion of the camshaft to the (3) push rod. The push rod transmits that motion to the (4) rocker arm to open and close the valve.

There are two types of valve lifters, slipper followers (right) and roller followers.
P
Roller followers have a hardened steel roller that rolls on the camshaft lobe.
Roller followers slide up and down in bores in the engine block and are kept aligned by special clips.
Slipper followers are usually one piece castings with a wear face that contacts the lobe.
The slipper followers slide up and down in bores in the engine block. Slipper followers rotate slowly while the engine is operating.
Some components which are most susceptible to wear are designed to be replaced. These include cylinder liners, piston rings, main bearings and connecting rod bearings..

Because of the extreme temperatures and pressures generated by combustion, cylinder liners become worn by pistons and rings and are designed to be replaced..
P
Because of high combustion temperatures and constant motion, piston rings will eventually wear, and are designed to be replaced as needed.
Main bearings will wear faster than the crankshaft because they are made of softer metal. Therefore, bearings are designed to be replaced when necessary.
Connecting rod bearings will wear faster than the crankshaft because they are made of softer metal. Therefore, bearings are designed to be replaced when necessary.

lessons.title: Cylinder Head Assembly
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn about cylinder head components and the function of each component.
You will also learn how an overhead cam engine operates and how its valve train differs from a push rod engine.
pages: The cylinder head and its components are designed to make sure that the valves open and close, and that fuel is injected at the proper time for peak engine performance.

The cylinder head is a separate casting which seals the top of the engine block and holds the valves, injector or precombustion chamber in place.

It also houses the valve train, some fuel system components and water passages for cooling the parts.
The cylinder head (1) is seated to the engine block with gaskets (2), a spacer plate (3) and bolts or studs.
Depending on the engine design, the cylinder head can either be a single casting that covers the top of the block, or several castings that cover one or more cylinders each.
You must remove the valve covers in order to reach the valve train components.

Rocker arms link the valves to the camshaft, and change the rotary motion of the camshaft to the reciprocating motion in the valves. As the push rod in the block pushes up on one end of the rocker arm, it pivots on the rocker arm shaft and pushes down on the valve mechanism causing the valve to open.

As the camshaft continues turning, the push rod lowers, and the force of the valve spring closes the valve. There is a separate rocker arm for intake and exhaust valves on every cylinder.

A rocker arm consists of:

1. Adjusting Screw - Adjusts valve lash.
2. Lock Nut - Locks screw in place to maintain lash.
3. Wear Seat - Hardened insert to prevent rocker arm wear.
4. Rocker Shaft Bushing - Provides a bearing between the rocker arm and the shaft.

The rocker arm pivots on a shaft that is usually fastened to the cylinder head. When the cam lobe starts to move the push rod upwards, there is usually a little gap or clearance between the rocker arm and valve bridge that assures the valve is able to close completely. This is called valve lash and is one of the more critical adjustments that must be made on the valve train.
Bridges are used if a cylinder has multiple intake and exhaust valves. On these engines, the bridge assembly transmits rocker arm motion to all intake or exhaust valves on a cylinder simultaneously.

1. Wear Seat - Reduces bridge wear.
2. Adjusting Screw - Compensates for differences in the height of the valve stems.
3. Lock Nut - Sets adjusting screw.
4. Bore - Rides on guide pin.
Bridges fit on bridge dowels. Bridge dowels fit into bores in the cylinder head.

The valves control flow of air and exhaust gasses through the combustion chamber. When the intake valve is open, air is allowed into the combustion chamber. When the exhaust valve is open, exhaust exits the combustion chamber.

E1. Keeper Grooves - Where keepers grip the valve stem to hold the spring on.
2. Valve Stem - Extends the length of the valve, rides in the valve guide.
3. Valve Fillet - Joins head of valve to stem.
4. Valve Seat - Has a hard facing which reduces wear and seals the combustion chamber.
5. Valve Face - Flat portion of valve.

To completely seal the combustion chamber, every valve has a valve seat insert located in the cylinder head. When the valve closes, the valve seat contacts the valve seat insert.

On most engines, the valve seat inserts are replaceable.

Valves move up and down inside valve guides which are mounted in the cylinder head. Valve guides keep the valves traveling in a straight line. The valve stem extends out of the guide on top of the cylinder head.

Valve springs keep the valves closed. Valve springs fit over the valves.

Valve springs are held in place by a combination of keepers (1) and either a retainer (2) or rotator.
Retainers or rotators fit over the end of the valve stem. Retainers lock the keepers into grooves in the valve, and provide a seat for the valve spring to press against.
Valve rotators turn the valve to prevent excessive wear in one spot.
The valves, valve seat inserts, and valve guides experience the most wear because of the high combustion temperatures and pressures. All are replaceable components.
Fuel nozzles or unit injectors are also located in the head. The nozzles fit between the valves.
Fuel nozzles are held in place with a sleeve, washers, adapters, and keepers.

XOverhead cam engines have a camshaft (1) in the cylinder head. Valve lifters (2) are linked to the top of the valve stem. As the cam lobe rotates, the lifter follows the motion and opens the valve. As the cam continues to rotate, valve spring (3) force closes the valve.

Overhead cam engines do not require push rods.
In a cam in head engine, the camshaft is located in the cylinder head. Rocker arms ride on the lobes. As the camshaft turns, the rockers push the valves open.

lessons.title: Gear Train Assembly
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about the components in the gear train and the function of each component.
pages: The gear train assembly is a series of gears that transfer power from the crankshaft to other major components in the engine. Gear trains may be located on the front and back of the engine. The gear train shown here is located on the front of the engine between the backing plate and timing gear housing.
The gear train synchronizes all the components in the engine so they work together during each stroke of the combustion cycle.

Here are the components of a typical gear train:

1. Crankshaft Gear
2. Idler Gear
3. Camshaft Gear
4. Fuel Injection Pump Gear
5. Oil Pump Gear
6. Water Pump Gear
7. Air Compressor
Timing marks are used to align the gears and help ensure proper timing.
The crankshaft gear is mounted on the crankshaft. As the crankshaft turns, the gear turns as well. All other components are timed and driven by the crankshaft and crankshaft gear.
The idler gear keeps the camshaft gear turning the same direction as the crankshaft gear. The gear ratios ensure that the camshaft turns at ½ the speed of the crankshaft.
idler gear. It turns at half the speed of the crankshaft to make sure the intake and exhaust valves open and close on the correct stroke.

The fuel pump gear is driven by the camshaft gear. Since they are the same size, they both turn at the same speed. The fuel pump gear turns the fuel pump camshaft, which works with the fuel system components to deliver fuel to the engine at the proper time.

Some engine models use balance shafts. The shafts are driven from the crankshaft. In this example, there is a balance shaft on each side of the engine. The balance shaft eliminates excess vibration of the crankshaft.
This is an example of a balance shaft and gear assembly.
The oil pump gear is driven by the crankshaft gear. The oil pump circulates oil throughout the engine.
The water pump is driven by the water pump gear and circulates coolant throughout the engine. The water pump gear is usually driven at the same speed as the crankshaft.

Some engines use an air compressor to supply air to brakes and other components. The air compressor is driven from gears in the gear train. The air compressor gear meshes with idler gears and turns at the speed recommended by the manufacturer.
A pulley assembly attached to the crankshaft drives other components like fans or alternators.
All the timing gears are protected by the timing gear housing. The timing gear housing seals the front of the engine block.

chapters.title: Engine Systems
intro: Chapter 2, Engine Systems, discusses the various diesel engine systems, their components, and how they operate. These systems include cooling, lubrication, air intake and exhaust, fuel, and the starting system. After completing this Cooling System topic, you will be able to identify cooling system components and their function, the flow of coolant through a cooling system and the characteristics of coolant.

lessons.title: Cooling System Components and Operation
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn to: 

1. Identify the primary purpose of the cooling system.
2. Trace the flow of coolant through the system.
3. Locate and identify the function of each component in an engine's cooling system.
4. Recognize different types of cooling systems.
pages: An engine's cooling system is responsible for maintaining adequate engine temperatures. If the cooling system fails, severe engine damage could occur. Let's look at the components and flow in a cooling system.
The cooling system circulates coolant throughout the engine to remove the heat created by combustion and friction. It uses the principle of heat transfer to do its job.

Heat always moves from a hot ‘source' (1) to a cooler ‘target' (2). Source and target could be metal, fluid or air. The key is the difference in relative temperatures between the two. The greater the difference, the more heat will transfer.

Every component in a cooling system plays a role in heat transfer.

The principle components in a cooling system are (1) a water pump, (2) oil cooler, (3) passages through the engine block and cylinder head, (4) temperature regulator and regulator housing, (5) radiator, (6) pressure cap, and (7) connecting hoses and pipes. In addition, a fan, usually driven by belts, is located near the radiator to increase air flow and improve heat transfer.
The water pump consists of an impeller with curved vanes in a housing. As the impeller turns, the curve of the vanes throws water outward and into the outlet formed by the housing.
This is a typical water pump on an engine. As you can see, it is mounted to the front of the block.

From the water pump outlet, coolant flows to the oil cooler. 

Oil coolers consist of a set of tubes in a housing. In this example, coolant flows through the tubes, removing heat from engine oil that surrounds the tubes.

The oil cooler removes heat from the lubricating oil, which preserves the oil's lubricating properties.

From the oil cooler, coolant flows either to the block or, if the engine is equipped with a turbocharger, it may flow to an aftercooler.

Some turbocharged engines use a jacket water aftercooler. If so, coolant flows there next.

The aftercooler removes heat from the intake air. On a jacket water aftercooler, the cooling system removes heat from the air.

An aftercooler is constructed just like a radiator, with tubes and fins. The heated compressed air coming from the turbocharger passes over the fins and transfers heat to the coolant in the tubes.
From the oil or aftercooler, coolant flows into the engine block and around the cylinder liners, removing waste heat from the pistons, rings, and liners. These cavities are called the water jacket.
Coolant travels from the engine block passages to the cylinder head, picking up heat from valve seats and guides.
Once it leaves the head, coolant enters the thermostat or regulator housing. A temperature regulator is mounted inside the housing.

The temperature regulator acts as the cooling system's “traffic cop.” The regulator's job is to maintain a proper range of operating temperatures. To do this, the regulator shunts coolant flow through the radiator, or through a bypass tube back to the water pump.

When the engine is cold, the regulator is closed. Coolant circulates back to the pump, bypassing the radiator. This helps warm up the engine.

As the engine heats up, coolant temperature increases until it reaches the opening temperature for the regulator. As the regulator opens, some coolant is directed into the radiator. The remainder bypasses to the water pump.

As temperatures increase, the regulator opens more, and more coolant is directed through the radiator. When the regulator is fully open, all the coolant flow is directed into the radiator.

You should test the regulator during cooling system maintenance, and replace it if necessary.

Opening temperatures are stamped on the regulator. If you should replace a regulator, make sure you use the one recommended for the engine, or else the cooling system will not operate properly.

If the regulator is open, coolant flows through pipes or hoses to the top of the radiator. Up to this point, the coolant has been picking up heat from all parts of the engine. In the radiator, the situation is reversed. Coolant transfers its heat to the cooler atmosphere.
In the radiator, coolant flows from top to bottom. Tubes and fins work together to dissipate heat. Radiators are usually mounted where they get the most air flow and best heat transfer.

Radiators also have pressure caps. The cap determines how much pressure will be present in the cooling system during operation.

Pressurized cooling systems help prevent water from boiling at higher altitudes.

As you climb above sea level, boiling temperature drops. If the cooling system was not pressurized, the coolant could boil, causing serious engine damage.

Radiator caps maintain pressure in the cooling system through two valves. If the difference between the cooling system pressure and atmospheric pressure exceeds the cap's opening pressure, an outlet valve opens. This allows a small amount of air to escape, reducing the pressure in the system. The system stabilizes.

When you stop the engine and it begins to cool, the pressure inside the cooling system drops below that of atmosphere. The cap's inlet valve opens, allowing some air into the radiator. This evens out and stabilizes the two pressures.
A variety of pressure caps can be used depending on the engine's operating altitude. The rated pressure is stamped on each cap.

You should test the pressure cap during cooling system maintenance, and replace it if necessary.

Topic 3 will describe how to perform this procedure.
If fan belt tension is too loose, fan speed can decrease. This decreases air flow across the radiator, and reduces the overall cooling capacity of the system.

Actually, a loose fan belt is more likely to produce symptoms of overheating and increased coolant temperatures. Because the fan is not turning at the correct speed, air is not moving across the radiator fast enough for good heat transfer.
Cooling systems are often modified to meet the special need of the engine application. Here, you will learn about different types of cooling systems.

A water cooled exhaust manifold is sometimes added to a cooling system to cool exhaust gas before it is expelled.

On marine engines, a water cooled exhaust is used to keep engine rooms cooler.

In a water cooled exhaust manifold, coolant flows through a housing which surrounds the exhaust gas passages.

Another option that may be present in some cooling systems is a coolant conditioner element.

A coolant conditioner element can be connected in parallel to the coolant flow. Corrosion inhibitors are placed into it and dissolve into the cooling system during operation.

On-highway trucks change engine speed frequently. Since the water pump is gear driven, this means the flow of water through the system also changes speed. The cooling system has been modified to accommodate these conditions.
Besides a water pump, oil cooler, coolant passages, temperature regulator, radiator and cap, fan, and connecting hoses, truck systems have an additional shunt line (1) linking the top of the radiator to the water pump. The shunt line protects the water pump from damage.

As the truck changes speed, the gear driven water pump changes speed. However, the coolant flow does not change speed as quickly, which causes a pressure differential at the water pump.

The shunt line provides sufficient water to the inlet side of the water pump to maintain pressure and prevent the coolant from boiling.

Water on the inlet side of the pump can boil because the pressure is reduced. On the outlet side of the pump, pressure is restored. This forces steam bubbles to implode. The bursting bubbles cause cavitation erosion at the water pump.

Marine engines have several unique cooling system components because the heat from the engine is transferred to water, rather than to air. Marine systems use a heat exchanger or keel cooling system. The basic coolant flow is the same, but a heat exchanger or keel cooler takes the place of the radiator.

The components of a keel cooler system include the same components as a conventional system. There's a water pump, coolant passages, and a surge or expansion tank which houses the temperature regulator. Instead of a radiator, the coolant flows through a keel cooler.

The keel cooler is a series of coiled tubes. It can be built into the hull of the ship, or mounted in channels and welded onto the hull. Coolant flows from the expansion tank (1) into the water pump (2), through the engine and through the keel cooling coil (3), where sea water cools the fluid.

The heat exchanger cooling system includes a water pump, engine coolant passages, a water cooled exhaust manifold, and an expansion or surge tank which houses the temperature regulator. There is also a heat exchanger. The raw water system has a raw water pump, and pipes and hoses which transport sea water to the pump and to the heat exchanger.

Zinc rods are used in marine applications to reduce corrosion. Zinc is much more susceptible to corrosion than other metals found in the cooling system. When the zinc is exposed to sea water, the zinc corrodes instead of other metal. 

This process is called galvanic corrosion. Zinc rods are called “sacrificial anodes” because they are designed to corrode instead of the other components. The rods must be checked frequently and replaced as needed.

In the segment, you will learn:

1. The three ingredients of coolant and recognize the purpose of each ingredient.
2. Recommended antifreeze and coolant conditioner concentrations.
3. Three factors which determine the operating range of a coolant.
Coolant is a mixture of water, antifreeze, and coolant conditioner. Each element serves a different purpose, and together they protect the engine from overheating, freezing, and corrosion.

Water is the main ingredient for all coolant because water transfers heat better than any other substance.

Water has several drawbacks as a coolant:
1. It boils easily.
2. It freezes.
3. It is extremely corrosive to metal.

Antifreeze, or ethylene glycol, and coolant conditioner are added to correct these deficiencies.
Antifreeze, or ethylene glycol, is used to raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point of water.
The amount of ethylene glycol affects the boiling point. The more antifreeze, the higher the boiling point.

If coolant freezes, it can not flow. therefore, it can not cool the engine. Frozen coolant can also expand and crack castings.

Freeze protection varies depending on the concentration of antifreeze.
Conditioner prevents corrosion by coating all the components in the cooling system. The thin coating prevents water and cavitation erosion from attacking the metal.

Operating altitude and system pressure affect the boiling point of water.

1. Increasing altitude lowers the boiling point of water.
2. Increasing system pressure increases the boiling point of water.

This is why most cooling systems operate under pressure. Pressurizing the system raises the boiling point. Since most engines operate above sea level they need this protection.

Three factors influence the operating temperature range of coolant:

1. Operating Altitude
2. System Pressure
3. Concentration of AntifreezeP

It is critical to prevent the coolant from boiling.

If coolant boils, steam bubbles form. These pockets of air do not transfer heat well, which leads to overheating.

Steam bubbles can also interfere with the water pump's ability to make coolant flow. This can lead to serious engine damage.
When the steam bubbles break, they can remove small particles of metal from components. This is called cavitation erosion.

To prevent cooling system problems you should maintain a proper antifreeze concentration. 
When you mix coolant, keep the antifreeze concentration between 30% - 60%P
Concentrations lower than 30% do not provide adequate protection, while concentrations above 60% start to reduce the heat removal properties.
Antifreeze concentrations higher than 60% also reduce the freeze protection and contribute to silica dropout, which destroys seals and clogs the cooling system.

Coolant conditioner is a good thing, but a little goes a long way.

Recommended coolant conditioner concentration: 3% - 6%P
If the coolant conditioner concentration is lower than recommended, engine components like cylinder liners can corrode or experience cavitation erosion.

Too much conditioner can cause silica dropout.

Silica dropout turns the coolant into a thick gel, which damages the water pump and clogs the radiator.

High concentrations of coolant conditioner also reduce heat transfer.
There are several ways to add conditioner to the cooling system. Use only one method at a time to prevent over conditioning, and check the concentration before making any further additions.

Make sure you add the proper amount of coolant to the system.

If the coolant level is low, there will not be enough water, antifreeze, and conditioner to protect the engine.

Check the Operation and Maintenance Manual for the correct fill level for the engine you are working on.

In general, the coolant level should always come up to the bottom of the filler pipe.

Good. In general, the higher the concentrations, the more freeze protection. However, this only applies up to a 68% concentrations of antifreeze. After this point, you can see on the chart that freeze protection begins to decrease.

topics.title: Lubrication System
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will understand the purpose of a lubrication system and be able to identify system components and their function. You will understand the key properties of engine oil and the flow of oil through the lubrication system.

lessons.title: Lubrication System Components
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about lubrication system components and their function. You will also be able to trace the flow of oil through the engine.
pages: The primary purpose of the lubrication system is to circulate oil throughout the engine. The oil cleans, cools and protects the engine's moving parts from wear.

The lubrication system consists of (1) an oil pan or sump, (2) a suction bell, (3) oil pump, (4) a pressure relief valve, (5) oil filter with a bypass valve, (6) engine oil cooler with a bypass valve, (7) main oil gallery, (8) piston cooling jets, (9) crankcase breather, connecting lines and pipes, and the oil itself.

The oil pan, or sump, acts as a reservoir for the engine oil.

The oil pan also dissipates heat from the oil to the atmosphere.

The oil pan is located on the bottom of the engine block.

From the oil pan, oil passes through an inlet screen and into the suction bell.

The inlet screen prevents large pieces of debris from entering the oil system.

The suction bell transports oil to the oil pump.

The oil pump creates flow, which circulates oil throughout the engine.

The oil pump is located in or near the oil pan. The pump is driven by the crankshaft via an oil pump gear.

A pressure relief valve is normally located near the oil pump.

The relief valve protects the lubrication system from high pressures.

From the oil pump, oil travels through the oil cooler. Oil coolers remove heat from the oil.
Oil fills the oil cooler housing. Inside the housing are tubes which carry engine coolant. Heat transfers from the oil to the coolant.

The oil cooler also has a bypass valve.

Oil flows from the oil cooler to the oil filter. Lubricating systems can use one or more oil filters, depending on the design. 

Filters remove debris and metal particles from the oil.

Filters use bypass valves as well.
In a full flow filter system, 100% of the oil goes through the filter. These systems must have a bypass valve.

A bypass filter system uses two oil filters. 90% of the oil flows through the primary filter and 10% flows through the bypass filter. Usually the bypass filter is more tightly woven, to trap extremely small particles. Bypass filtering systems also use bypass valves.

1. Primary (regular) filter
2. Bypass filter
3. Oil pump
4. Engine or component

On some turbocharged engines, oil flows from the filter to the turbocharger through an inlet line. An outlet line returns oil to the oil pan.

On other engines, clean oil leaves the oil filter(s) and enters the main oil gallery.

The main oil gallery is located in the block. This is the primary oil passage through the block.

From the oil gallery, the oil flows to all moving parts of the engine, including the main bearings and crankshaft.

1. Outlet
2. InletP

Oil flows from the gallery to the crankshaft, which then lubricates the main and connecting rod bearings.

1. Crankshaft Main Bearings
2. Oil Manifold
Caterpillar crankshafts have drilled oil passages which deliver oil to the connecting rod and main bearings.
Oil reaches the cylinder walls as it is slung out of the rod bearings and splashed off the piston undercrowns.

Oil travels through passages to lubricate all moving parts, including the valve train, injection pump housing, timing advance unit and other accessory components. Oil drains back to the oil pan through passages.

The oil lines, passages and bearings restrict the flow of oil, which creates oil pressure. Most of the oil system pressure is created by the main bearings. The oil pressure reading on a gauge is the result of this normal restriction.
Piston cooling jets spray oil to the underside of each piston, and will help lubricate the cylinder walls.

Crankcase breathers vent combustion gases that leak past piston rings.

This maintains stable pressures within the crankcase.

Breathers are often mounted on top of the engine.
This equalizes pressure inside the engine crankcase with pressure on the outside and permits oil to easily drain back to the oil pan.
In the lubrication system, the oil filter requires the most maintenance. It does get dirty and, if not properly maintained, can cause lubrication system problems.

Lubrication systems use several bypass and relief valves to protect the engine. Oil pumps (1) use pressure relief valves (2), while oil coolers (3) and oil filters (4) use bypass valves (5). The name of the valve describes how the valve operates. Pressure relief valves reduce system pressure, and bypass valves allow oil to flow around a component instead of through it.

The pressure relief valve is usually located near the oil pump. The relief valve is commonly a spring actuated valve. The relief valve opens when system pressures exceed the spring force on the valve. As long as pressure remains high, the valve remains open.

When the relief valve opens, some oil drains back to the oil pan. When oil pressure drops below the spring opening force of the valve, the valve closes.

The oil cooler bypass valve is a directional valve that opens when the pressure differential across the oil cooler is higher than the opening force required to open the valve. When the valve opens, oil diverts around the oil cooler. This ensures that some oil reaches vital engine parts even if there is an oil cooler problem. When the oil is cold, it may not flow well. This would open the valve. The oil cooler bypass valve is often built into the oil cooler.

The oil filter bypass valve is a directional valve that opens when the pressure differential across the oil filter exceeds the valve spring opening force. If the oil is thick, such as at engine startup, or if the filter is clogged, the filter bypass valve opens. Oil diverts around the filter, which ensures that some oil always reaches the bearings and other engine components. This protects the engine from oil starvation damage.

lessons.title: Engine Oil: Viscosity, Viscosity Index and TBN
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about viscosity, viscosity index, and TBN.
pages: Engines require the right type, the right viscosity and the correct quantity of oil in order to operate properly. Oil must lubricate, clean, and cool engine components under a variety of operating conditions. Oil must flow and lubricate in cold climates and be able to withstand heat without thinning or breaking down

The Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) has developed a classification system to describe an oil's ability to withstand extreme conditions without breaking down.

Oil is described according to its type and viscosity.
Oil type describes performance characteristics, such as detergency, dispersancy, and resistance to breakdown.

Oil type is identified with alphabetical letters like CE or CF-4.

Different engine models require different types of oil. Make sure you use the type of oil recommended for the engine.

Refer to the most recent literature for the correct recommendations.

Viscosity describes a base oil's resistance to flow. Flow relates directly to how well the oil coats and protects parts.

Viscosity changes with temperature. The higher the temperature, the lower the viscosity and the thinner the oil.

Viscosity Index, or VI, is a measure of a base oil's ability to resist viscosity changes with temperature changes.

1. High VI oil changes viscosity less as temperatures change.
2. Low VI oil changes viscosity more as temperatures change.

It is important that the oil not become too thin at high temperatures. Thin oils do not provide enough protection against wear.

Multiviscosity oils have been chemically altered to extend their operating range.

A lower viscosity base stock is blended with an additive which thickens the oil as temperature increases.

As multiviscosity oils deteriorate, viscosity reverts back to the lower viscosity of the base oil.
The oil label tells you much about the type and viscosity of the oil.

The Society of Automotive Engineers classifies oil according to the letters SAE followed by a number. The number describes the viscosity grade.

Single weight oils have only one number. Multiviscosity oils have two numbers.

Lower numbers mean the oil is thinner, and higher numbers mean the oil is thicker.

For multiviscosity oils:
• First number is the cold viscosity grade
• Second number is the hot weather viscosity grade.

Viscosity grade numbers with a “W” are considered winter oils, tested to have correct viscosity at 8 degrees Farenheit.

Numbers without the “W” are considered hot weather oils, tested to have correct viscosity at 210 degrees Farenheit.

Base oils are usually produced by refining crude oils.

Base oil cannot provide enough protection and lubrication for today's high performance engines.
Certain oil additives have been created to improve and strengthen the oil.

These are common oil additives:

1. Detergents help keep the engine clean.
2. Anti-wear Agents reduce friction.
3. Dispersants keep contaminant particles in suspension.
4. Alkalinity Agents neutralize acids in the oil.
5. Oxidation Inhibitors prevent the oil from oxidizing when it is exposed to air. Oxidation causes development of organic acids and carbonaceous matter.
6. Pour-Point Depressants keep the oil fluid at low temperatures. Petroleum base oils contain wax, which crystallizes at low temperatures. The depressants keep wax crystals from forming.
7. Viscosity Improvers keep the oil from becoming too thin at high temperatures.

The most common oil additive you will work with is Total Base Number, or TBN.

TBN is produced by adding alkalinity agents to the base stock.

The more alkaline the oil, the higher the TBN and the more acid it can neutralize.

The amount of alkalinity additive in an oil is indicated by the Total Base Number, or TBN. 
Diesel fuels may contain sulfur. When these fuels burn, the sulfur helps create acids. These highly corrosive acids contaminate the oil.

The alkalinity additives within the oil neutralize these acids. This prevents the sulfuric acid from corroding metal parts. The TBN number of the oil indicates how well it neutralizes acids. Since different fuels contain different amounts of sulfur, it's important to use an oil with a high enough TBN. Follow the recommendations of the engine manufacturer.

Over time, the oil additives degrade, and the oil's ability to lubricate decreases. 

If you do not change the oil frequently enough, the oil will oxidize, additives will deplete and sludge may form.

topics.title: Air Intake and Exhaust System
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will be able to identify the major components in an air intake/exhaust system and describe how they operate.

lessons.title: Air Intake and Exhaust Components
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn about the components in the air intake/exhaust system and identify the purpose of each.

You will be able to identify different air intake systems including NA, T, TA, ATTAC, JWAC, and SCAC.
