pages: Diesel engines require large quantities of air to burn the fuel. The air intake system must provide enough clean air for combustion. The exhaust system must remove heat and combustion gases. Any reduction in the flow of air or combustion gases through the system reduces engine performance.

A common intake/exhaust system includes a precleaner (1), an air filter (2), a turbocharger (3), an intake manifold (4), an aftercooler (5), exhaust manifold (6), exhaust stack (7), muffler and connecting pipes (8).

In order to service and troubleshoot the air system on an engine, it is important to understand the flow of air through the system and the function of each component. It is also important to know what the components look like and how they work.

Precleaners are often used in the air systems of diesel engines. 

The precleaner screens out heavier, larger contaminants suspended in the air.

Clean air is critical for peak engine performance. Dirt can increase wear and damage engine components.
Precleaners are often used in the air systems of on-highway trucks. The precleaner screens out heavier, larger contaminants suspended in the air.

Air leaves the precleaner and enters the air filter.
The air filter prevents smaller dirt and debris from entering the engine.

Clean air is critical for peak engine performance. Dirty air can increase wear and damage engine components.

The air filter housing holds the filter element.

From the air filter, the air flows into the turbocharger.

Turbochargers:
1. Help maintain engine power at high altitude.
2. Increase horsepower.

Turbochargers provide the engine with more air, enabling it to burn more fuel.

A turbocharger has two parts:

1. Air inlet side or compressor.
2. Exhaust side or turbine.

Exhaust gases from the exhaust manifold turn the exhaust turbine of the turbocharger.

Exhaust gases spin the turbine side. Since the compressor and turbine wheels are on the same shaft, the compressor turns as well. The faster the compressor side turns, the more air is “packed” into the air system, increasing air pressure and density. The increase in air pressure is called boost.

Waste gates are part of some turbochargers. If boost is higher than recommended, the waste gate opens to vent exhaust around the turbine. The reduced exhaust gas flow slows down the turbine and compressor, controlling boost pressure.

The turbocharger provides more air to improve combustion. As the air compresses, it heats up and expands, becoming less dense. This means there may not be enough air for good combustion at higher fuel settings. Most turbocharged engines use an aftercooler to reduce the temperature of the intake air.

Turbochargers increase the temperature of intake air to roughly 300 degrees F.

The hot intake air is less dense.

The aftercooler removes heat from the inlet air.
As the air cools, it becomes more dense. This means that more air can be packed into each cylinder.

Aftercoolers get their names because they cool the air after it passes through a turbocharger. Some aftercoolers are located between the turbocharger and inlet manifold. Others are found inside the intake manifold.

From the aftercooler, air flows into the intake manifold and to the intake valve ports for each cylinder.

The intake manifold is mounted on the cylinder head.

Air enters the combustion chamber where it burns.

Combustion gases exit the exhaust ports and enter the exhaust manifold.

The exhaust manifold is mounted on the cylinder head and fits over the exhaust ports.

From the turbocharger, exhaust gases are piped through the muffler and exhaust stack.

The muffler deadens exhaust noise and makes the machine quieter.

After exhaust gases pass through the muffler, they enter the exhaust stack.

The stack vents the exhaust away from the operator.

Exhaust gases enter the atmosphere from the stack.
In addition to the basic components you have just learned about, marine and industrial engines may use (1) a water cooled exhaust manifold and (2) a water cooled turbocharger.
2Precleaner, air filter, compressor, aftercooler, intake manifold, exhaust manifold, turbine, muffler, exhaust stack.
2Air filter, compressor, precleaner, intake manifold, aftercooler, turbine, exhaust manifold, muffler, exhaust stack.
2Precleaner, air filter, intake manifold, compressor, aftercooler, turbine, exhaust manifold, exhaust stack, muffler.
2Air filter, compressor, intake manifold, precleaner, turbine, exhaust manifold, aftercooler, muffler, exhaust stack.

Naturally Aspirated (NA) System 
Air intake systems that have neither a turbocharger nor an aftercooler are known as “naturally aspirated” systems. They are also known as “NA” intake systems.
Some air intake/exhaust systems have turbochargers but no aftercoolers. These are known as turbocharged or “T” systems.
This is what a typical T system looks like on an engine.

One of the most common air intake systems is known as a “turbocharged aftercooled system.” 
(This type of system is also known as a “TA.”)
These systems have a turbocharger and an aftercooler. Different types of aftercoolers can be used.

A jacket water aftercooled, or JWAC system, uses engine coolant to cool the inlet air.
The aftercooler housing fits inside the intake manifold. Engine coolant circulates and removes heat from the intake air before it reaches the intake manifold.

JWAC systems are used on many mobile applications.

Some air intake systems use outside air to cool the inlet air. This system is called “Air to Air After Cooled,” or “ATAAC.”

The aftercooler looks like a small radiator mounted in front of the coolant radiator. Ambient air blows over the aftercooler, cooling the warm inlet air.
This is what a typical ATAAC air system looks like on an engine.

“Separate Circuit After Cooled” or SCAC systems are most commonly found on marine applications.
Water cools the inlet air, but the SCAC and engine cooling systems are separate. An SCAC system has its own heat exchanger, pump, and water supply.
This is what a typical SCAC air system looks like on an engine.

topics.title: Fuel System
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will be able to identify fuel system components and their operation.

lessons.title: Fuel System Components
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn the purpose of the fuel system and how it operates.

You will learn to identify the components used in a pump and lines system and an electronic unit injection system, and identify the function of each component.

You will be able to trace the flow of fuel through the system.
pages:
The amount of fuel the engine burns is directly related to the amount of required horsepower and torque. In general, the more fuel the engine receives, the more torque is available at the flywheel. The fuel system delivers clean fuel, at the right time and in the right quantity, to meet engine horsepower demand.

The fuel system components match fuel delivery to engine horsepower demand by altering how much fuel is injected, and when it is injected. These functions are handled by the heart of the fuel system, the fuel injection pump.
There are two broad categories of fuel systems, the pump and lines system, and the electronic unit injection system.

cA pump and lines fuel system consists of:

1. a fuel tank
2. fuel filters
3. transfer pump
4. injection pump
5. governor
6. timing advance mechanism
7. fuel ratio control
8. high pressure fuel lines
9. low pressure fuel lines
10. nozzles 
11. a return lineP

The fuel tank stores fuel.

Fuel tanks are available in different sizes.

You can find fuel tanks located in a variety of places, depending on the application.

Fuel begins to flow when you turn the key to start the engine.

As you turn the key, a solenoid is actuated which allows fuel to flow from the transfer pump to the injection pump.

The fuel transfer pump pulls fuel from the tank, through the primary fuel filter.

The primary fuel filter removes large debris from the fuel.

Some fuel systems also have a water separator.

The water separator allows any condensation or trapped water to settle out.

Water in the fuel can cause serious engine damage.

From the primary filter, fuel enters the transfer pump.

The transfer pump provides flow throughout the low pressure portion of the fuel system.

The primary purpose of the fuel transfer pump is to keep an adequate supply of clean fuel in the injection pump.

Fuel exits the fuel transfer pump and enters the secondary or final fuel filter.

This filter screens minute particles and contaminants from the fuel, which could damage nozzles or plug injectors.

Final filters are located between the transfer pump and the injection pump housing.
Unlike oil filters, the fuel filters have no bypass valve. If the filters get clogged, fuel flow stops and the engine will not run. This protects the engine from dirty fuel.

Most final fuel filters incorporate a fuel priming pump in the base.

You can use the pump to prime the system if you have removed the fuel pump housing for a major service.

The pump is also used to prime the fuel system after changing the fuel filter.

Fuel exits the final filter and flows into the fuel gallery within the injection pump housing.
Pumps in the housing measure and pressurize the fuel.

The housing is generally located near the front of the engine, because the pump is gear driven from the camshaft.

A timing advance unit, mechanical governor, and fuel ratio control are attached to the housing.

On pump and lines systems, steel high pressure fuel lines connect fuel injection pumps to nozzles.
The high pressure side of the fuel system consists of the high pressure lines and the nozzles.

Proper quantities of pressurized fuel travel through the high pressure fuel lines to the fuel nozzles.

Nozzle fuel travels through high pressure fuel lines to the nozzles.

Nozzles are located in the cylinder head.

Nozzles have valves that open when fuel pressure gets high enough. When the valve opens, fuel is atomized and sprayed into the combustion chamber. At the end of injection, there is a rapid pressure drop which closes the valve.

More fuel is available in the fuel injection pump housing than the engine can use.

The return line:
1. Directs excess fuel back to the tank
2. Removes air from the fuel
3. Cools the fuel by keeping it in motion. The fuel system will not operate correctly without a fuel return line.
Every fuel system has either electronic or manual methods of turning off the fuel supply.

Electronic unit injection (EUI) systems use some of the same components as a pump and lines system. EUI systems use (1) a fuel tank, (2) primary fuel filter, (3) fuel transfer pump, (4) final fuel filter, and (5) a return line. The fuel injection pump is the point where EUI systems differ from pump and lines systems.

Fuel exits the final fuel filter and enters a fuel manifold.

The fuel manifold is usually part of the engine block. The manifold is filled with fuel.

The fuel injection pump, high pressure lines, and nozzles are replaced by a single component called a unit injector.

Electronic unit injectors are mounted in the cylinder head.

Fuel in the manifold enters the injector, which meters, pressurizes, and injects the fuel.
Electronic unit injectors can be recognized by the solenoid attached near the top.

On an EUI system, the mechanical governor, timing advance, and fuel ratio control are replaced by electronics.

EUI systems use an electronic control module (ECM) to house some of the electronics and programming information.

The combustion chamber design affects fuel efficiency and engine performance. The design of the piston and the method used to inject fuel into the cylinder determine how quickly and completely the fuel burns.

In pump and line systems, there are two types of combustion chamber design: (1) precombustion chamber or PC, and (2) direct injection or DI.
In EUI fuel systems there is only one basic type of combustion chamber, the DI.
In a direct injection combustion chamber design, fuel is injected directly into the cylinder through the nozzle.

In a PC system, the nozzle injects fuel into a precombustion chamber where it ignites. This forces the remaining fuel into the main chamber, where full combustion takes place. In some engines, glow plugs are used to warm the air when starting the engine.
To prevent burning a hole in the top of the piston, PC pistons have a steel heat plug mounted near the center.

lessons.title: Injection Pump, Governor and Timing Advance
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn how a fuel injection pump, governor, and timing advance unit operate. 
You will learn the advantages of a unit injection system.

And, you will understand the meaning of low-idle speed, high-idle speed, overspeed, full load speed, and lug.
pages:
Over the years, CAT has made significant design changes in the fuel system. The new designs have improved engine performance and reduced emissions.

This topic explains two basic methods of fuel injection: mechanical systems (left) which use a governor, timing advance unit and fuel ratio control, and (right) electronic unit injection systems.

In diesel engines, fuel is injected during the compression stroke, before the piston reaches top dead center. The basic principle of fuel injection is that the right amount of fuel must be injected at the right time to satisfy engine horsepower demands.

Fuel requires time to burn. The right amount of fuel must be injected at the appropriate point in the compression stroke so that it burns completely. This is known as (1) the “burn window,” and is measured in degrees of crankshaft rotation. Degrees of rotation means the number of degrees the crankshaft rotates while fuel is being injected.

The burn window is defined by the starting point of injection, or timing, and the length of time injection occurs, or duration. Both (2) timing and (3) duration are measured in degrees of crankshaft rotation.

In a mechanical fuel system, the (1) fuel injection pump, (2) timing advance, (3) governor, and (4) fuel ratio control all work together to control fuel injection. These components have a direct effect on engine performance. 

As engine load and engine speed change, varying amounts of fuel must be injected at different times in order to maintain the proper burn windows. A timing advance unit controls when fuel is injected, and the governor controls how much fuel is delivered to the engine, or duration.

The fuel injection pump is the heart of the fuel system. Understanding how the pump operates is a critical first step in understanding fuel injection. In pump and lines systems, fuel injection pumps usually have (1) a plunger inside (2) a barrel. The plunger moves up and down, following the motion of the fuel pump camshaft.

Low pressure fuel in (3) the gallery flows to and from the barrel through (4) ports.

The plunger has a groove or (5) scroll machined into it. When this scroll aligns with the ports, fuel can flow from the inlet port, through (6) the pumping chamber, to the outlet port.

When the scroll blocks the ports, the fuel in the pumping chamber is trapped and forced to the nozzle. It is at this point that injection begins. This point is called injection timing and is controlled by changing the position of the fuel pump camshaft. It is the beginning of the burn window.

Injection occurs during the time the ports are closed off by the scroll. This length of time is called (1) duration. The longer the duration, the more fuel is injected. Duration is controlled by rotating the plunger in its bore.

This changes the amount of scroll that exists between the ports. The ports are either shut off sooner (fuel off) or left open longer (fuel on).

Injection duration is controlled by the governor and rack. All the fuel pumps are linked to the governor by the fuel control rack. When the engine requires more fuel, it can only get it if injection duration increases. The governor senses the need for fuel and moves the rack.

The rack is a straight gear that meshes with gears on each plunger.

Moving the rack causes the plungers to rotate.

The plungers rotate slightly in their bores so that the scroll keeps the ports closed longer, increasing duration. This is called the FUEL ON position (1).

As demand for fuel lessens, the rack moves toward the FUEL OFF position (2) and the ports open sooner.

Mechanical governors use a system of flyweights and springs to move the control rack. The springs always try to move the rack to Fuel On. The flyweights always try to move the rack to Fuel Off. When the forces are balanced, the engine operates at a stable rpm.

Fuel delivery directly affects engine speed and horsepower output. Increased fuel delivery increases engine output.

Governors regulate fuel delivery to control engine speed between a low rpm setting and a high rpm setting, called low and high idle. Governors are usually mounted on the rear of the fuel injection pump.

A timing advance unit “advances” or “retards” fuel injection by altering the fuel pump camshaft rotation.

Fuel injection timing can be advanced or retarded.

Advance Timing means fuel is injected sooner.

Retard Timing means fuel is injected later.

The fuel system cannot operate in isolation from other engine systems. In particular, the air intake system is critical. Fuel will not burn completely unless there is enough air.

The fuel ratio control ensures there is the right amount of fuel injected for the amount of air present in the cylinder. It senses boost pressure, and will “override” the governor to prevent excess fuel from being injected. This helps control emissions and improves fuel efficiency.

The fuel ratio control is mounted on the governor.
On an EUI system, the rack, the mechanical governor, timing advance, and fuel ratio control are replaced by the electronic control module (ECM) and several solenoids or sensors.
In place of a timing advance mechanism, a timing wheel and sensor monitor engine speed electronically.

All of the functions performed by the mechanical units are handled electronically, giving better accuracy and reliability.
The ECM senses engine speed and load and adjusts timing and duration automatically.

Up to this point you have learned about the various components of the fuel injection pump and how the timing advance unit and governor work to adjust the burn window.

Now, let's look at how it all works together during engine operation.

During actual operation, the engine is usually working under load. The governor determines what engine rpm is correct for the applied load and moves the rack to fuel ON or fuel OFF to establish the right rpm. The timing advance mechanism senses the increase or decrease in rpm and varies the injection timing to start the burn window at the correct location.

Low idle is the lowest speed at which the engine is allowed to run under no load. 

The fuel injection pumps are positioned so that minimum amounts of fuel are delivered to the engine.
High idle is the maximum rpm the engine is allowed to run under no load.

All diesel engines are given a rating called Full Load at rated speed.

This is the rpm at which the engine delivers rated horsepower when fully loaded.

The engine is operating under load, and the governor flyweights and springs are stabilized to provide a constant rpm.

Sometimes engines are operated in such a way that the rpm is forced to exceed the high idle rpm.
The governor shuts the fuel off but the engine still exceeds the high idle speed.

This is called overspeed or overrun and is usually the result of operator error.

Sometimes engines are loaded too heavily, and even though the governor moves the rack to the full FUEL ON position, the engine rpm does not increase. This is called lug operation.

Under these circumstances, the governor is unable to match the horsepower requirements since no more fuel is available.
The engine operates under a variety of conditions. Match each term to its definition.
The rpm where the maximum rated horsepower is developed.q
The maximum speed (no load) at which a governor allows the engine to run.
The lowest speed (no load) at which a governor controls the engine speed.

lessons.title: Fuel Properties
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn about specific gravity... viscosity... cloud point... sulfur... and contaminants. 

You will understand API rating and how it affects engine performance. And, you will understand Cetane Index and how a low rating affects engine ignition.
pages: Fuel produces power in a diesel engine when it is atomized and mixed with air in the combustion chamber. Pressure caused by the piston rising in the cylinder causes a rapid temperature increase. When fuel is injected, the fuel/air mixture ignites and the energy of the fuel is released. A perfect fuel would burn completely, leaving no residue or smoke products. However, there is no perfect fuel.

Fuel quality affects the performance and maintenance of any diesel engine.

It is important to understand basic fuel properties to be able to judge fuel quality.

These properties have an impact on the operation of a diesel engine and its fuel handling and fuel treatment systems.

The specific gravity of diesel fuel (1) is the weight of a fixed volume of fuel compared to the weight of the same volume of water (2), at the same temperature.

The higher the specific gravity, the heavier the fuel. Heavier fuels have more energy or power per volume for the engine to use.

Specific gravity can be measured on the American Petroleum Institute (API) scale.
The scale is inverse to the specific gravity.
The higher the API number, the lighter the fuel. Fuel with a low API number provides more horsepower.

Caterpillar recommends 35 degrees API (minimum) fuel. Kerosene might have a measurement of 40 - 44 degrees API.

Columns 1 and 2 (gravity):
(1) measures degrees API at 15 degrees C (60 degrees F)
(2) measures specific gravity at 15 degrees C (60 degrees F)
 Column 3 (density):
(3) measures pounds per gallon

Viscosity is a measure of a liquid's resistance to flow.

High viscosity means the fuel is thick and does not flow as easily.

Fuel with the wrong viscosity, either too high or too low, can cause engine damage.

Cloud point is that temperature at which a cloud or haze appears in the fuel.

This appearance is caused by the temperature falling below the melting point of waxes or paraffins that occur naturally in petroleum products.

The cloud point of the fuel must be below the lowest outside, or ambient, temperature to prevent filters from plugging.

Cloud point is determined by the refiner.
Sulfur is an element which occurs naturally in all crude oils. You should be aware of you fuel sulfur content. Sulfur over 0.5% can severely reduce engine life unless proper steps are taken.

When diesel fuel containing sulfur is burned in an engine's combustion chamber, oxides of sulfur form and react with water vapor to create sulfuric acid.

If these acid vapors condense, they chemically attack the metal surfaces of valve guides, cylinder liners, and may affect bearings.

?To limit sulfuric acid formation:

1. Keep engine temperature above 175 degrees F, or 80 degrees C, to limit condensation.
2. Use oil with a TBN sufficient to counteract acid formation.

The Cetane Index is a measure of the ignition quality of fuel which affects engine starting and acceleration. The higher the Cetane rating, the more quickly the fuel will ignite. Cetane is rated using an index.

Caterpillar recommends:
35 Cetane for precombustion chamber fuel systems.
40 Cetane for direct injection fuel systems.

Fuel with a low cetane number can cause:

1. Ignition delay, starting difficulties and engine knock.
2. Poor fuel economy, a loss of power and sometimes engine damage.
3. White smoke and odor at start-up on colder days.

Cetane improver additives can often reduce white smoke during engine start-up in cold weather.

Contaminants in the fuel can also affect engine performance.

Contaminants are foreign elements which can get into fuel and cause problems.

The two most common contaminants are water and sediment.

Water can become a contaminant:
1. If it is introduced into the fuel during shipment.
2. If condensation occurs.

Excess water in fuel can cause:
1. Fuel pump damage if fuel is used to lubricate the pump.

Sediment consists of items like:

1. Rust
2. Scale
3. Weld Slag
4. Dirt
5. Other debris that often get into fuel tanks and cause problems.

All fuel should be cleaned by the primary and final fuel filters on the engine.

topics.title: Starting Systems
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will understand common diesel engine starting systems, and identify the components of each system.

lessons.title: Electrical and Air Starting Systems
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn that cranking speed is more important than cranking duration for a diesel engine.

You will learn about electrical and air starting systems, and understand the unique components used in each system.
pages:
Starting systems operate by cranking the engine to build up enough compression and heat to ignite the fuel. On all starting systems, a cranking motor turns the ring gear and flywheel. As the flywheel turns, air is compressed inside the cylinders. 

Cranking speed is more critical to starting than cranking duration, because speed determines the amount of heat generated in the cylinder.

Cranking motors are powered by electricity or air.

An electrical starting system has:

1. Batteries
2. Cranking motor with a solenoid switch
3. Starter switch
4. Wires and cable.

When the key start switch is on, the battery provides electrical power to the components in the starting system. The cranking motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy.

You might also find a master switch, which disconnects the batteries, or a neutral switch, which prevents the starting circuits from closing when the transmission is in gear.

An air starting system uses compressed air to run the cranking motor. They have a faster cranking speed than an electric starting system.

Air systems are common on off-highway trucks. The drawback with an air system is that you have only one or two attempts before exhausting the air supply.
The air tank holds the compressed air. Control or relay valves open and close, allowing air to flow to the cranking motor.
An on/off push button valve starts the air flow to the relay valve diaphragm.
The relay valve opens, sending air from the air tank to the cranking motor.
The compressed air enters the cranking motor, turning it.
Air is also directed on to a servo, which engages the pinion with the ring gear, turning it.

title: Systems Tests and Maintenance Procedures
overview: Chapter 1, Engine Systems Tests, will teach you how to properly perform a variety of routine test procedures on the various systems of a diesel engine. After completing this topic, you will understand the cooling system tests that are used during maintenance. You will also know the lubrication system tests, the air system tests, as well as fuel system tests you might have to perform during routine maintenance.

lessons.title: Cooling System Tests
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will be able to recognize cooling system tests and the procedures for conducting them.

You will be able to interpret results from antifreeze and coolant conditioner concentration tests and determine an appropriate corrective action.
pages: Because the cooling system is so critical to the life of the engine, there are several test procedures to ensure the cooling system is operating properly.

Check the coolant level frequently. The cooling system can be under pressure. Loosen the cap slowly to prevent injury. Always check the Operation and Maintenance Manual for the proper fill level. The coolant level should come up to the bottom of the filler pipe.

There are various methods to test the coolant.

A Caterpillar Coolant and Battery Tester tells you the freeze protection provided by the solution.

To use the coolant tester: 

Open the hinged cover and clean the site glass, place a drop of coolant on the glass, close the hinged cover, hold the tester up to natural light. Make sure the hinged cover is on top of the tester.

The freeze protection temperature is indicated by the line between the light and dark portions in the site glass. Read the temperature alongside the ethylene glycol scale.

To determine the antifreeze concentration using the results from the coolant tester:

Obtain Caterpillar SEDB0518-07 "Know Your Cooling System" or Caterpillar SEDB0978-01 "Coolant and Your Engine." 

1. Refer to the Freezing Point Curve chart located in either publication.
2. Locate the freeze protection temperature from your test result on the chart.
3. Trace a line from the temperature on the left scale of the freeze protection curve. Trace another line from the intersection point on the freeze curve to the antifreeze concentration on the bottom scale.
4. Read the antifreeze concentration.

Another method to test antifreeze concentration requires the use of the Coolant Test Kit. Floating balls in a dropper provide an approximate concentration of ethylene glycol.

To perform the test: fill the dropper with coolant to the test line, observe how many balls float. Compare your test results with the instruction card from the test kit. In general, the more balls that float, the higher the concentration.

You should determine the antifreeze concentration before you test the coolant conditioner concentration.

To read the test results accurately, you must know how much antifreeze is in the coolant.

To test coolant conditioner concentration, use the Caterpillar test kit. To perform the test:

1. Put 1 milliliter of coolant into the vial. 
2. Add water to the 10 milliliter mark.
3. Add three drops of Solution A and mix it.
4. Add Solution B one drop at a time, mixing after each addition. Count the drops. 
5. When the color changes from red to green, gray or blue and stays that way, the test is done.

Compare the number of drops of Solution B you added to the vial to the numbers on the chart.

The antifreeze concentration of the sample determines which scale to use.

Read and note the concentration of coolant conditioner.

After measuring the concentration of antifreeze and coolant conditioner, determine whether the coolant mix needs adjustment.

1. If the coolant level is low, but the concentrations are acceptable, mix new coolant and fill the system.

2. If the concentrations are too high, drain some coolant from the system and add the correct amount of new coolant.

Retest the new mixture after operating the engine long enough for the coolant to get fully mixed.

Do not add more conditioner if the coolant conditioner concentration is acceptable.
P

During maintenance of the cooling system, visually examine the coolant.

Oil (1), fuel (2), or debris (3) in the coolant indicates a problem that needs investigation.

If the coolant shows evidence of a leak, inspect the engine.

Leaks provide a way for air and foreign fluids to enter the cooling system.

Excess air reduces cooling capacity and can produce cavitation erosion.

Test the radiator cap during your routine cooling system maintenance. The test makes sure the cap will open at the correct pressure. The opening pressure is stamped on the cap.

To test the pressure cap for the pressure that makes the cap open:

1. Remove the cap from the radiator.
2. Put the pressure cap on the recommended Cooling System Pressurizing Pump Group for the engine.
3. Operate the pump and look at the gauge for the exact pressure that makes the pressure cap open.
4. Make a comparison of the reading on the gauge with the correct pressure at which the pressure cap must open.
5. If the cap is defective, install a new one.

Check the seal.

Look for damage to the seal or to the surface that seals. Any foreign material or deposits on the cap, seal or surface that seals, must be removed.

If the cap is worn or damaged, replace the cap.

When you perform major maintenance on a cooling system, test the regulator to make sure it is working properly.

A regulator failure can cause overheating or overcooling, which may result in serious engine damage.

Examine the regulator for external damage or rupture.

Then, test it to make sure it opens at the proper temperature.

Regulator Testing Procedure:

1. Remove the regulator from the engine.
2. Note the opening temperature stamped on the side of the regulator, or in the manual.
3. Hang the regulator in water. The regulator should not touch the sides or bottom of the container.
4. Heat the water to the opening temperature.
5. Remove the regulator, measure the opening distance, and compare it to the specifications for the regulator.

lessons.title: Lubrication System Tests
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn when an Scheduled Oil Sample should be taken and the type of information it provides. You will understand why monitoring oil level, oil pressure and oil consumption are important service procedures.
pages:
There are several system tests you can do to make sure the engine lubrication system is performing properly: 

1. Oil Pressure
2. Scheduled Oil Sampling
3. Oil Level
P

Every time you start the engine, check the oil pressure on the oil pressure gauge. Oil system pressure can indicate whether the components in the system are operating normally. For the most accurate oil pressure reading, attach a pressure gauge to the recommended oil pressure test site. Start the engine, and read the gauge. Compare the reading to specifications in the service manual. 
P

Every time you change the oil, you should collect a scheduled oil sample.

The oil sample is sent to a lab for analysis. An S·O·S provides information on engine wear and oil condition.

For more information on S·O·S and sampling procedure, please review General Maintenance Procedures, later in this course.

Check the oil level daily to monitor engine oil consumption.

Diesel engines do consume oil, and you will have to add new oil periodically. This is normal.

If you check the level every day, you will be able to spot changes in oil consumption which could indicate a problem.

You and the operator share this responsibility.
To check the oil level, pull out the dipstick and wipe it off. Insert the dipstick back into its port. Pull the dipstick out and read the oil level.

Many dipsticks have different markings on each side. Make sure to read the right one.

1. If you measured the oil level with the engine stopped, read the side of the dipstick that says Engine Stopped.
2. If you measured the oil with the engine running, read the side of the dipstick that says Engine Running.

On each side of the dipstick are two lines.

One line says "Low" or "Add" and the other says "Full."

In many cases, the distance between the lines indicates a quantity of oil, such as a gallon.

Therefore, if the oil level was on the "Low" mark, you could estimate that the engine needs a gallon of oil.

Some dipsticks have no "Low" or "Full" markings when the engine's shipped to the customer.

This is because the engine may be mounted at an angle, and a premarked dipstick would be inaccurate.

In a case like this, the operator must mark the dipstick so it indicates the correct oil quantity in his engine.

Check the dipstick to make sure it is the correct part number for the engine.

It is not uncommon to find that someone has switched dipsticks.

This can lead to under or over-filling because the stick reads the wrong level.

If too much oil is added, the design of the engine will blow oil out of the seals.

As the oil level increases beyond the specified level, it covers the front and rear seals on the crankshaft.

While the engine is running, the seals spill the excess oil.

This leads to the impression that the engine is consuming too much oil.

lessons.title: Air Intake and Exhaust System Tests
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn about air intake and exhaust system tests such as boost, inlet restriction, and smoke density.

You will also learn the step by step procedure for a snap idle smoke test.
pages:
½Any change in the flow of air or exhaust through the system will affect engine performance. A variety of tests can be used to determine if the air intake and exhaust system is functioning normally. These tests include:

1. Checking the air filter indicator
2. Checking boost
3. Smoke density test
4. Checking for an inlet restriction

Some engines are equipped with an air filter indicator.

The indicator can be mounted in the cab, the engine compartment, or on the air filter housing.

A diaphragm inside the indicator moves in response to vacuum inside the air filter.

The greater the vacuum or restriction, the higher the diaphragm is pulled.

You can reset the diaphragm by pressing the Reset button.

Since the air filter indicator can be reset anytime, there may be an inlet restriction even though the indicator appears normal.

If the indicator diaphragm is in the "replace" zone, inspect the air filter element.

It is best to rely upon visual inspection of the filter to make sure it is not clogged.

If the filter is clogged, replace it.

To determine if enough air is entering the intake manifold, use a boost pressure test. Boost is measured with the Caterpillar engine pressure gauge group. Boost is a measurement of the difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure within the intake manifold.

To measure boost, make sure the engine is off. Connect line and adapter to recommended test plug on intake manifold. Check service manual for exact location. Connect line to the compound pressure gauge. Run engine until it reaches normal operating temperature. Load the engine. Read boost from gauge and compare to specifications. Boost pressure can be affected by air restrictions in the filter or leaks between the compressor and intake valve.
5Always check the service manual for the engine you are working on to determine which pressure gauge to use. The H2O gauge shown in the
previous demonstration may not be appropriate for some boost measurements.A

Smoke tests measure how thoroughly the engine is burning fuel.

The smoke density tool works by gauging the amount of light blocked by smoke as it passes through a sensor.

Density results are displayed as a percentage.

For example, 04 means 4% of the light is blocked by smoke.

Smoke density is measured using a Snap Idle Test.

Snap Idle Test Procedure:

1. Start engine and put transmission in neutral.
2. Press accelerator 3 times to clear stack.
3. Connect sensor to top of stack and connect meter.
4. Turn on meter.
5. Accelerate to high idle 3 times.
6. Average the two closest readings. Compare your result with regulations.
P

An inlet restriction can affect engine performance.

Inlet restriction tests check the pressure drop across a component.

The most common cause of a restriction is a clogged air filter, but other components can also become plugged.

To perform an inlet restriction test using the Caterpillar Engine Pressure Group:

1. Make sure the engine is off. 
2. Connect a line to the test plug on the air filter housing. You may have to remove the air filter indicator. Refer to the special instructions for exact location. 
3. Connect the line to the vacuum gauge. 
4. Start the engine and read the gauge. 
5. Compare the results to manual specifications.

lessons.title: Fuel System Tests
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn:

1. How to measure dynamic timing.
2. How to interpret the results of a dynamic timing test. 
3. The procedure for timing advance start and stop adjustment.
4. The pin timing procedure.
5. How to identify test results that indicate a failed injector.
P
pages:
Because the fuel system is so critical to engine performance, many tests have been developed to make sure the components are working properly.

Many of these tests are diagnostic, or are used after a complete engine overhaul.

Some tests are performed on a routine basis. This segment covers common tests used during performance testing or during an overhaul. The tests covered in this segment include dynamic testing, adjusting timing advance, pin timing and nozzle testing.
P

Dynamic timing measurements provide information on fuel injection for all cylinders. Dynamic timing indicates whether (1) reference timing and (2) timing advance start and (3) stop are within specification. Dynamic timing also reveals whether the timing advance unit is operating normally.

Before you conduct a timing measurement, plot the timing specifications for the engine on a graph. The timing specifications are available from the service literature system.

Use the recommended timing indicator for the engine model. The indicator uses transducers to measure two signals: when fuel is injected and when the piston reaches Top Dead Center. It calculates the time difference between the two signals and displays a reading in "degrees before Top Dead Center."P

1. Attach fuel line transducer

2. Attach top dead center transducer

3. Connect indicator to power

4. Start engine and check fuel pressure

5. Begin dynamic timing measurement at 1000 RPM

6. Plot timing every 100 RPM

7. Connect all points with a lineP

Your timing measurements must fall within the specified range for reference timing, timing advance start, and timing advance stop.

1. Timing advance must occur smoothly throughout the specified speed range.

2. Sudden jumps indicate component problems.
2The time between fuel injection and top dead center.
2The time between fuel ignition and the end of the power stroke.
2The time between the start of fuel injection and the end of fuel injection.
2The time between fuel injection and fuel ignition.

After you have performed a dynamic timing measurement you will be able to evaluate automatic timing advance unit operation. You cannot truly evaluate timing advance operation without performing a dynamic timing test.

The timing points must fall within the specifications for (1) reference timing, (2) timing advance start, and (3) timing advance stop.
You can easily tell if timing advance start and stop is (1) too early or (2) too late. Timing advance start and stop can be adjusted if necessary.

To adjust Timing Advance:

1. Loosen locknut.
2. Turn large screw clockwise to increase timing advance start.
3. Turn small screw clockwise to decrease stop RPM.

If you adjust timing advance start, you must also adjust timing advance stop. When you turn the "start" screw (1), the "stop" screw (2) rides along with it which resets timing advance stop automatically.

You must back out the "stop" screw to reset the timing advance stop to the correct RPM. After adjusting timing advance start or stop, recheck the dynamic timing.

If dynamic timing indicates that the reference timing of the engine (1) is not within specification, you should check the mechanical alignment of the components. Pin timing is the factory reference point, and is based on the correct alignment of the engine components.

Pin timing physically aligns engine components with metal pins. To perform the procedure:

1. Place No. 1 piston at TDC (Top Dead Center) on compression stroke.
2. Pin the fuel injection pump housing to fuel pump camshaft with timing bolt.
3. Pin the flywheel to flywheel housing with timing bolt.

If both pins fit at the same time, timing is correct.

Fuel nozzles should be inspected and tested before installation.

During an overhaul, all nozzles are usually tested.

Nozzles must be tested off the engine on the recommended test stand.
P

Nozzles are tested for:

1. Valve opening/closing pressure
2. Valve seating
3. Back leakage
4. Spray patternP
Nozzles that do not open (or open at the wrong pressure) should be replaced.
Replace nozzles that do not mist fuel properly.
Replace the nozzle if too much fuel leaks off.
Replace nozzles if too little fuel leaks off.
2They are not tested; if a malfunction is suspected they are replaced.

chapters.title: General Maintenance Procedures
intro: Chapter 2, General Maintenance Procedures, will teach you how to properly perform a variety of routine procedures that are critical to the performance and life of an engine.

topics.title: General Safety Guidelines
topics.summary: After completing this topic -- General Safety Guidelines -- you will understand the basic safety guidelines which apply to all diesel engine shops. You will know about personal protective devices, environmental safety guidelines, and safe engine work practices.

lessons.title: Personal Safety
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about personal safety devices which may be required in a diesel engine shop.
pages: There are safety warnings everywhere. Read them and understand all safety precautions and warnings for the engine and for any products or tools you use on it. Most accidents are caused by failure to observe basic safety rules or precautions. By following a few general guidelines, you will work more safely.
Do not take safety precautions lightly. The types of injuries that could result from improper procedures are serious, and could even result in death.

If you use a tool, procedure or operating technique that is not specifically recommended, make sure that it is safe for you and others, and will not damage the equipment. 

Caterpillar cannot anticipate every possible situation that might involve a potential hazard. Use your best judgement to ensure that your actions will not injure you, others, or damage the equipment.

There are many things you can do to protect yourself and others from injury. First and foremost, become familiar with the safe job practices and safety equipment requirements for the work you are performing. If you do not know what they are, ask for help.

There are several protective devices such as safety glasses, rubber gloves, steel tipped shoes, ear plugs, hard hats, and aprons that may need to be worn depending on the work location. Be familiar with the safety equipment requirements for the work area.

Some chemicals used with engines can be hazardous. Battery acid, for example. Become familiar with the hazardous chemicals used in your work area and know what personal safety devices you should use when working with them.

Mines, construction sites, and other hazardous or noisy work areas may require special safety equipment...gloves to protect your hands, hard hat and steel-toed boots to protect your head and feet, and ear plugs to block out the loud noise. Always use the protective devices appropriate for the job you are doing.
Never wear jewelry, loose fitting or torn clothing that can get caught in moving parts. This technician could get his shirt caught in a moving component of the engine.

Although it may seem a quick way to clean up your clothes and skin, the pressure of compressed air to spray away dirt could force oil and fuel particles under your skin. So, do not clean your clothing or skin with compressed air.
This technician could really hurt his back lifting this way. Do not lift heavy equipment or components without help. Use a hoist when necessary.
Remove rings before doing mechanical work because they can get caught in moving parts and can short-circuit electrical connections and cause severe burns.
Always use recommended procedures and equipment when climbing on and off of machinery.

You can protect yourself from injury by using good work habits. Be careful around the engine. If you get a hand or finger caught when moving heavy components, you could really hurt yourself. It is also easy to slip and fall when climbing on or off of machinery.

lessons.title: Safe Work Environment
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn about safe and unsafe work environments. You will also learn the procedures and guidelines required to prepare the engine for a service procedure.
pages: Environmental safety means keeping the area you work in free of hazards.
Keep your work area well ventilated to minimize exhaust fumes. If you have permanent exhaust systems, use them to vent fumes outside.
Clean up any spills immediately to prevent contaminating the environment or causing injury to someone who might slip on them. Put working tools and equipment in their proper place.
If the engine is in a truck, block the wheels. If the engine is used in some other type of equipment, block or stabilize hydraulic and mechanical systems.
Put warning tags on the engine and in the operator's compartment. Tag the steering wheel so it is clear that work is in progress and that no one should try to start the engine.
Be sure to observe all NO SMOKING areas since a cigarette could cause an explosion by igniting hydrogen gas fumes in battery compartments.

lessons.title: Safety Precautions Before Service
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn the common safety precautions which should be followed before performing any service procedure.

You will also learn the proper test procedures for safely checking pressurized systems and working on a diesel engine. P
pages:
Because some diesel engine systems generate high pressures and temperatures, special precautions are necessary to prevent injuries. 

Always follow the service manual procedures for the specific engine.
Although there are some exceptions, almost all service procedures should be done on a cool engine.
Batteries should be disconnected and isolator switches turned OFF before starting work to prevent accidental starts and components shorting out. It also protects you from burns and shocks.

Never use your bare hand to check high pressure fuel lines for leaks. Fuel under pressure can pierce your skin and cause blood poisoning. 

Use a shop towel to help test for leaks in pressurized systems. Wipe the suspect fitting, and watch for leaks from a safe distance.

Never bend or hit a fuel injection line when you remove or install it. The lines carry fuel at extremely high pressures, and any damage increases the risk of leaks.

When the engine is turned off, most systems drop pressure quickly. Check the service manual to see if any systems stay pressurized when the engine is off.

Cooling systems generally drop pressure more slowly, be extra careful when working with them. To avoid being burned by hot, pressurized spray, cover radiator caps when you open cooling systems.

When using lifting equipment, attach the hooks with the hook ends facing out (left photo). When the hook faces out, the load is distributed straight through the chain. This reduces damage to the equipment.
Attach hoist chains so they are as perpendicular as possible. The more vertical the chains, the more load they can safely carry.
Operate the hoist slowly because the component might start to swing. Positioning the hoist directly over the component reduces the swing.
Make sure the rated lifting capacity is higher than the load.

topics.title: Engine Identification and Inspection
topics.summary:
After completing this topic, you will be able to identify engine information plates, identification tags and service meters. You will understand the types of information available from these sources. 
You will also be able to conduct a visual inspection of an engine.

lessons.title: Identification Tags and Information Plates
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn how to locate an identification tag and information plate on an engine.

You will also learn to calculate a service interval using hours, miles, and gallons of fuel consumed.
pages:
Whenever you service an engine, you should always perform a visual inspection. A visual exam will tell you a lot about the general condition of the engine.
P

On Cat engines, the information plate provides most of the information you will need. Information plates are often located on the intake manifold or valve cover. For the exact location, check the manual.
Electronic engines use plates plus computer software to store performance information.

Every piece of data on the information plate is useful when you service or test an engine. The serial number is a unique number which identifies each engine. 

P
The arrangement number is a six digit number used with the serial number to access the Caterpillar parts and ordering system.
Use the performance specification or zero-T (0-T) number to access the Fuel Settings and Related Information Fiche. With the zero-T number, you can look up specifications for a particular engine.
In addition to the information plate, the serial number and model number are located on an ID tag on the block. The serial number is also stamped into the block.
Make sure you keep the original information plate. The plate and ID tag must match. Otherwise, you could look up information for the wrong engine.

Besides the data from the information plate, you have to know how long it has been since the engine was serviced. There are three ways to calculate the service interval: service hours, mileage or fuel consumption. 

Every engine model can have different service intervals. Make sure to check the service manual to find out if the engine is due for service.

To calculate the service interval using the fuel consumption technique, add the total gallons of fuel used since the last service. Fuel consumption is the most accurate method to determine the service interval because it compensates for engine load. 

You must have accurate operator logs in order to use this method.

Calculating Service Intervals by 
 Fuel Consumption
To calculate the service interval using the mileage method, take the current odometer reading (1), and subtract the previous reading (2) found in the service logs.

lessons.title: Visual Inspection
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn the purpose and procedures of a visual inspection. You will learn to identify problem areas when given sample components to inspect. And, you will learn the different methods of checking belt tension.
pages: Visual inspections tell you about the general condition of the engine. They help identify engine problems before they become engine failures. You need to perform a visual inspection every time you service an engine.

When you perform a visual inspection, you will want to do basic operation checks and inspect the engine systems for leaks and other obvious problems. 

During the inspection, write down any problems you find. Let your service adviser know about major items.
Leaks can appear as wet spots, corroded spots, or stains. On a large leak you might see fluid dripping or pouring out.
Check the battery and case for corrosion, cracks, leaks at the cell covers, and the condition of the posts, connections, terminals and harnesses. Chalky deposits also indicate a problem.

Check the electrolyte level on regular and low maintenance batteries. You cannot do this on a sealed battery. 

Finally, check the cables and connections to make sure they are not damaged and are the correct size. Clean the connections and put heavy protective grease on them to stop corrosion. 

Check the electrical harnesses, too. Wiggle them to make sure they are not loose, and look for any frayed wires that could cause a short.
You need to inspect the oil pressure, temperature, alternator and other gauges to make sure they are working.

Check all the cooling hoses and clamps. If they feel soft and mushy, or hard and brittle they should be replaced. Twist, pinch and squeeze the hoses to make sure they are not too soft or too hard. Wiggle the hoses at the connections to make sure they are clamped on tight.
You also need to check the radiator fins. A large area of bent or clogged fins could reduce cooling efficiency. Inspect all the components for damage and leaks.
Check the coolant level and also make sure there is no debris or obvious discoloration.
Inspect the air intake system for leaks, restrictions and damaged components.
Check the fuel system for leaks, bent or dented fuel lines and missing clamps.

If the engine has belt driven components, check both the belts and pulleys. Even small cracks and ridges can cause a belt to fail during engine operation. If a belt is worn or loose, components will not turn at the correct speed which can lead to major engine failure.
If one belt is worn, replace all the belts in the set.
To check belt tension with the engine off, twist or deflect the belts by hand. In general, you should not be able to deflect the belt more than the width of the belt or one inch.
You can also use a belt tension tool to get an accurate measurement of the belt tension.
While you are checking the belts, inspect the pulleys for wear, cracks or damage.
Pulley grooves should have flat, angled sides. If a pulley has dished sides or other damage such as cracks, replace it.
Goal of visual inspection: to spot problems before they become failures.

topics.title: Changing Fluids and Filters
topics.summary: After completing this topic, you will understand the maintenance procedures performed on the oil, cooling, air and fuel systems. You will recognize the procedures required to change the oil, air and fuel filters.

lessons.title: Oil and Oil Filters
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn the recommended service interval for changing oil and filters.

You will also learn the steps required to perform the oil and filter change procedure.
pages: Changing the oil, coolant, air and fuel filters regularly reduces wear and prolongs the life of the engine. Changing the oil and filters at correct intervals helps maintain good oil quality.
Different engines have different oil change intervals. Check the operations and maintenance manual for the engine you are working on.
The engine may also require a Scheduled Oil Sample. This procedure is explained in detail in a later topic.
When you change the oil filter, cut the old filter open and examine the debris trapped inside it. Particles of metal indicate some part of the engine may be wearing abnormally fast.
Large quantities of metal indicate abnormal wear or a pending failure, so if you see this, contact your supervisor.

Here are the steps in the Oil Change Procedure:

1. Stabilize machine
2. Run engine until warm
3. Turn engine off
4. Drain oil into container
5. Reinstall the drain plug
6. Remove filter
7. Examine filter debris
8. Install new filter
9. Fill system with oil
10. Check for leaks and level
After stabilizing the machine, can you perform an oil change from start to finish? Place these steps in their proper order by each action on the right to the appropriate step number on the left.

lessons.title: Coolant and Coolant Conditioner
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn the two methods for adding coolant conditioner and the procedures used for each method.

You will learn the procedures used to perform routine maintenance on the cooling system and those required for a major service.
pages:
Cooling systems have a different maintenance schedule than air, fuel or oil.

There are four checks you need to perform on the cooling system:

1. Coolant Level
2. Coolant Appearance
3. Antifreeze Concentration
4. Coolant Conditioner Concentration

Cooling systems are pressurized and take a little while to cool off after the engine is stopped. Follow the safety guidelines in your shop before working on the engine. Loosen the radiator cap slowly to de-pressurize the system.
Always check the appearance of the coolant. Foamy or dirty coolant indicates a leak in the system.
Check the antifreeze concentration. Use the test kit recommended by the manufacturer.
Test the concentration of the coolant conditioner.
If you have to add coolant, make sure it is the proper mix of water, antifreeze and conditioner.
There are two methods to add coolant conditioner: a spin-on element or liquid conditioner.

Follow these steps to change a coolant conditioner element:

1. Turn off the engine and let the engine cool.
2. Turn off the inlet and outlet valve.
3. Loosen the conditioner element.
4. Clean the gasket or seal.
5. Install the new element.
6. Tighten it until the gasket meets the base.
7. Turn the element 3/4 of a turn more by hand.
8. Open the inlet and outlet valve.
9. Remove the radiator cap and check the level.
10. Replace the cap and check for leaks.
If the engine does not have a coolant conditioner element, add liquid coolant conditioner to the filler pipe. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the correct amount.
Excessive coolant conditioner creates silica dropout, which can turn the coolant to a thick gel that blocks the coolant passages. Conditioner should not exceed 6%.
After inspecting the coolant, check the radiator cap. If the gaskets are worn or damaged, replace the cap.

To Flush Coolant:

1. Turn Engine Off 
2. Disconnect Batteries 
3. Remove Drain Plugs
4. Open Heater Valves
5. Remove Water Pump Drain
6. Check Water Pump Filter
7. Install Clean Drain PlugsP

To Test Regulator:

1. Remove Regulator
2. Test Regulator
3. Install New Seal
4. Install New Regulator
5. Replace Gasket and Install HousingP

To Clean Cooling System:

1. Fill System
2. Install Radiator Cap
3. Run Engine
4. Stop Engine and Let Cool
5. Drain Cleaner
6. Flush System with Water
7. Install Drain Plugs

?To Replace Coolant and Test Engine:

1. Refill coolant no faster than 5 gallons per minute to avoid an air lock
2. Check coolant level
3. Inspect radiator cap
4. Check for leaks
P
On some marine engines you need to check the condition of the sacrificial zinc rods. The rods should be checked frequently and replaced as needed.

lessons.title: Air Filter and Indicator
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn how to locate and identify an air filter indicator and an air filter on an engine.

You will be able to determine whether the air filter should be changed based on an air filter indicator.
pages: Basic air intake service includes inspecting and cleaning the precleaner and the air inlet pipes. Air filters are replaced as needed.
Many engine performance problems stem from a dirty air filter. Symptoms such as black smoke, low power or excessive fuel consumption could indicate a problem with the air filter.
The indicator can be mounted in the cab, engine compartment or on the filter element. The indicator has a window which is green, yellow or red, and a scale which displays vacuum in inches of water.

As the filter gets dirty, less air flows through the filter. This increases the vacuum inside the indicator which causes the diaphragm and piston to move. When the piston enters the "maximum restriction" area, it is time to change the air filter.
For engines without an air filter indicator, the operating conditions dictate how often the filter should be serviced.

LThese are the steps in the air system service procedure:

1. Prepare engine
2. Service precleaner
3. Change air filter
4. Examine new air filter
6. Reset air filter indicatorP

lessons.title: Fuel Filters
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn to identify primary and final fuel filters on an engine.

You will also learn the procedures used for cleanable and replaceable fuel filters. P
pages:
Fuel systems require regular maintenance to ensure clean fuel is delivered to the engine. Servicing the fuel system requires several steps. 

You have to:

1. Check for Water.
2. Change Fuel Filter.
3. Prime Fuel System.

To drain water from the water separator and fuel tanks:

1. Turn off the engine and fuel supply
2. Disconnect batteries
3. Open the valve on the water separator
4. Drain water
5. Close the valve
6. Locate the fuel tank drain valve
7. Open the valve
8. Drain water from the fuel tank
9. Close the valve

After draining the water from the fuel system, change the primary and final fuel filters.

1. Primary filters are normally located between the tank and transfer pump.

2. The final filter is usually located fairly close to the fuel pump.

Do not fill new fuel filters with fuel when you install them. This introduces unfiltered fuel into the engine which could cause damage.

Primary fuel filters are available in both cleanable and replaceable styles.

Final fuel filters are always replaced.

To clean a canister primary filter:

1. Turn off engine and close fuel supply.
2. Loosen the bolt on the housing and remove the filter case.
3. Take the filter element out of the case. 
4. Clean the filter with nonflammable solvent according to manual specifications.
5. Clean the filter case. 
6. Install the clean, dry, or new filter element into its case.
7. Reconnect the case.
8. Tighten the bolts to the recommended torque.

To change a primary and final spin-on fuel filter:

1. Turn off engine and close fuel supply.
2. Remove and discard the fuel filter.
3. Clean off the surface of the filter base.
4. Replace the filter with the type and size recommended in the service manual.
5. Lubricate new filter gasket with clean fuel. Do not put fuel in the filter.
6. After the filter contacts the base, hand tighten the filter 3/4 of a turn. 
7. Open fuel supply valve. If the engine has a fuel shutoff solenoid, this step is not necessary.

Prime the fuel system to remove air bubbles.

1. Unlock the priming pump located on top of the final fuel filter.
2. Operate the pump until you feel resistance.
3. Lock the pump.
4. Start the engine.

lessons.title: Collecting an S·O·S Sample
lessons.objective:
In this segment, you will learn when an S·O·S should be collected.

You will learn the two preferred sampling sites for an engine oil sampling.
P
pages: Scheduled Oil Sampling provides valuable wear trend information that can tell you about major engine problems before they cause engine failure.
An S·O·S sample should be collected at every oil change. The engine should be warm to ensure that wear materials are suspended in the sample.
There are two recommended sampling sites: the dipstick port and the oil sample port (arrow) on the engine.
Use clean sampling equipment. Dirty tubes or bottles contaminate the sample and give inaccurate results.

7To collect an S·O·S sample:

1. Run the engine until it is at operating temperature.
2. Take the sample before you drain the oil. 
3. Insert the tube into one of the ports. Use the pump, if necessary, to fill the sample bottle.
4. When the sample bottle is full, disconnect the hose and pump.
5. Cap the bottle tightly.
6. Fill out the label

lessons.title: What S·O·S Indicates
lessons.objective: In this segment, you will learn to identify information obtained through an S·O·S.
pages: An S·O·S report is a picture of the overall health of the engine. The S·O·S has three types of tests: wear analysis, chemical and physical tests, and oil condition analysis.
Wear analysis reveals components that might be wearing faster than normal.
Chemical and physical tests detect the presence of water, fuel and coolant in the oil.
An oil condition analysis determines the presence and amount of contaminants such as soot, sulfur products, oxidation, and nitration products.
Reading an S·O·S is quite easy since the report is divided into (1) owner information, (2) an oil history, (3) wear materials, (4) chemical and physical tests, and (5) oil condition results.

TEST INSTRUCTIONS

Your results will be presented on a summary page at the end of the test.

Click on the Continue button to begin.

Good luck!
After stabilizing the machine, can you perform an oil change from start to finish? Place these steps in their proper order by each action on the right to the appropriate step number on the left.
To view a report detailing your results, click on the Report button.
To navigate to a topic, click on the highlighted text. To return to the summary, click on the Summary button.

title: Concepts and Components
overview: This chapter on "Basic Hydraulic Concepts" contains information you need to know to effectively discuss or repair Caterpillar hydraulic components or systems. It is important to review these system and safety fundamentals since they provide the foundation upon which the rest of this course is built.

chapters.title: Basic Hydraulic Concepts
intro: In this chapter, you will learn the names and functions of components in simple hydraulic circuits and how hydraulic energy is put to work. This chapter also includes a segment on safety.

The Components chapter is an in-depth study of hydraulic components used on Caterpillar machines. It explains the different types of pumps, motors, valves and other components -- how they work, wear and fail; their repair options; and significant sales features.

lessons.title: Hydraulics at Caterpillar
lessons.objective: This lesson examines the role of hydraulics in Caterpillar construction and material handling equipment. And, it introduces you to the content covered in this course.
pages:
The power to lift... to push. The power to move mountains, or build them. In the world of construction and material handling equipment, the power that gets the job done is hydraulics. It wasn't until the 1950s that hydraulics were widely used on Caterpillar equipment. 

Since then, this form of power has become essential to the operation of virtually every machine in the Caterpillar line.

Cylinders of every type and size give life to buckets, blades, backhoes and truck beds. 

Hydraulic motors drive tracks, wheels, carbodys and conveyors. Brakes, steering, transmissions, suspensions and a host of other vehicle systems rely on hydraulics for power and control.

This course is an introduction to mobile hydraulic systems. You will learn how these systems work and why they are used on Caterpillar machines. 

Sales people taking this course will focus on the features and benefits of Caterpillar systems. You will be better prepared to talk knowledgeably with your customers about the advantages of Caterpillar hydraulics. 

Service people will explore the function, wear and failure of hydraulic systems and the options for repairing them. 

The course will prepare you for Level Three courses on hydraulic systems for specific Caterpillar machines. 
P

topics.title: Hydraulic Principles
topics.summary: Upon completing this topic, you will be able to identify fundamental hydraulic system components, define basic hydraulic terms, and discuss the properties of hydraulic fluids.

lessons.title: System Components
lessons.objective: Objective: Given a basic diagram of a mobile hydraulic system, you will be able to identify and use the correct names for system components. P
pages:
In this lesson, you learn about basic hydraulic components and how the system operates. This diagram represents a basic hydraulic system. Note that the hydraulic lines are different colors. The red, blue and green represent different pressures within the system. Common system components include:

A Fluid 
B Tank
C Filter
D Pump
E Control Valve
F Actuator
G Lines
H Relief Valve
I CoolerP

The fluid in a hydraulic system transmits energy. This is possible because liquids are virtually incompressible. As fluid is pumped through the system, force is exerted equally on all surfaces.

Since liquids conform to any shape, the hydraulic fluid can flow in any direction and into all open passages. Oil is the most commonly used hydraulic system fluid in Caterpillar machines.

The primary functions of a hydraulic tank are:

* stores oil
* cools oil
* allows air to separate from oil
* allows particles to settle
Filters remove contaminants from the hydraulic fluid. This prevents component damage and ensures proper system operation. The location and type of filters in a system vary.
The pump converts mechanical energy into fluid energy in the form of flow. It is driven by an external power source.
The directional control valve determines the path fluid takes through the system. This is the means by which the operator controls the machine.

The actuator converts hydraulic energy to mechanical energy in order to perform work. Cylinders produce linear motion, used to operate buckets, blades, booms and other implements. Hydraulic motors produce rotary motion, used for motive, steering and other vehicle systems.

Lines are hoses or tubes through which hydraulic fluid moves. Flexible hoses allow for motion, absorb vibration, reduce noise, and are easy to route and connect. Tubes provide more rigid connections, compact routing and better heat dissipation.
The relief valve (or pressure control valve) limits system pressure. The valve opens if pressure exceeds a predetermined set point.
A cooler removes heat from the hydraulic fluid. This improves component life.

This animation will help demonstrate how the system operates. The control valve is now in the Raise position. Follow the arrows as they trace flow through the system. When the control valve is shifted into the hold position ..... Note how the system operates differently when the control valve is in the Lower position.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.objective: Objective: Given a basic diagram of a mobile hydraulic system, you will be able to identify both series and parallel circuits.
pages: This diagram represents a simple hydraulic system with one valve and one actuator. Most machines require multiple components which can be connected in series or parallel. This lesson examines the difference between these two types of circuits.

1. When components are connected in series, fluid flows from one component to the next. There is one path for flow. 

2. When components are connected in parallel, fluid flows through each component simultaneously. There are two or more paths for flow.
In a series circuit, fluid flows from one component and through one or more additional components before returning to the tank. In this circuit, valve B gets pump flow before valve A.
In a parallel circuit, components have equal access to pump flow. In this circuit, valves A and B receive flow simultaneously, permitting independent operation.

lessons.title: Introduction to Cat Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: Using commonly available service literature, you will be able to locate and identify hydraulic system components in Caterpillar machines -- particularly those systems in track loaders, backhoe loaders, and excavators.
pages:
The track loader is representative of machines with simple hydraulic systems. Here you can identify each of the major components.

1. Cooler
2. Pump
3. Lift Cylinders
4. Hydraulic Tank
5. Tilt Cylinder
6. Control ValvesP
The cooler removes excess heat from hydraulic return oil before it flows to the tank. Air from the engine fan carries the heat away.
The pump draws oil from the tank and supplies it to the control valves.
The lift cylinders receive oil from the lift control valve to raise and lower the bucket.
The hydraulic tank serves as a reservoir of supply oil to the system. This tank contains two oil filters which clean the oil before it is combined with reserve oil.
The tilt cylinder receives oil from the tilt control valve to rack back and dump the bucket.

The control valves provide the operator control of lift and tilt cylinders by directing oil to the appropriate cylinder ports. Oil flows from the cylinders, through the valves and cooler, then returns to the tank.

The backhoe loader is a small machine, but it features a complex, sophisticated hydraulic system. This diagram identifies the major components.

1. Backhoe Cylinders
2. Stabilizer Cylinders
3. Swing Cylinders
4. Steering Cylinder
5. Pump
6. Tilt Cylinder
7. Lift Cylinders
8. Hydraulic Tank
9. Control ValveP
The backhoe cylinders include the boom, stick and bucket cylinders which control the operation of the backhoe.
Stabilizer cylinders extend to the ground to steady the machine during backhoe operation.
Swing cylinders move the backhoe from left to right.
The steering cylinder pivots the machine's front wheels left and right.
The tilt cylinder racks back and dumps the bucket.
The lift cylinders raise and lower the bucket.
The hydraulic tank serves as a reservoir of supply oil to the system. Housed inside the tank are two oil filters which clean the oil before it is combined with reserve oil.
The control valves direct oil to various cylinders.

Caterpillar hydraulic excavators depend on powerful, efficient hydraulic systems to do their jobs. As you can see from this diagram the system has several major components. This diagram identifies the location of:

1. Control Valves
2. Track Motors
3. Pumps
4. Hydraulic Tank
5. Boom Cylinders
6. Stick Cylinder
7. Bucket CylinderP
Control valves direct oil to the cylinders and track motors.
The track motors provide rotary power to drive the tracks.
The pumps draw oil from the tank and supply it to the control valves.
The hydraulic tank serves as a reservoir of supply oil to the system. The filter, located inside the tank, removes contaminants from the oil which is returning to the tank.
The two boom cylinders raise and lower the boom.
The stick cylinder extends and retracts the stick.
The bucket cylinder opens and closes the bucket.

lessons.title: Fluid Properties and Additives
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to discuss the properties of hydraulic fluid.
pages: Hydraulic fluid is the key component in any hydraulic system. It is the means by which energy is transmitted throughout the system. Certain fluid properties determine how well it does its job. This lesson discusses critical properties and fluid additives used to improve them.

Hydraulic fluid has many functions. The fluid must:

• transmit energy throughout the system
• provide lubrication for moving parts
• protect components from rust and corrosion
• carry heat away from components

One of the most critical properties of oil is viscosity. This refers to an oil's thickness or it's resistance to flow.

Viscosity is directly related to how well an oil will protect and lubricate components.

High viscosity oil can result in sluggish operation and may require additional power. Low viscosity oil may decrease the fluid's ability to lubricate and cause components to wear faster. It also increases the possibility of leakage.

Temperature can affect the viscosity of oil, so it is important to use the proper weight of oil for your machine and climate.

Always refer to your operator's and maintenance guides for the recommended oil.

Additives are used to control viscosity and other important characteristics of hydraulic oil. They are used to reduce wear, increase chemical stability, inhibit corrosion and oxidation, keep components clean, and suspend particles until they reach the filter. These are additional reasons why you should always use the recommended hydraulic fluid in Caterpillar machines.

topics.title: Putting Hydraulics to Work
topics.summary: Upon completing this topic, you will be able to solve mathematical equations relating to force, pressure, and area, and you will be able to convert hydraulic-related units of measure from English to Metric and vice versa.

lessons.title: Power Conversion
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to trace the conversion of power in a mobile hydraulic system.
pages:
In order to perform useful work, a hydraulic system must convert and control energy as it flows from one component to the next. This graphic represents the key conversion and control points in the system.
P
A hydraulic system must receive input energy from some source. This is usually in the form of rotating mechanical energy from an engine or vehicle gear train.
The hydraulic pump converts mechanical energy to hydraulic energy in the form of flow.
Valves control the transfer of hydraulic energy through the system by controlling fluid flow and direction.
The actuator converts hydraulic energy to mechanical energy in the form of linear or rotary motion and force. This energy is used to perform work.

lessons.title: Calculating System Performance
