lessons.title: ISO Symbols and Why They Matter
lessons.objective: Objective: Upon completing this segment, you will be able to define the significance of International Standards Organization (ISO) symbols and their importance in reading Caterpillar hydraulic schematics.
pages:
Understanding and troubleshooting the complex hydraulic systems on today's machines requires the ability to read and interpret hydraulic schematics.

The simpler systems on older Caterpillar machines could be easily represented by orthographic schematics -- which contain two-dimensional, engineering drawings and cutaways of the major components. 

As systems became more and more complex this type of schematic became too cumbersome and difficult to read. So, newer, more complex systems are often depicted by ISO schematics, which use international graphic symbols to represent the various components. 

These symbols, which were developed by the International Standards Organization, provide a single, worldwide method of representing different types of hydraulic components. 

Caterpillar service manuals frequently contain both ISO and orthographic schematics. 

After completing this module, you will be able to recognize components and trace flow through complex hydraulic systems by reading and correctly interpreting both types of schematics.

In Module One, you learned that color is sometimes used to indicate system pressures. Caterpillar service publications and service training materials often use these colors to represent the pressure and function of fluid and components.

1. Highest Pressure Supply Oil is red
2. Intermediate Pressure Supply Oil is indicated by red and white diagonals
3. Lower Pressure Supply Oil is dotted with red or colored pink.
 A. Lowest pressure supply oil is pink.
4. Return Oil is indicated with green.
5. Pilot or Signal Oil with orange.
6. Trapped Oil is identified by blue.
7. Static Components are shown in gray.
8. Moving Component Parts are shown in yellow.

You will see these colors used frequently in diagrams such as for this valve.

1. Highest Pressure Supply Oil
2. Static Component
3. Moving Components
4. Return Oil
5. Intermediate Pressure Supply OilP

ISO (International Standards Organization) schematics use these simple basic shapes to represent the following components and characteristics:

1. Pumps and Motors
2. Fluid Conditioners
3. Control Valves
4. LinesP

These symbols are used in combination with the basic shapes to give you more information about the components. 

1. Variable Control
2. Direction of fluid or energy flow
3. Direction of rotation or flow
4. For example, a simple pump symbol can be modified like this to more precisely identify the pump characteristics. P

topics.title: Component Symbols and Drawings
topics.summary: Upon completing this topic, you will be able to: identify the ISO symbols for lines, reservoirs, conditioners, pumps, motors, valves, cylinders, and other components; trace the flow through the valves; and given ISO and orthographic drawings, state the operation of each valve type.

lessons.title: Lines, Reservoirs and Conditioners
lessons.objective: In this lesson you will learn the ISO symbols for lines and connections, tanks and accumulators, coolers and filters. P
pages:
These are the ISO symbols for different types of hydraulic lines:

1. Main system working line.
2. Pilot, signal, vent and drain lines (symbol can be shown either way)
3. On some Caterpillar schematics, you will see lines drawn in solid, with color indicating the type of line. P

When reading ISO schematics, you must be able to determine when lines are joined and when they simply cross one another. These are some common ways to represent crossing and joining lines.

The symbols on the left in drawing 1 show crossing lines, in drawing 2 are common symbols for joining lines.

You will note that different schematics may use the same symbol to represent either a crossing or a joining line. However, use of a symbol will be consistent within any given schematic.
P

The simplified ISO symbol for a hydraulic tank is an open box with a return line. The return line may be shown above or below the oil level. Some schematics may show pressurized tanks as a closed box.

Although most hydraulic systems have only one tank, the symbol may be used several times on the schematic to reduce complexity.

1. Below oil level
2. Above oil level

P

On some schematics, tanks will be shown as orthographic drawings.
P

1. This is the basic symbol for an accumulator.

Internal symbols may be added to indicate the type of accumulator. 

2. Spring-Loaded

3. Gas-Charged

4. Weighted

The open triangle in the gas-charged accumulator represents the direction of pneumatic energy.
This is an orthographic of a gas-charged accumulator.

1. This is the basic ISO symbol for a fluid conditioner.

2. The addition of a dashed line is the symbol for an oil filter.

3. This is the symbol for an oil cooler. The solid triangles represent heat dissipation.

4. Some Caterpillar schematics will show the cooler represented as a labeled box.
This is a typical orthographic drawing of a hydraulic oil filter.

lessons.title: Pumps and Motors
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify the ISO symbols for pumps and motors.
pages: In this lesson you will learn the ISO symbols for pumps and motors, and see some examples of orthographic drawings.

1. The basic ISO symbol for a pump or motor is a circle.

2. Triangles may be added to the basic symbol to indicate direction of fluid or energy flow.

Pumps are sometimes shown connected to the component that is driving them, such as an engine or electric motor.

The component shaft is shown as a short solid line connected to the component outline. The arrow indicates the direction of rotation.

ISO schematics indicate component function, not design or type. For example, this ISO symbol (identified as number 1 on the graphic) can be used to represent either of these fixed displacement pumps.

Number 2 depicts a vane pump and number 3 a piston pump.

lessons.title: Valve Basics
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify the ISO symbols for valves and be able to trace flow through the valves in their various positions.
pages: After completing this lesson you will recognize the ISO symbols for valves and be able to trace flow through the valves in their various positions. You will see both ISO and orthographic drawings and be able to review the operation of each valve type.

The basic ISO symbol for a valve is a box, or envelope.

Directional control selector valves are usually shown as multiple envelopes, with the number of envelopes representing the number of valve positions.

1. Basic Valve Envelope
2. Two Position
3. Three Position

Short lines drawn perpendicular to the envelope indicate external port connections.

1. Two-Way
2. Three-Way
3. Four-Way

Ports are sometimes labeled. When this is done, T means Tank, P means Pump, and A and B signify working ports.

An arrow inside the envelope indicates direction of flow.

ISO symbols are shown in their normal, or hold position.

1. Normally Open
2. Normally ClosedP

The three basic types of valves are flow, pressure, and directional control valves.

1. Flow control and check valves
2. Pressure control valves
3. Directional control valvesP

lessons.title: Flow Control and Check Valves
lessons.objective: This lesson teaches you more specifics about how to recognize flow control and check valves on both orthographic and ISO schematics.
pages:
1. The basic symbol for a flow control valve begins with an envelope and line.

2. Two curved lines on either side of the straight line indicate a restriction, or orifice.

3. Adding a diagonal arrow signifies that the orifice is variable. A simple infinitely variable gate valve can be represented by symbol number three.

This is the ISO symbol for a pressure compensated flow control valve. 

There are two pilot sensing lines (shown as dashed lines). The downstream pilot line is working with the spring to keep the valve closed. The other pilot line senses upstream pressure and is working to open the valve.

The valve maintains constant flow by maintaining a constant pressure drop across the orifice. Excess flow is dumped to the tank.

You will usually see pressure compensated flow control valves in this simplified form. (Shown on the right.)

The vertical arrow indicates that the valve is pressure compensated and replaces the pilot lines and other pressure compensating elements.

Some flow control valves do not vent to the tank.

This is an orthographic drawing of a flow control valve on a small wheel loader.

A relief valve shares the same valve body as the flow control valve.

1. Relief Valve
2. Dump Valve and Spring
3. Orifice

The flow control valve provides a predetermined maximum flow rate to one circuit, and bypasses excess flow to another circuit or back to tank. It consists of an orifice, a dump valve and a light spring. These valves can control flow to a fine degree.

The orifice is designed to pass a certain flow at a specified pressure differential. As oil flows through the orifice, a pressure differential is created.

Higher pressure pushes against the upstream side of the dump valve.

However, the lower pressure plus the spring force act against the downstream side of the dump valve, keeping it closed.

When the flow rate increases through the orifice, the differential between the two pressures also rises. The downstream pressure and spring force are no longer greater than upstream pressure, so the valve opens, bypassing excess flow. The flow through the orifice will then be maintained at the required value.

If the downstream flow is blocked, equal pressure on both sides of the orifice keeps the dump valve closed.

A more common type of flow control valve combines the action of the orifice and dump valve in one moving part.

1. The basic symbol for a check valve ball and seat. Normal flow from left to right unseats the ball. Flow from right to left is blocked.

2. Many check valves are equipped with springs to help keep the ball seated.
This is an orthographic drawing of a check valve group.

A check valve can be classified as either a directional or flow control valve. Its primary function is to allow flow in only one direction. The most common design is a piston, or ball, and a spring. The check valve is often used in combination with other valves.

Pressure on the upstream side of the valve is sufficient to overcome the force of the spring, pushing the piston away from the seat and allowing flow through the valve.

Flow in the opposite direction lets pressure work with the spring, closing the valve and blocking flow.

Some check valves work in two directions. They are called double check valves, resolvers, or shuttle valves.

1. This valve symbol shows that the highest pressure from circuit A or B is allowed to pass to circuit C.

2. Some Caterpillar schematics will show a shuttle valve symbol this way.

This is an orthographic drawing of a typical shuttle valve.

1. Inlets
2. Outlet

This is the ISO symbol for a make-up valve, which is a special type of check valve.

System supply pressure works with the spring to keep the ball seated. When return pressure exceeds supply pressure plus the force of the spring, the valve opens, allowing flow in the opposite direction.
Many make-up valves are housed inside other valves. For example, this make-up valve shares a housing with a directional control valve.

A make-up valve is a type of check valve that allows return oil to flow directly to actuator lines whenever return pressure is greater than inlet pressure to the actuator. This prevents cylinders from voiding when dropping blades or buckets drain the cylinders faster than the pump can supply oil.

The make-up valve consists of a check valve and a light spring.

When oil pressure drops to approximately two pounds per square inch less than the return line pressure, the valve unseats, allowing oil to flow to lines. P

lessons.title: Pressure Control Valves
lessons.objective: This lesson teaches you more specifics about how to recognize pressure control valves on both orthographic and ISO schematics.
pages: One symbol for a simple relief valve is a ball, a seat and a spring that acts against system pressure.
This is the main relief valve on a differential steer track-type tractor. In other systems you will find simple relief valves housed within other valve bodies.

A simple relief valve consists of a valve body, piston, and spring. The piston is normally held closed on the seat by a predetermined spring force.

If system pressure is greater than the spring force, the valve will open, allowing oil to pass to the tank. Simple relief valves do not provide precise control of pressure, and in certain applications, the valve chatters.

The general symbol for a relief valve shows a single valve envelope, which is normally closed to flow. The symbol can represent a direct acting relief valve or a pilot-operated relief valve.

The internal or external pilot pressure acting on one side of the envelope works against the spring force. The diagonal arrow on the spring indicates the spring force can be varied.
This orthographic drawing includes a typical pilot-operated relief valve.

Pilot-operated relief valves are used in many high pressure systems, where it is important to maintain uniform pressure under different flow rates. The valve consists of a small pilot valve (1) that is used to control the larger unloading valve (2).

The pilot-operated relief valve consists of a pilot valve spring that controls the maximum system or circuit pressure, and an unloading valve with an orifice that is held shut during normal operation by a large, weak spring. With system pressure less than the pilot valve set point, the pilot valve remains closed. The unloading valve spring chamber is filled and since there is no flow, oil pressure on both sides of the unloading valve orifice are the same. Therefore, the unloading valve spring holds the unloading valve closed.

When oil pressure rises to the relief valve setting, the pilot valve opens and dumps oil from the unloading valve spring chamber to the return line. Since more oil can flow past the pilot valve than through the unloading valve orifice, the pressure drops in the unloading valve spring chamber.

The higher system or circuit pressure pushes the unloading valve open, allowing pump flow to be dumped into the return line. This gives precise pressure control in high pressure systems using a small spring and small mechanical construction.
A modulating relief valve adds a check valve and orifice arrangement and load piston cavity containing a piston and spring. These valves are used to allow a gradual buildup of pressure.
This is an orthographic drawing of a modulating relief valve.

A modulating relief valve is used to allow a gradual buildup of pressure. It is sometimes found in transmissions to facilitate smooth shifting.

A modulating relief valve usually consists of the parts pointed out on this illustration. Number 1 is the slug, 2... the spring, 3 ...the modulating relief valve, 4... the orifice and check valve arrangement, ... 5. the load piston cavity ... and 6 the torque converter circuit. 

At machine startup the springs between the load piston and modulating relief valve are at full extension. The pump supplies oil to the slug chamber, moving the modulating relief valve to the right. This allows some oil to enter the converter circuit.

Oil is also sent through the orifice check valve to the chamber on the right side of the load chamber. As oil fills the chamber, pressure builds, moving the load piston to the left and closing off the modulating relief valve to the converter circuit. Pressure builds in the modulating relief valve slug cavity again, moving it to the right.

The movement of the modulating relief valve and the load piston against each other compresses the spring more and more until the load piston reaches its maximum travel. A passage opens, venting oil in the load piston chamber to tank. At this time maximum pressure has been reached. The orifice controls the rate of flow to the load piston. By controlling the rate flow to the load piston, we control how fast the pressure rises in the system. The check valve allows for a rapid dump of the load piston chamber when the supply oil pressure drops, such as between shifts. This allows the modulation cycle to start again when the springs are fully extended.
The symbol for a pressure reducing valve resembles a pilot-operated relief valve, except it is normally open and the pilot line senses downstream pressure.
This is an orthographic drawing of a pressure reducing valve.

Pressure reducing valves are used when circuit pressure requirements are less than supply pressure.

1. Spring
2. Spool
3. Piston

The pressure-reducing valve consists of a piston, spring, and spool. The force of the spring determines maximum downstream pressure. The valve is normally open.

As flow passes the spool, downstream pressure builds. As the pressure in the piston cavity builds, it acts against the piston and spool, overcomes the force of the spring and begins closing off the opening.

When downstream pressure matches the resistance of the spring, movement stops, maintaining the reduced downstream pressure. P

This is the symbol for a pressure differential valve.

This valve has two pilot lines with one sensing upstream pressure and working against the spring, while the other pilot line senses downstream pressure and works with the spring.
This is an orthographic drawing of a pressure differential valve.

The pressure differential valve consists of a spring and a spool. 

On this drawing, the spring is identified by the number 1 and the spool by the number 2. Also note that the number 3 corresponds to the location of the primary circuit. The secondary circuit is number 4.

The spool initially blocks flow from the primary to the secondary circuit. Once flow requirements to the primary circuit are met, pressure rises, moving the spool against the spring and allowing flow into the secondary circuit and the spring chamber.

As secondary pressure builds, the valve moves back to the right. The valve will constantly adjust its position so that pressure in the secondary circuit equals the pressure in the primary circuit, less the force of the spring. P

lessons.title: Directional Control Valves
lessons.objective: This lesson teaches you more specifics about how to recognize directional control valves on both orthographic and ISO schematics.
pages:
Generally, directional control valves are shown with two or more envelopes.

The port connections are made to the envelope that shows the neutral, or hold position.

This symbol represents an open-center control valve. In the normal position, flow from the pump returns to tank and both work ports are blocked.

The right-hand envelope in this open-center control valve indicates the valve position that sends pump flow to work port B and flow from work port A is sent back to tank.

The valve position indicated by the left-hand envelope reverses flow, sending flow from the pump to port A, and returning flow from port B to tank.

Adding parallel lines to either side of a valve symbol indicates that the valve is capable of infinite positioning between certain limits.

This is an orthographic drawing of a typical open-center directional control valve.

1. Relief Valves
2. Check Valve
3. Directional Control Valve Spool

Selector valves typically consist of three or more positions. Each position changes fluid flow to the actuator. 

In a three position, open center valve, the middle, or neutral, position holds the actuator in place. Ports A and B are blocked and supply oil is returned to the tank.

With the valve positioned to extend the actuator, oil is sent through port B to the actuator. 

With the valve positioned to retract the actuator, oil is sent through port A to the actuator. 

A closed center valve is similar to an open center valve, except that pump flow is blocked in the centered, or neutral, position.
This ISO symbol represents a closed-center directional control valve. In the neutral or hold position, all four ports are blocked.

This is an orthographic drawing for a closed-center directional control valve.

1. Directional Control Valve Spool
2. Combination Line Relief and Make-Up Valves
3. Pressure Reducing Valve

A symbol added to the side of a directional control valve indicates the way in which the valve operates. The valve in illustration number 1 is manually operated.

Illustration number 2 shows the symbols for some common manually controlled mechanisms. A depicts a hand lever, B depicts a push button, and C a pedal mechanism.

The addition of a spring symbol to both sides of the directional control valve indicates that the valve is spring-centered and automatically returns to the hold position when the operator releases the lever or deactivates a solenoid. Illustration number 3 is an example of this type.

Here are additional controls sometimes used.

1. Remote Supply 
2. Remote Return 
3. Solenoid
4. Internal Supply 
5. Internal Return 
6. Electric Motor
7. Servo Control Unit 
8. Thermal 
9. Detented

Combination controls are also used. One control symbol on top of another indicates one OR the other. Both controls in the same box indicate one AND the other.

Illustration 1A depicts a solenoid or manual control. 1B on the other hand, denotes both solenoid and pilot control.

Sometimes more than one valve is controlled by the same device, as the joystick control for excavator operation. Schematics may show these controls using symbol number 2.

lessons.title: Cylinders
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify the ISO symbols for hydraulic cylinders.
pages: This lesson covers ISO symbols and orthographic drawings of hydraulics cylinders.

1. The basic symbol for cylinders is a rectangle representing the cylinder barrel, and a T-shaped representation of the piston and rod.

2. Sometimes the rod and piston are shown in more detail.

3. This is the symbol for a single-acting cylinder. A single port is indicated, and the end of the symbol opposite the port is left open to indicate the cylinder is vented.
This is an orthographic drawing of a single-acting cylinder.
A single acting cylinder is hydraulically powered in only one direction. Oil entering a single port forces the actuator to extend. The weight of the load retracts the actuator.

1. This is the symbol for a double-acting cylinder. Two ports indicate that flow moves the cylinder in both directions.

2. A double-rodded cylinder is shown like this.

1. This is an orthographic of a double-acting cylinder.

2. This is an orthographic of a double-rodded cylinder.

A double-acting cylinder is hydraulically driven in two directions. Pressure oil enters at the cap end of the cylinder to extend it. Oil is forced from the rod end and returned to tank. To retract the cylinder, high pressure oil is directed to the rod end.

The symbol for a telescoping cylinder indicates the number of rods the cylinder has.

A single port and open ended rods indicate a single-acting cylinder (1). Double-acting cylinders are shown with two ports and the rod ends are closed (2).
This orthographic represents a double-acting telescoping cylinder.

1. A cylinder snubber is represented by a small rectangle on either or both sides of the piston.

2. A diagonal line through the rectangle indicates that the snubber has a variable flow restriction.
This orthographic drawing represents one type of a cylinder snubber.
Very good. The orthographic is a double-rodded cylinder, which is represented by symbol A.

lessons.title: Other Components
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify the ISO symbols for external power sources, gauges, and other occasionally used schematic graphics.
pages:
This lesson discusses a few additional ISO symbols that you will occasionally encounter on Caterpillar hydraulic system schematics.

1. EngineP

Some ISO schematics have a symbol for external power sources.

1. An engine is indicated by either of these symbols.

2. An electric motor is indicated by this symbol.

This is the symbol for a pressure switch. It indicates that pressure is working against a spring.

If the pressure becomes high enough, the connecting bar swings to the right to make contact to the lower right terminal post, opening or closing the switch.

The vertical line and jagged arrow represent an indicator light.

These symbols represent pressure and temperature gauges.

1. Pressure Gauge
2. Temperature GaugeP

This is the symbol for a quick connect test port. 

Oil pressure and the spring will keep the ball against the seat, sealing off the port.

When a gauge is connected the 'T' is depressed to keep the ball from seating. This opens the port and allows pressure to be measured.

lessons.title: Interpreting Schematics
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to interpret schematics using common orthographic drawings and ISO symbols.
pages:
Once you learn to recognize the various ISO symbols and orthographic drawings for individual hydraulic components you are ready to move on to schematics of entire systems. This lesson will teach you how to trace flow through a system and to correctly interpret how the components work together.

We will start with a simplified orthographic schematic of a tilt circuit.

The circuit consists of a hydraulic oil tank with a filter, a pump, a valve group consisting of an inlet manifold with a main relief valve, an open centered directional control valve, an end cover, and a double acting cylinder. Other valve spools that would normally be in this valve stack have been omitted for simplicity.

To trace flow through a circuit, start at the tank and follow the fluid flow through the various components, ending back at the tank. The path will vary, depending on the position of valves in the circuit. We will start with the control valve in the neutral or hold position.

Fluid is drawn from the tank by the pump and flows toward the inlet manifold. The oil fills the cavities, and moves through the directional control valve.

It is important to note that some of the oil passages are below the plane of this orthographic cross-section. These are shown with dotted lines.

Oil flows through these passages to the end cover where it is directed back through the return passages of the directional control valve, to the return line, through the filter and back to the tank.

Now we will imagine the control valve is shifted to the dump position. Supply oil from the pump is directed through the spool, where it unseats the check valve and flows to the cylinder to extend the piston and rod. Return oil from the cylinder comes back through the directional control valve and returns to the tank.

Once the piston fully extends, pressure builds in the inlet manifold, causing the relief valve to unseat and dump supply oil back to the tank.

Imagine that now we have shifted the spool to the rackback position. Supply oil is directed through the control valve to the rod end of the cylinder and the piston and rod retract.

Shifting back to the hold position will keep the piston in place.

Now we will replace these orthographic drawings with the appropriate ISO symbols. ......The pump, .....the filter,.....the relief valve,.....the directional control valve,.....and the cylinder.

We will first show flow with the directional control valve in the hold position. Note that the center position is colored yellow. This is to help indicate the active envelope.
In this illustration the valve is in the rackback position. Study the schematic carefully and trace flow through the circuit.
Here you can trace the changes in circuit flow when the valve is shifted to the dump position.

Sometimes at Caterpillar, you will see schematics with a combination of both ISO and orthographic symbols, as you see here. Can you identify the appropriate circuit pressures for this system using the ISO color codes?

Test your knowledge by coloring the lines on this drawing. This valve is shown in the hold position. Click on a color from the palette in the question box then click on the line you want to color. When you have colored all the lines, click on the enter button in the question box to see if your answer is correct.

For more practice, you can shift the valve to the dump position by clicking on the small right arrow directly above the shift mechanism on the drawing. Then, color the lines to indicate how pressure changes as the cylinder extends.

When you have finished the exercise, click on the Exit Simulation button. To replay these directions, click on the audio icon twice.

The practice sequence will also ask questions that will require you to read and interpret more complicated ISO schematics -- such as this circuit which is typical of one you might find on a Caterpillar Backhoe Loader.

lessons.title: Open- and Closed-Center Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify and discuss the differences and similarities between open- and closed-center hydraulic systems.
pages:
Hydraulic systems on Caterpillar machines are often referred to by the various types of components or features present in the system. For example, a pilot-operated system is one that incorporates pilot-operated valves.

The most commonly-used terms used to classify mobile hydraulic systems includes open and closed center, fixed and variable displacement, manual and pilot operated, pressure compensated and load sensing. Hydraulic systems that incorporate electronic control devices are often called electronic over hydraulic systems.

This lesson explains the operation, characteristics and use of these systems in Caterpillar machines.

PIn this first lesson, we look at open and closed-center systems. 

An open or closed-center system refers to the type of directional control valve that operates the actuator. The hold or neutral position of an open-centered valve directs full pump flow to the tank. Ports A and B are blocked.

When the valve shifts to this position, oil flows from the pump to port B, extending the actuator. 

When the valve is shifted to this position, oil flows from the pump to port A, retracting the actuator. 

When the cylinder is stalled out the main relief valve opens, returning pump flow to the tank and protecting the system from excessive pressure.

PThis ISO schematic represents the lift, tilt, and auxiliary circuits on a small Caterpillar wheel loader. Note that the direction control valves are open-centered, permitting pump flow to return to tank in a neutral, center position. See if you can trace flow through the circuits in each of the valve positions. 

On this schematic, you should be able to identify the supply line from the pump which is indicated by number 1; the lift circuit is shown by 2; flow to the lift cylinders is marked by the number 3; the number 4 shows the tilt circuit; and, 5 indicates flow to the tilt cylinders. Number 6 identifies the auxiliary circuit and 7 shows flow to the attachment cylinders. Finally, the number 8 indicates flow to the tank.
rences and similarities between open- and closed-center hydraulic systems.

On this simple closed-center system, the hold or neutral position blocks pump flow, which causes the main relief valve to open. 

When the valve shifts to this position, oil flows from the pump to port B, extending the actuator. 

When the valve is shifted to this position, oil flows from the pump to port A, retracting the actuator. 

When the cylinder is stalled in either extreme, the main relief valve functions the same as in the open-centered system, protecting the system from excessive pressure.

This is part of the ISO system schematic for a Caterpillar backhoe loader. The two closed-centered valves control the bucket and boom cylinders. See if you can identify all the various types of valves and trace flow through these two circuits.

1. Pump Supply
2. Signal to Pump
3. Bucket Cylinder
4. Boom Cylinder

lessons.title: Fixed- and Variable-Displacement Systems
lessons.objective:
Objective: You will be able to identify and discuss the differences between fixed- and variable-
displacement hydraulic systems. P
pages:
A fixed or variable displacement system refers to the type of pump that supplies flow. The output of a fixed-displacement pump is only affected by its operating speed. When the machine is running at high idle, the pump is always producing maximum flow; consequently, these are very responsive systems.

Many operators like fixed-displacement systems because they can use the sound of the engine lugging to determine how hard they are working the hydraulics. 

There are some limitations to fixed-displacement systems. Heat can build up because the pump is always running, passing flow through the system. And fixed displacement pumps require engine horsepower that could be used for other purposes when hydraulic power is not needed.

Variable-displacement systems use pumps that supply flow on demand. In this system, a pump control valve senses workport pressure and adjusts the output of the pump to supply only the amount of oil required. This type of hydraulic system is more fuel efficient. It also generates less heat, resulting in longer component life.

This is a simplified schematic of a variable-displacement hydraulic system. Notice that a pump control valve is connected to both workports by a double check valve, or shuttle valve. When the directional control valve is in the center, or hold position, pump flow to the workports is blocked. The pump control valve senses the lower workport pressure and adjusts the pump so it only outputs sufficient flow to maintain minimum system pressure. This condition is called low pressure standby.

When the directional control valve shifts, the higher pressure in the workport closes the double check valve, sending the higher pressure back to the pump control valve. This signals the pump control valve to upstroke the pump, sending more flow to the actuator.

This orthographic cross-section represents a variable-displacement pump and its control valve. When the implement directional control valve is in the hold position, flow to workports is blocked and no signal pressure is being sent to the pump control valve. 

Since there is no signal pressure, pump supply pressure is enough to keep the margin spool up. This directs pump flow to the large actuator, which maintains the pump swashplate at a minimum angle. This state is called "low pressure standby." 

In this condition, the pump is producing just enough flow to compensate for system leakage and maintain adequate system pressure to insure good implement response.

1. Signal Pressure From Workports
2. Pump Supply To Control Valves
3. Large Actuator
4. Swashplate
5. Small Actuator & Bias Spring
6. Margin Spool

When the implement directional control valve is shifted, pressure from the selected workport is sent through the signal line to the pump control valve. This additional pressure works with the spring to push the margin spool down, allowing flow to the large actuator to drain to tank. 

The small actuator and bias piston can now move the pump swashplate to a higher angle, increasing pump output. This condition is called upstroking. As pump flow increases, system pressure also increases.

As system flow requirements are satisfied, the margin spool moves to maintain a constant pressure differential between pump output pressure, or system pressure, and signal pressure. This pressure differential is called margin pressure and is equal to the value of the spring above the margin spool. In this condition, pump flow is relatively constant and being directed to the actuators.

If the operator wants to slow the implement, the implement directional control valve is throttled back toward the hold position, reducing flow to the workports. This change in flow requirements results in a higher pressure below the margin spool, moving the spool up and allowing more flow to be directed to the large actuator. 

The increased pressure to the large actuator is greater than the force of the small actuator and bias spring, so the swashplate moves to a reduced angle, reducing pump flow. This is called destroking. When the desired system pressure is achieved, the pump again returns to a constant flow condition.

This pump control valve has another control stem that reacts to pump supply pressure and is set to open at a given maximum pressure. Called a pressure compensator or pressure cut-off spool, this valve works to destroke the pump to limit maximum system pressure. During normal operation, the spool is forced down by the pressure compensator spring. In a stall, or maximum system pressure state, signal pressure is equal to pump supply pressure. The combination of signal pressure and margin spring forces the margin spool down. This would usually cause the pump to upstroke. However, since supply pressure was great enough, the pressure compensator spool is forced up. This permits supply oil to flow to the large acuator destroking pump and reducing flow. This feature eliminates the need for a main system relief valve in some systems. Maximum system pressure is set by the pressure compensator adjustment screw.

lessons.title: Manual and Pilot-Operated Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to distinguish between manually-operated and pilot-operated hydraulic systems found in Caterpillar machines.
pages:
The directional control valves on Caterpillar machines are often manually or pilot-operated.

On manually-operated systems, control valves are moved directly by the operator's hand or foot, usually through some type of mechanical linkage.

Many small Caterpillar machines use manually-operated systems. Typically, manual operation allows more precise control of implements.

Pilot-operated systems use small pilot valves to control the movement of the main directional control valve. They are used on valves that would be difficult for the operator to control...
or on directional control valves that are remotely located on a machine.

Larger machines often use pilot-operated systems. These systems reduce operator effort, resulting in less fatigue.

lessons.title: Load-Sensing Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to discuss the function of load-sensing hydraulic systems and their application in both fixed- and variable-displacement systems.
pages:
Many Caterpillar machines are equipped with load sensing hydraulic systems. That means the hydraulic system can determine how much load there is on the various implements and provide only the amount of system pressure and flow necessary to do the work.

These systems generate less heat, have better component life and, in variable-displacement applications, provide better fuel economy.

Load sensing refers to any system that regulates flow to maintain a pump supply pressure at a fixed value above the highest workport pressure requirement.

Load sensing can be achieved on both fixed and variable-displacement systems.

Load sensing in a fixed-displacement system is accomplished through the use a flow control or dump valve. This valve senses pump supply pressure and workport pressure and maintains a pressure differential between the two equal to the value of the spring. In a closed-center system with the directional control valve in the hold position, the dump valve is open, returning pump flow to the tank at a lower pressure than the relief valve setting.

When the directional valve is shifted, the load on the cylinder causes the dump valve to close and pump flow is directed to the cylinder. As the flow requirements of the cylinder are met, system pressure increases. The dump valve will open to meter excess flow to tank to maintain a set pressure differential between the cylinder pressure and system pressure.

If flow requirements change, the dump valve will move to maintain the required flow rate to the cylinder and the differential between load and system pressure.

This ISO schematic represents a typical fixed-displacement, load-sensing hydraulic system. See if you can locate the flow control or dump valve and trace flow through the system as the load varies on the actuators. P

Load sensing in a variable-displacement system is accomplished through the use of a variable-displacement pump and pump control valve. 

The pump control valve senses pump supply pressure and workport pressure and regulates pump flow to maintain the desired pressure differential. 

The operation of this system is discussed in the lesson on fixed- and variable-displacement systems. P
This ISO schematic represents a variable- displacement, load sensing hydraulic system. See if you can trace flow through the system with the directional control valve in all three positions.
2constant differential pressure between the pump output pressure and highest workport pressure.
2constant differential pressure between the pump output pressures and the relief valve setting.
Good. A load sensing system maintains constant differential pressure between the pump output pressure and the highest workport pressure.

Good. A flow control (dump) valve is required in a load sensing, fixed-displacement system. The valve maintains a desired pressure differential between pump supply pressure and highest workport pressure, dumping excess pump flow to tank when it is not required.

lessons.title: Pressure-Compensated Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify and discuss the characteristics of pressure-compensated hydraulic systems.
pages: Many Caterpillar machines are equipped with pressure compensated systems. This term is often used to describe certain pumps and valves and generally refers to conditions that limit output pressure. At Caterpillar, the term usually refers to control systems that produce a constant implement speed for a given lever displacement. P

Pressure compensation can be accomplished through the use of a pressure reducing valve between the pump and the directional control valve. This valve senses downstream pressure at the control spool and higher workport pressure from the rod or head end of the cylinder. 

The pressure reducing valve varies flow to the control valve in order to maintain a constant pressure differential across the control valve. This reduces lever efforts and gives the operator more precise control.

In this example of a pressure compensated system, the pump is producing more flow than the cylinder requires. Pump output pressure is 2700 psi, workport pressure is 1000 psi and the pressure created by the spring in the reducing valve is 50 psi

Under these conditions, the pressure reducing valve limits pressure to the directional control valve to 1050 psi, regardless of pump output pressure. The excess 1650 psi is dissipated as heat.

Since workport pressure is 1000 psi, there is only a 50 psi pressure drop across the directional control valve. If workport pressure increases or decreases, the pressure reducing valve will continue to maintain a constant pressure drop across the control spool.

Since pressure drop is controlled, lighter centering springs can be used in the directional control valve...resulting in reduced lever effort and operator fatigue. It also eliminates the effects of varying engine speeds and changing workport loads on cylinder speed.

lessons.title: Electronically Controlled Systems
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to discuss typical applications of computer- or electronically- controlled hydraulic systems.
pages:
Some Caterpillar machines are equipped with sophisticated, computer or electronically controlled hydraulic systems. These types of integrated systems give the operator more precise control over the machine and are generally more productive and more efficient.

This lesson is an introduction to electronic/hydraulic systems. We will examine two typical applications of this technology: an Electronic Power Unit Control and a Work Mode Selector.

The electronic power unit control (EPUC) is a microcomputer-based electronic device used to control hydraulic fluid flow. Its main function is to limit the hydraulic horsepower range of variable-displacement pumps.

The EPUC matches hydraulic horsepower to available engine horsepower, improving machine performance, noise levels and fuel efficiency.

The Work Mode Selector permits the operator to configure a machine for particular operations. This excavator Work Mode Selector, for example has three settings:

• Loading
• Sidewall Crowding
• Leveling

These settings determine which hydraulic circuits get priority. The benefit is increased implement control and higher production.

Good. The Electronic Power Unit Control limits the horsepower range of variable-displacement pumps. The EPUC matches hydraulic horsepower to available engine horsepower, improving machine performance, noise levels and fuel efficiency.

lessons.title: Characteristics of Cat Hydraulics
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to apply your knowledge of Caterpillar Hydraulic Systems to your job by recognizing the characteristics of the hydraulic systems most commonly used on Cat backhoes, excavators and wheel loaders.
pages:
A wide variety of hydraulic systems are used on Caterpillar machines. Even machines in the same family may have significantly different features and characteristics.

The reason for this is that each machine must perform certain kinds of work and compete in certain types of markets.

Although each machine system is unique, the systems on these three machines are representative of those typically found on Caterpillar machines.

The hydraulic system on the 910E is representative of those found on Caterpillar's smaller, utility-sized machines that have fairly simple hydraulic requirements.

There are five primary circuits in the system: steering, brakes, bucket lift, bucket tilt and an auxiliary attachment circuit.

A two-section, fixed-displacement gear pump provides flow for the entire system. The front section powers the implements, and the rear section supplies flow for steering and brake circuits.

The system has a pressurized tank, fluid filter and an oil cooler is optional.

The implement control valves are open-centered and manually operated. The lift and tilt valve spools are equipped with electro-magnetic detents in the raise and rack-back positions. 

These detents work with electronic sensing devices on the lift arms and cylinders to provide automatic bucket positioning and lift-kickout. This feature eliminates the need to visually check bucket position and frees the operator's hands for maneuvering the machine. 

The 910E uses threaded gland lift and tilt cylinders...and all connections are fitted with O-Ring face seals.

This type of hydraulic system provides good, reliable service on machines that must compete in highly competitive, price-sensitive industries such as building construction.

Some small, utility-type machines, such as Backhoe Loaders, require fairly complex, sophisticated hydraulic systems. 
 
This 426, for example, has a variable-displacement, load-sensing, pressure-compensated system that provides optimum performance for both the backhoe and loader functions.

The hydraulic tank on the 426 is pressurized to prevent system contamination. The hydraulic filter assembly is located inside the tank. It consists of two filter elements: one for pump case drain oil and the other for return oil from the implement valve groups.

All system flow requirements are met by a variable-displacement axial piston pump. A pump control valve senses the highest pressure requirement from the loader, backhoe and steering circuits and adjusts the pump to provide adequate flow.

Implement control on the 426 is provided by closed-centered, manually-operated selector valves. The backhoe and loader valves are pressure-compensated to reduce lever effort and improve controllability.

The backhoe control valve stack has six standard valves for stick, bucket, swing, boom and stabilizer control. Two optional valves can be added for extended stick and auxiliary control. 

The loader control valve stack has four standard valves: bucket lift and tilt, and auxiliary circuit for optional attachments, and steering. The tilt control valve spool is fitted with an electro-magnetic detent and is mechanically connected to the tilt cylinder linkage. 

This system provides for automatic bucket leveling and the return-to-dig feature that improves loader productivity.

Caterpillar XT-3 hose, threaded gland cylinders and O-ring face seals on all connections ensure a durable, dry hydraulic system. The swing cylinders are equipped with snubbers that cushion and slow the backhoe before it contacts the frame stops.

Caterpillar Backhoe Loaders are versatile utility machines that excel at many digging and lifting jobs. The hydraulic system on these machines are designed for maximum efficiency. They can deliver full implement forces at any engine speed and feature low lever efforts, low heat generation and low fuel consumption.

The E-series excavators, typical of Caterpillar's large, high production machines, are equipped with sophisticated, computer-controlled hydraulic systems. These systems provide fast, aggressive production cycles, responsive implement control and efficient operation.

This particular model features variable-displacement, pressure-compensated, load-sensing pumps. Main implement control valves are open center and pilot operated.

There are five primary circuits: boom, bucket, stick, swing, travel; and a sixth, auxiliary circuit for attachments. Main system flow requirements are supplied by two tandemly-mounted, variable-displacement axial piston pumps. They are coupled directly to the engine flywheel.

The pilot system is supplied by a single stage gear pump, which is driven by the rear piston pump. An accumulator in the pilot circuit provides smooth control of the implement circuits during multiple implement operation. It also allows limited gravity-assisted implement control when the engine is not running.

Travel and swing motors are both fixed-displacement, axial piston-type motors. The travel motor has an integral brake that is automatically set when pressure is no longer applied to the motor. This model is also equipped with a straight travel feature that keeps the excavator moving straight during simultaneous travel, implement and swing operations.

Hydraulic pump output is computer-controlled and equipped with a Power Mode Selector. The Electronic Power Unit Control, or EPUC, is a microcomputer that continually monitors hydraulic pressure, engine rpm, Power Mode Selector and governor setting...and adjusts pump output to maintain a desired hydraulic horsepower or engine rpm. 
This improves fuel efficiency and ensures that nearly 100% of engine horsepower is available to the hydraulic system. The EPUC is also equipped with self-diagnosis capability.

The Power and Work Mode Selectors permit the operator to tailor the hydraulic system to match the job requirements. These controls work by adjusting pump output and controlling the priority of various circuits.
Although two of these machines have sophisticated, load sensing systems with pressure compensated pumps -- the one you are looking for also has pressure compensated control valves. Try Again.

Good. The variable-displacement, load sensing, pressure compensated hydraulic system on the 426 provides optimum performance for both the backhoe and loader functions, and is designed for maximum efficiency. It can deliver full implement forces at any engine speed and features low lever efforts, low heat generation and low fuel consumption.

lessons.title: The Eight-Step Troubleshooting Approach
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to identify the "Eight Step Troubleshooting Approach."
pages:
Troubleshooting is an organized, logical method of identifying problems and solving them. This is a critical skill, because your effectiveness and efficiency in repairing Caterpillar hydraulic systems depends upon your ability to quickly and correctly determine the cause of problems.

This topic describes an eight-step approach to troubleshooting that will help you save time, energy and money.

The first step in the troubleshooting process to make sure a problem really does exist. Inexperience with a machine's characteristics and improper operation are sometimes mistaken for problems.

One of the best ways to determine if a problem exists is to ask questions and listen. Operators, mechanics and others familiar with the machine you are troubleshooting are good sources for information.

Find out when the problem started.
Was it a sudden or gradual problem?
Is the problem continual or sporadic?
Does it occur at all speeds, gears, loads, and temperatures?

Find out when the machine was last serviced...by whom...and what was done. If it is available, check the service record of the machine.

Ask more than one person and see if you receive the same information. And remember that a friendly, tactful attitude will usually gain you more and better information.

Once you have determined that a problem really exists, the second troubleshooting step is to state the problem by writing it down in simple terms.

This will help you more clearly understand the exact nature of the problem.

Be sure you do not put a solution in the statement. It is too early to make a diagnosis and guessing at a solution at this stage will only waste time.

The third troubleshooting step is to visually inspect the machine. Check for obvious damage, such as leaks, loose bolts and cracks.

Check all fluid levels.

If possible, watch the machine in actual operation. Try to observe the problem as it happens.

Do not guess at anything that can be visually inspected. Check it out yourself.

Step four is to list all possible causes of the problem. Be sure to include all of them, from the simplest to the most unlikely and difficult.

Use the service manual and system schematics to make sure you have considered all possibilities. And remember to apply the basic principles you have learned in this course. It will help ensure that the real cause of the problem is on your list.

Step five is to run tests and record data. The information you gathered in steps one through four, plus the machine's service manual, will help you determine which tests need to be performed.

Be sure to note the test specifications and procedures in the service manual.

You may need to check cycle times...
pressures...
temperatures...
and other machine characteristics.

Remember to record all appropriate data from the tests.

Now, use all the data you have collected so far to do step six...eliminate and isolate.

Take the list of possible causes you made in step four and based upon the input from the operator and others, your inspection and test results, eliminate everything that could not create the problem.

You have now isolated the most probable cause or causes of the problem.

Step seven is to fix the problem.

If there is more than one possible cause left on your list, start with the simplest and easiest to fix.

Once you have repaired the machine, rerun any appropriate tests. Make sure you have really fixed the problem. If possible, try to observe the machine in operation. Wait for the machine to reach operating temperature and watch it work under normal conditions. If the repair fails, let it happen while you are there.

Even after the machine is repaired, there is one final troubleshooting step: analyze the failure. Why did the problem occur in the first place?

This procedure may be simple...if the source of the problem is straightforward; or it may require more sophisticated failure analysis methods. 

Include this analysis on your service report, along with all pertinent information about the machine.

Doing this final step will provide valuable information to those designing and supporting the machines. And it will also make you a better troubleshooter because your knowledge about Caterpillar hydraulic systems will grow with each analysis.

While asking questions will eventually help you accomplish this step, it is not sufficient. Asking the operator or machine owner questions about the problem should be part of the first step of troubleshooting. Try Again.
2The pump is not generating sufficient flow to move the bucket.
When the operator tries to lift the bucket, something in the control valve prevents flow from getting to the cylinders.
Good. The best statement is: "The machine cannot lift a loaded bucket." It states the problem in simple terms and does not suggest a solution.

lessons.title: A Field Service Call
lessons.objective: Objective: You will be able to apply the "Eight-Step Troubleshooting Approach" to the field service call illustrated in this lesson.
pages:
In this topic you meet Jim Thomas, a field service mechanic with the local Cat dealership. According to his Service Manager, Jim is the best troubleshooter in the field. He is on his way out to a customer's job site. They called earlier today; said they were having trouble with one of their 980s.

You are invited to go along with Jim and help him troubleshoot the machine. So hop aboard, buckle up and good luck.

You and Jim arrive at the job and are met by the customer. He is upset because the 980 they are having problems with was in the shop at the dealership only a month ago. One of the main implement pumps was replaced.

The 980 seems to be acting the same way that it did before the first failure, and the customer is convinced it is the same problem. He insists that you save everybody's time and just replace the pump.

Jim asks the customer when the problem started; he says you will have to talk to the operator.

After talking with the operator, you learn that they first noticed some problems with the loader about a week ago. The implement hydraulic system didn't have enough power. At first it wasn't too bad, but it has been getting a lot worse lately. In fact, the loader can now hardly lift a full load.

The operator also believes the pump is faulty, since the lack of power is continuous. What do you think your next step should be?

1. Inspect the machine
2. Replace the pump and save time
3. Look at the service records
4. Ask the operator to run the machine so that you can see the problem first hand.

If you answered, "3. Look at the Service Records," you are correct. You are still in the first troubleshooting step of making sure a problem really exists. The service records are a good source of information. On many field service calls, you might check service records before you leave the dealership. In this case, the customer has kept his own detailed service records.

Checking the service records you learn that the hydraulic pump was replaced about six weeks ago. It had over six thousand hours on it, which is considered a reasonable pump life. Since the failed pump showed some signs of excessive wear, the tank and some of the valves were disassembled and cleaned to make sure no debris was left in the system.

The new pump has only 230 hours of operation. However, the operator is experienced and the symptoms are obvious, so you are confident that a problem does in fact exist. The next step is to write down the problem as a simple statement. Which of these best states the problem? 

1. The hydraulic system lacks power
2. The machine is not working properly
3. The pump is not producing adequate flow to fully power the implements

TIf you chose statement number one, "The hydraulic system lacks power," you are correct. It states the problem in the simplest terms. 

While it is true the machine is not working properly, statement number two is vague, you should be as specific as possible. However, you can be too specific, as is the case with the third choice. 

Statement number three suggests a solution to the problem by naming the pump as the cause. At this point we are not sure what is causing the problem.

Now that you have written down the problem in its simplest terms, what is your next troubleshooting step?

1. Inspect the machine
2. Fix the problem
3. Run tests and record data

You will need to run tests, collect data and fix the problem eventually. But you should first inspect the machine.

A thorough visual walk-around of the machine reveals no leaks or obvious damage of any kind... and fluid levels are correct.

Jim then asks the operator to start up the machine so you can see for yourself exactly how the hydraulic system performs.

The problem is exactly as you have described it: the hydraulic system lacks power.

So, the next step is to make a list of all possible causes of the problem. After checking the schematics in the service manual he brought along, Jim prepared this list of causes. Think about how each of these items could cause the problem you have observed.

Is the cause an incorrectly adjusted engine RPM? If the engine RPM is set too low, the pump would produce less flow, adversely affecting implement performance.

What about a faulty control valve? A worn or broken control valve could be leaking internally, diverting some of the flow intended for implement circuits.

Or, a faulty or incorrectly adjusted relief valve? A relief valve could be opening at too low a pressure, diverting some of the flow back to the tank.

The problem could stem from a faulty pump. If flow loss is too great, pump output will not be sufficient at higher pressures, adversely affecting implement performance. Several pump conditions could contribute to flow loss.

Now that you and Jim have prepared a list of possible causes, it's time to perform some tests. Based on the information you have collected so far, you decide to check the RPM setpoint...you measure cycle times and drift...
and you measure both system and pilot pressures.

You could also check pump flow, but since that takes a little longer, you decide to postpone that test until after you eliminate some of the possible causes.

With the engine running at high idle under normal conditions for operation, an engine set point indicator group was used to take RPM readings with and without a load on the engine. The difference between the two readings was 7 RPM. Acceptable tolerance is plus or minus 10 RPM.

On this machine excessive implement drift can indicate faulty make-up valves, worn valve stems in the control valve sections or worn piston seals in the cylinders. 

With hydraulic oil temperatures of 100° to 120° F (38° to 40° C), maximum permissible lift cylinder drift is 0.50 inches (13 mm) in 5 minutes. Maximum permissible tilt cylinder drift is 0.75 inches (19 mm) in 5 minutes. Measured drift was within these limits.
Main system pressure was measured at 1985 psi. Correct system pressure is 3000 psi plus or minus 50 psi.
Pilot system pressure was measured at 320 psi. Correct pressure is 335 psi plus or minus 15 psi.

Now that you have finished testing and data collection, it is time to eliminate items from your list of possible causes and isolate the real problem.

Which of these items do you think we can eliminate, based on everything we know so far? 

1. Incorrectly adjusted engine RPM
2. Faulty control valve
3. Faulty or incorrectly adjusted relief valve
4. Faulty pump

If you eliminated incorrectly adjusted engine fuel pump and faulty control valve, you are correct! Engine RPM set point was measured and found to be within tolerance, so this item cannot be the cause of our problem. Since the lift and tilt circuit cycle times and drift were within specifications, it is unlikely that the control valve is a problem.

By eliminating the first two items from your list, you have isolated two possible causes: the main relief valve and the pump.

When you are left with more than one possible cause, start with the easiest and fastest to check or replace. In this case, the relief valve.

When starting to readjust the main relief valve, Jim thought the plunger turned much too freely, so he replaced it...then finished adjusting system pressure.

The hydraulic system responded immediately; the problem had apparently been fixed.

The operator took the machine out and was satisfied with its performance.

The repairs were apparently successful, but is the troubleshooting task completed?
